Loss-of-function mutations in these genes impair zinc-regulated signaling in keratinocytes and lymphocytes, compromising T-cell function and predisposing to EV lesions.

972039.long_answer: Large international cohort and meta-analysis data indicate that carriers of pathogenic CDKN2A variants have a cumulative melanoma penetrance of roughly seven in ten—about 70 %—by 80 years of age.

338909.long_answer: Among the PAX (paired-box) transcription-factor family, eye malformations that lead to vision loss are classically linked to PAX6 (e.g., aniridia, foveal hypoplasia) and to PAX2 (renal-coloboma syndrome). PAX7, in contrast, is best known for its role in skeletal-muscle and neural-crest development and for somatic PAX7-FOXO1 fusions in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma. Germ-line variants or inherited defects in PAX7 have not been implicated in congenital or progressive ocular disorders that impair vision. Consequently, the scientific and clinical literature does not support an association between PAX7 and eye conditions that produce mild to severe visual impairment.

845932.long_answer: The ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) gene that encodes the ALK receptor tyrosine-kinase is located on the short arm of human chromosome 2 at band 2p23. Rearrangements of this locus—most commonly the t(2;5)(p23;q35) translocation—drive expression of ALK fusion proteins, giving rise to ALK-positive anaplastic large-cell lymphoma.

600724.long_answer: Microcephaly-lymphedema-chorioretinal dysplasia (MLCRD), now usually referred to as “microcephaly with or without chorioretinopathy, lymphedema, or intellectual disability” (MCLMR; OMIM #152950), has been molecularly linked to heterozygous pathogenic variants in the KIF11 gene. All convincingly documented and genetically confirmed cases show autosomal-dominant segregation, often arising from de-novo mutations but capable of vertical transmission with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance. No reproducible evidence exists for autosomal-recessive, X-linked, or any other mode of inheritance. Therefore, according to current scientific consensus, this condition follows a single inheritance pattern—autosomal dominant.

265353.long_answer: Cleidocranial dysplasia—a skeletal disorder characterized by hypoplastic or absent clavicles and delayed closure of cranial sutures—is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the RUNX2 (CBFA1) gene, a transcription factor essential for osteoblast differentiation and bone formation. Disruption of RUNX2 impairs intramembranous ossification, producing the distinctive clavicle and skull abnormalities seen in the condition.

573802.long_answer: Heimler syndrome is a very mild peroxisome-biogenesis disorder most often caused by pathogenic variants in the PEX1 gene. The human PEX1 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 7 (region 7q21–q22). Mutations in this chromosome-7 gene disrupt peroxisomal biogenesis, leading to the characteristic features of Heimler syndrome such as sensorineural hearing loss and amelogenesis imperfecta.

707102.long_answer: Mutations in the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor gene (GNRHR) are a well-established cause of normosmic congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. The GNRHR gene is located on human chromosome 4 (band 4q13.2); therefore, chromosome 4 is the chromosome that houses the gene whose mutation leads to this condition.

726978.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which is located on the long arm (q arm) of human chromosome 7 at position 7q31.2.

100553.long_answer: Usher syndrome type 1F and a form of nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive deafness (DFNB23) are both caused by mutations in the PCDH15 gene (protocadherin-15). The PCDH15 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 10 (cytogenetic band 10q21.1), making chromosome 10 the chromosome that contains the gene responsible for these conditions.

329222.long_answer: Neuhauser syndrome, also called the hydrocephalus–endocardial fibroelastosis–cataract (HEC) syndrome, is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder whose diagnostic triad is congenital hydrocephalus, diffuse endocardial fibroelastosis of the heart, and bilateral congenital cataracts—an ocular lesion that can lead to blindness. This distinctive combination of CNS, cardiac and ocular findings defines the syndrome.

960032.long_answer: Prolonged heavy alcohol consumption often leads to malnutrition and impaired intestinal absorption of thiamine (vitamin B1). Thiamine deficiency produces Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a neurological disorder of the central nervous system characterized by confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and memory disturbances. Thus, lack of thiamine is the vitamin deficiency classically linked to alcohol-related CNS disease.

517955.long_answer: Modern QuikClot Combat Gauze is impregnated with kaolin, an aluminosilicate clay. When blood soaks the dressing, kaolin directly activates coagulation Factor XII (Hageman factor), triggering the intrinsic clotting cascade and accelerating formation of a stable fibrin clot—an effect exploited to control bleeding from injuries such as stab wounds.

141115.long_answer: Hypomelanosis of Ito—also called incontinentia pigmenti achromians—was first reported in 1952 by the Japanese dermatologist Minoru Ito, who described a series of patients with streaked, whorled hypopigmentation following the lines of Blaschko. His detailed clinical and histopathologic observations led to the eponym "Ito’s disease."

355051.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the Heat-Shock-Transcription-Factor-4 (HSF4) gene produce an autosomal-dominant ocular syndrome characterised by bilateral congenital cataracts together with iris coloboma. HSF4 is a lens-specific transcription factor; missense mutations such as p.Arg116His impair its regulatory activity during eye development, leading to defective lens fiber differentiation (resulting in cataracts) and incomplete optic fissure closure (producing iris coloboma).

401286.long_answer: Galactokinase deficiency is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the GALK1 gene (galactokinase 1). Cytogenetic and molecular mapping have localized GALK1 to band 17q24 on human chromosome 17, so the pathogenic gene resides on chromosome 17.

670112.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the PITX2 homeobox transcription factor cause Axenfeld-Rieger (Rieger) syndrome. This autosomal-dominant disorder is characterised by anterior-segment dysgenesis with iris and ocular hypoplasia/microphthalmia, in addition to dental and umbilical anomalies. Thus, PITX2 mutation is the genetic change classically associated with a condition that includes hypoplasia of the eyes.

658933.long_answer: Congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1N (CDG-1N) is caused by pathogenic variants in the DPM3 gene (dolichyl-phosphate mannosyltransferase subunit 3). The DPM3 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 1q22 on human chromosome 1; therefore, chromosome 1 contains the gene responsible for CDG type 1N.

989121.long_answer: Blomstrand chondrodysplasia results from loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding the type-1 parathyroid hormone/parathyroid hormone-related peptide receptor (PTH1R). Because the mutation blocks the action of parathyroid hormone, the endocrine system functionally affected is that of the parathyroid gland, whose hormone can no longer act on its target tissues.

446810.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the TTC8 gene—also known as BBS8—located on chromosome 14q24.3 cause Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 8. This ciliopathy is classically marked by progressive retinal dystrophy leading to visual impairment and by limb anomalies such as post-axial polydactyly, along with other systemic features.

156605.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the COMP (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein) gene give rise to disorders such as pseudoachondroplasia and multiple epiphyseal dysplasia type 1. These conditions are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, meaning one mutated COMP allele inherited from an affected parent is sufficient to cause disease.

989261.long_answer: The hereditary startle disease hyperekplexia, which causes marked muscle stiffness and exaggerated muscular jerks, is most often produced by mutations in the α-1 subunit of the glycine receptor gene GLRA1 located on chromosome 5q32-q34. Clonazepam, a benzodiazepine that enhances inhibitory GABAergic tone, is the standard treatment used to reduce the hypertonia and startle–induced muscle spasms in this disorder, linking the disease—and thus chromosome 5—with therapy using clonazepam.

392843.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1, cause Marfan syndrome—a systemic connective-tissue disorder. The deficient or dysfunctional fibrillin-1 weakens elastic microfibrils, producing skeletal manifestations that characteristically include scoliosis, joint hypermobility, long limbs, and other musculoskeletal deformities.

314508.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the POMGNT1 gene, which encodes protein O-mannose β-1,2-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 1, cause the subtype POMGNT1-CDG (formerly CDG type IId) of the congenital disorders of glycosylation. The same defect in O-mannosyl glycosylation of α-dystroglycan leads to the clinical picture of muscle–eye–brain disease.

414106.long_answer: Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus is transmitted to humans primarily by Dermacentor ticks. Public-health guidelines, including those from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, advise applying insect repellent containing DEET (N,N-diethyl-meta-toluamide) to exposed skin and clothing because DEET effectively repels ticks and thereby helps prevent the tick bites that can spread Omsk hemorrhagic fever.

983522.long_answer: Infantile systemic hyalinosis results from biallelic mutations in the ANTXR2 (CMG2) gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 4 (4q21).

757488.long_answer: The gene F8, recorded in the OMIM database (OMIM #300841), encodes coagulation factor VIII, a key protein of the intrinsic coagulation cascade. Cytogenetic mapping places F8 at Xq28, indicating that the human X chromosome harbors this coagulation-related gene.

940223.long_answer: Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome is an inherited prion disease caused by pathogenic mutations in the PRNP gene (prion protein gene). The human PRNP gene is located on chromosome 20 (20p13), so chromosome 20 is the chromosome associated with this dementia-causing syndrome.

717940.long_answer: Fukutin physically associates with the fukutin-related protein (FKRP) in the O-mannosyl glycosylation pathway that is disrupted in Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy. The FKRP gene that encodes this interacting protein is mapped to human chromosome 19 (19q13.3).

496672.long_answer: Muscle–eye–brain disease (MEB) belongs to the group of α-dystroglycanopathies, a subset of congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) that disturb O-mannose glycosylation of α-dystroglycan. Genes that have been definitively implicated in MEB or closely related conditions (e.g., Walker-Warburg syndrome, limb-girdle muscular dystrophy 2M) include POMGNT1, POMGNT2 (GTDC2), POMT1, POMT2, POMK, FKRP, FKTN, LARGE1, LARGE2, ISPD/CRPPA and several others. Extensive clinical-genetic studies, databases such as OMIM, ClinGen and GeneReviews, and the current CDG classification lists do not report any human disorder attributable to mutations in a gene called “POMGNT7.” In fact, no human gene with the official symbol POMGNT7 is recognized; the only characterized human POMGNT genes are POMGNT1 and POMGNT2. Consequently, there is no evidence—either in the medical literature or in curated genetic databases—that variants in a nonexistent or uncharacterized “POMGNT7” gene cause any congenital disorder of glycosylation, let alone the muscle–eye–brain disease phenotype. Therefore, the statement that mutations in POMGNT7 cause a CDG subtype leading to MEB is not supported by established scientific consensus and is considered incorrect.

887567.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 (IDH1) gene found in acute myeloid leukemia produce an aberrant enzyme that converts α-ketoglutarate to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate. The accumulated 2-hydroxyglutarate competitively inhibits α-ketoglutarate–dependent epigenetic enzymes such as TET DNA demethylases and histone demethylases, thereby altering DNA and histone methylation profiles and contributing to leukemogenesis.

377451.long_answer: Adult-onset citrullinemia, also called citrullinemia type II, is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC25A13 gene. SLC25A13 encodes the mitochondrial aspartate–glutamate carrier protein “citrin”; its deficiency disrupts the urea cycle and energy metabolism, leading to episodic hyperammonemia that primarily manifests with central nervous system symptoms in adults.

223815.long_answer: Horseshoe kidney is classically seen in Turner syndrome (45,X). The most characteristic congenital heart defect in Turner syndrome is coarctation of the aorta, making this cardiac lesion closely associated with the same genetic condition that produces horseshoe kidney.

944539.long_answer: The dipeptide β-alanine–histidine (carnosine) is hydrolysed by the enzyme carnosinase (carnosine dipeptidase 1). In humans, inherited carnosinase deficiency (carnosinemia) results from mutations in the CNDP1 gene. CNDP1 is mapped to cytogenetic band 18q22.3, i.e., it resides on human chromosome 18; therefore chromosome 18 contains the gene whose alteration causes this enzyme deficiency.

535997.long_answer: The cystic fibrosis gene, CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator), is located on the long arm of chromosome 7 at position 7q31.2. Mutations in this gene disrupt chloride ion transport in epithelial cells, leading to the characteristic pulmonary and pancreatic manifestations of cystic fibrosis.

698939.long_answer: Congenital contractural arachnodactyly (Beals-Hecht syndrome) is caused by pathogenic variants in the FBN2 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-2. The FBN2 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 5 (cytogenetic band 5q23–q31). Therefore, chromosome 5 carries the gene responsible for this disorder.

412619.long_answer: Mutations in the LIPA gene abolish or markedly reduce lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) activity—the enzyme responsible for hydrolyzing cholesteryl esters and triglycerides delivered to lysosomes within low-density lipoprotein particles. Loss of LAL function causes accumulation of these lipids, manifesting clinically as Wolman disease or cholesteryl ester storage disease.

342043.long_answer: The neural cell adhesion molecule-1 (NCAM1) gene, which has been implicated in certain congenital cases of esophageal atresia and functions in neural cell adhesion and guidance, maps to the long arm of human chromosome 11 (11q23).

783707.long_answer: Activating (gain-of-function) mutations in the FGFR3 gene, most commonly the G380R missense change, cause achondroplasia and related FGFR3-linked skeletal dysplasias. Constitutive FGFR3 signalling suppresses growth-plate chondrocyte proliferation and maturation, producing severely shortened long bones, limb deformities and disproportionate short stature—clinical features of severe dwarfism.

866526.long_answer: The zinc transporter gene SLC39A8 (also known as ZIP8) modulates cellular and serum zinc levels and has been linked to several inflammatory conditions; this gene is located on human chromosome 4 (region 4q24). Thus, chromosome 4 harbors the gene that influences zinc homeostasis and inflammation.

403312.long_answer: Congenital contractural arachnodactyly (Beals syndrome) is caused by pathogenic variants in the fibrillin-2 gene (FBN2). The FBN2 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 5, band q23-q31. Consequently, chromosome 5 is the chromosomal location that harbors the gene responsible for this disorder.

279112.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the Nav1.7 voltage-gated sodium channel required for nociceptive neuron firing, cause congenital insensitivity to pain. Because these patients do not perceive painful pressure or tissue ischemia, they often remain in one position too long and develop recurrent pressure (decubitus) ulcers as well as other painless injuries.

218881.long_answer: Caroli syndrome is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PKHD1 gene (polycystic kidney and hepatic disease 1). The PKHD1 locus is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 6 (6p12), making chromosome 6 the chromosomal location linked to this syndrome.

975336.long_answer: Glycogen-synthase-kinase-3 beta (GSK3B) is a repeatedly implicated susceptibility gene in bipolar disorder. The GSK3β kinase binds to and phosphorylates STAT1, the signal-transducer that is directly activated by pegylated interferon-α—one of the classic, widely used treatments for chronic hepatitis C. Because GSK3B physically interacts with STAT1, the protein that interferon-α targets, it satisfies the relationship described in the question.

689756.long_answer: Human papillomavirus (HPV) carries a circular double-stranded DNA genome. In the host cell nucleus it is copied by the cellular DNA polymerase through a theta-type, bidirectional mechanism: replication initiates at a single origin and proceeds simultaneously in two opposite directions around the circle. This bidirectional replication model is a well-established feature of Papillomaviridae.

313631.long_answer: A classic lysosomal storage disease, Tay-Sachs, is caused by absence of the lysosomal enzyme β-hexosaminidase A. The gene that encodes the enzyme’s α-subunit (HEXA) is located on human chromosome 15 (15q23 – q24). Mutations on chromosome 15 therefore give rise to the enzyme deficiency responsible for this prototypical lysosomal storage disorder.

552849.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ATR gene cause Seckel syndrome. This autosomal-recessive disorder is classically characterized by severe intrauterine growth retardation, marked microcephaly, and distinctive craniofacial dysmorphisms ("bird-headed" appearance). ATR encodes a key DNA-damage-response kinase; its deficiency disrupts cell-cycle checkpoints during development, leading to the microcephaly and craniofacial abnormalities seen in the syndrome.

788907.long_answer: Triple-A (Allgrove) syndrome is caused by mutations in the AAAS gene, which encodes the ALADIN nucleoporin. The AAAS gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 12q13 on human chromosome 12; hence, chromosome 12 carries the gene responsible for Triple-A syndrome.

548165.long_answer: Hailey-Hailey disease (familial benign chronic pemphigus) presents with recurrent blisters and erythematous rashes. It is produced by mutations in the ATP2C1 gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 3 (3q21-q24). Thus, the gene responsible for this blistering skin disorder resides on chromosome 3.

992351.long_answer: Friedreich ataxia is caused by a GAA-trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene that encodes the mitochondrial protein frataxin. Loss of frataxin disrupts mitochondrial iron handling, leading to oxidative damage in neurons and cardiac muscle. The resulting hypertrophic cardiomyopathy frequently progresses to heart failure, making the FXN mutation a well-established genetic cause of cardiomyopathy and cardiac death.

896969.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked DMD gene, which encodes dystrophin, cause Duchenne (and Becker) muscular dystrophy. This disorder classically produces progressive weakness of the proximal limb-girdle muscles—those of the pelvic and shoulder regions—owing to degeneration of muscle fibers lacking functional dystrophin.

707732.long_answer: Hypochondrogenesis results from dominant mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes the α1 chain of type II collagen essential for cartilage development. COL2A1 is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 12 (12q13.11-q13.2), so chromosome 12 is the chromosome that carries the gene responsible for this disorder.

133544.long_answer: Mutations in the SBDS gene cause Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, a hereditary disorder characterized by exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, skeletal anomalies and bone-marrow failure that often manifests as neutropenia and progressive pancytopenia.

473545.long_answer:
Extensive clinical and epidemiological research shows that exposure to severe or repeated traumatic events in childhood—such as physical, sexual, or emotional abuse, domestic violence, or other overwhelming stressors—is a well-established risk factor for developing both post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and dissociative disorders, including dissociative fugue.  

• PTSD: Childhood trauma is one of the most robust predictors of later PTSD. DSM-5 and large cohort studies consistently list early-life abuse or neglect as a precipitating factor, and prevalence of PTSD is markedly higher in individuals traumatized during childhood than those first traumatized in adulthood.  

• Dissociative fugue: Although rare, dissociative fugue (now coded as a specifier of dissociative amnesia in DSM-5) has repeatedly been linked to severe stress or trauma, especially when that trauma occurred early in life. Case series, clinical reviews, and dissociation research (e.g., Spiegel et al., 2011; International Society for the Study of Trauma and Dissociation guidelines) note that many patients with fugue states report histories of childhood abuse or neglect, and high scores on childhood trauma inventories.  

Because childhood trauma is a documented etiological or risk factor for both conditions, the statement that it is associated with both dissociative fugue and PTSD is supported by the scientific consensus.

112922.long_answer: The main susceptibility genes that have been implicated in isolated or syndromic forms of esophageal atresia (for example SOX2 on chromosome 3q, CHD7 on 8q, MYCN on 2p, and others) are not located on chromosome 5. Likewise, the well-known neural cell-adhesion genes (L1CAM on Xq28, NCAM1 on 11q23, NRCAM on 7q31, CHL1 on 3p26, etc.) are situated on chromosomes other than chromosome 5. No gene on chromosome 5 is recognized by the scientific community as both (i) a neural cell-adhesion molecule and (ii) a gene whose mutation or dosage change is causally linked to esophageal atresia. Therefore, the claim that chromosome 5 harbors a neural cell-adhesion gene associated with esophageal atresia contradicts established genomic and clinical evidence.

443034.long_answer: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) is classically caused by pathogenic variants in any one of several genes that regulate pancreatic β-cell function (e.g., HNF1A, HNF4A, GCK, HNF1B, PDX1, KLF11, among others). In virtually all well-characterized forms of MODY, these mutations are transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion: a single pathogenic allele is sufficient to cause the phenotype, and the condition typically appears in multiple successive generations. Autosomal recessive inheritance, which would require two pathogenic alleles and often skips generations, is not the accepted mode of inheritance for MODY. Therefore, the statement that MODY-causing gene mutations are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner is incorrect.

428932.long_answer: Acute intermittent porphyria results from pathogenic variants in the HMBS (porphobilinogen deaminase) gene. These mutations are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner with incomplete penetrance, meaning a single mutated allele is sufficient to confer disease risk, though not all carriers develop symptoms.

384427.long_answer: Bowen–Conradi syndrome is caused by a recessive missense mutation (Thr36Met) in the EMG1 (essential for mitotic growth 1) gene. The human EMG1 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 12p13.32 on chromosome 12, so the disease-causing gene resides on human chromosome 12.

803096.long_answer: Shwachman–Diamond syndrome is caused by mutations in the SBDS gene, which is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 7 at band q11. Consequently, the gene responsible for the disorder resides on chromosome 7.

748347.long_answer: Missense mutations in the SPTLC1 gene, which encodes a subunit of serine-palmitoyltransferase, cause Hereditary Sensory Neuropathy type I (HSN-I). This dominantly inherited disorder selectively damages peripheral sensory nerves, producing a progressive loss of pain and temperature sensation in the distal limbs and leading to chronic ulcers and neuropathic complications.

300888.long_answer: Mohr–Tranebjærg syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TIMM8A (DDP1) gene, which is located at the Xq22 locus on the X chromosome; hence, the disorder follows an X-linked inheritance pattern.

207599.long_answer: Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, a hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, was first described in 1886 by the French neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot, who published the initial clinical account with his student Pierre Marie; an independent description by the English neurologist Howard Henry Tooth followed later the same year, which is why the disorder bears all three names today.

900957.long_answer: Erythropoietic protoporphyria is most commonly produced by loss-of-function mutations in the FECH gene, which encodes ferrochelatase, the terminal enzyme of heme biosynthesis. The human FECH gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 18 (18q21), so pathogenic variants on chromosome 18 lead to the clinical disorder.

521665.long_answer: The most frequently mutated gene in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia is TET2; this gene is located at cytogenetic band 4q24 on human chromosome 4. Hence, chromosome 4 harbors the gene whose mutation is common in CMML.

659920.long_answer: The scalp disorder cutis verticis gyrata was first described in 1837 by the French dermatologist Jean-Louis-Marc Alibert, who reported the characteristic thickened, convoluted folds of the scalp; the descriptive term “cutis verticis gyrata” itself was coined later by Unna in 1907.

830484.long_answer: Mutations in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4, produce autosomal dominant muscle channelopathies (e.g., paramyotonia congenita, hyperkalemic periodic paralysis). These disorders arise because SCN4A gain-of-function mutations alter sodium channel gating in muscle fibers, leading to impaired membrane excitability and episodic weakness or myotonia.

601626.long_answer: Mutations in the IHH (Indian hedgehog) gene cause brachydactyly type A1, a congenital limb malformation characterized by marked shortening of the middle phalanges, resulting in shortened interphalangeal joints of the fingers and toes.

168713.long_answer: The French barber-surgeon Ambroise Paré (1510–1590) gave the earliest recorded medical description of children born with fused fingers and toes in his 1573 treatise on congenital "monsters," thereby identifying syndactyly as a birth anomaly.

188716.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the KCNQ1 gene (encoding the cardiac/inner-ear IKs potassium-channel α-subunit) cause Jervell-Lange-Nielsen syndrome. This disorder follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern and is clinically characterized by congenital, often severe sensorineural hearing loss together with a prolonged QT interval and risk of arrhythmias.

526691.long_answer: The clinical picture matches epidermolytic ichthyosis (epidermolytic hyperkeratosis), an autosomal-dominant cornification disorder produced by heterozygous mutations in the suprabasal keratin genes KRT1 (keratin 1) and KRT10 (keratin 10). These mutations destabilize the keratin intermediate-filament network, leading to neonatal skin fragility and, later, the characteristic generalized, persistent brown hyperkeratosis with sharply demarcated plaques.

865982.long_answer: Toxicity to the chemotherapeutic drug irinotecan is strongly linked to polymorphisms in the UGT1A1 gene (notably the *28 allele). UGT1A1 encodes the enzyme that glucuronidates the active metabolite SN-38; reduced activity leads to high SN-38 levels and a markedly higher risk of severe diarrhea and neutropenia. The UGT1A1 gene is located on human chromosome 2 (band 2q37), so chromosome 2 carries the risk-modifying gene.

790271.long_answer: Genu valgum is a common limb deformity in hereditary multiple osteochondromas (hereditary multiple exostoses), an autosomal-dominant skeletal disorder. This condition is classically produced by loss-of-function mutations in the EXT1 gene (exostosin-1) on chromosome 8, which encodes a glycosyltransferase required for heparan-sulfate biosynthesis in the growth plate. Disruption of EXT1 causes abnormal osteocartilaginous outgrowths around the physes, leading to angular deformities such as genu valgum.

267642.long_answer: Alien hand syndrome has been described in patients with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a demyelinating brain disease produced by the JC virus (John Cunningham polyomavirus). The virus infects and destroys oligodendrocytes, creating callosal and parietal lesions that can disconnect motor control from conscious volition, thereby producing the involuntary limb movements characteristic of alien hand syndrome.

285923.long_answer: The most common form of autosomal-dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG4) is caused by mutations in the SPAST gene, which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 2 (region 2p22-p21).

148681.long_answer: Hereditary hyperekplexia (startle disease) is caused most commonly by mutations in the GLRA1 gene situated on human chromosome 5 (5q34). The characteristic exaggerated startle and stiffness are effectively controlled with the benzodiazepine clonazepam, making chromosome 5 the chromosome linked to a clonazepam-responsive disease.

517827.long_answer: Mutations in the LAMA3 gene (encoding the α3-chain of laminin-332) cause laryngo-onycho-cutaneous (LOC) syndrome—a very rare epithelial disorder whose hallmark triad is laryngeal granulation tissue, nail dystrophy (onychodysplasia), and chronic skin erosions or granulation over the face and extremities. Loss of functional laminin-332 disrupts epithelial basement-membrane adhesion, accounting for the combined abnormalities in the larynx, nails, and skin.

449455.long_answer: 5α-Reductase type 2 deficiency is caused by mutations in the SRD5A2 gene, which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 2 (band 2p23). Alterations in this chromosomal locus impair conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, producing the characteristic clinical phenotype.

115420.long_answer: The APRT gene, whose loss-of-function mutations cause adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) deficiency and consequent 2,8-dihydroxyadenine kidney stones and nephropathy, is located on the long arm of human chromosome 16 (region 16q24.3).

106674.long_answer: Mutations in the SPAST gene are the most common cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG4), a rare neurological disorder marked by progressive spasticity and stiffness of the lower limbs. SPAST encodes the microtubule-severing protein spastin; loss-of-function variants disrupt axonal transport in corticospinal neurons, leading to the characteristic lower-limb stiffness of the disease.

987629.long_answer: Malignant hyperthermia arises when mutations (e.g., in the RYR1 channel) trigger uncontrolled release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the specialized endoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle fibers that stores and liberates calcium for contraction.

478521.long_answer: The syndrome classically producing syndactyly-type hand and foot deformities together with a flat facial profile is Apert (acrocephalosyndactyly) syndrome, produced by gain-of-function mutations in the FGFR2 gene. This disorder is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner (although most cases arise de novo), so the characteristic inheritance pattern linked to these hand- and foot-plus-flat-facies anomalies is autosomal dominant.

729968.long_answer: The t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation characteristic of the Philadelphia chromosome fuses the ABL1 proto-oncogene from chromosome 9 with the BCR gene on chromosome 22. ABL1 is the key oncogenic partner that drives leukemogenesis in BCR-ABL1-positive acute myeloid leukemia. Hence, the AML-associated gene involved in the t(9;22) translocation is located on human chromosome 9.

530687.long_answer: The MKKS gene (also called BBS6) maps to cytogenetic band 20p12.2 on human chromosome 20. Mutations in this locus produce the chaperonin-like protein defects responsible for McKusick–Kaufman syndrome and the associated limb malformations such as polydactyly.

677497.long_answer:
Separation of the digits during human limb development is produced by programmed cell death (apoptosis) in the interdigital tissue. The key signals that trigger this apoptosis are Bone-Morphogenetic Proteins, especially BMP-2, BMP-4 and BMP-7.  
• BMP2 is encoded by the BMP2 gene on chromosome 20p12.3.  
• BMP4 is encoded by the BMP4 gene on chromosome 14q22-q23.  
• BMP7 is encoded by the BMP7 gene on chromosome 20q13.3.  
Loss-of-function mutations or experimental inhibition of these BMPs leads to syndactyly in animal models, confirming that they are the major pro-apoptotic signals required for digit separation.  

Although chromosome 6p (the short arm of chromosome 6) does contain the BMP6 gene and many immune-system genes, BMP6 is not the critical factor for the interdigital apoptosis that prevents syndactyly, and the principal BMP genes involved are not located on 6p.  

Therefore the statement that “the gene of the protein that is responsible for the apoptosis that prevents syndactyly is located on the short arm of chromosome 6” is not consistent with established embryological and genetic evidence.

507990.long_answer: Diamond–Blackfan anemia is a congenital (inherited) red-cell aplasia characterized by macrocytic anemia presenting in infancy. The disorder is often accompanied by congenital limb abnormalities (e.g., thumb or radial defects) and carries an increased lifetime risk of developing bone cancers such as osteogenic sarcoma, making it the anemia classically linked to the described syndrome.

337475.long_answer: PMM2 deficiency (CDG-Ia) is caused by pathogenic variants in the PMM2 gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 16p13.2 on human chromosome 16.

882372.long_answer: Nezelof syndrome is a congenital thymic dysplasia that impairs development of thymus-dependent lymphocytes. The resulting selective deficiency of mature T cells compromises cell-mediated immunity; without adequate T-cell help, B cells are present but produce poorly functional immunoglobulins, predisposing patients to recurrent severe infections.

830989.long_answer: The most common form of ectodermal dysplasia is X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (HED), caused by mutations in the EDA (ectodysplasin-A) gene. EDA is located on the human X chromosome (region Xq12-q13.1). Therefore, the gene underlying the most prevalent type of ectodermal dysplasia resides on the X chromosome.

919350.long_answer: The vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) gene encodes VEGF-A, the classic “vascular permeability factor” that enhances leakage across epithelial and especially endothelial barriers, leading to tissue edema. In humans, the VEGFA gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 (6p12), so chromosome 6 contains the gene responsible for this permeability-regulating protein.

590448.long_answer: The characteristic abnormal cranial growth patterns seen in McGillivray syndrome reflect the principles of craniosynostosis that were first described by the German pathologist Rudolf Virchow in 1851; he showed that premature fusion of a calvarial suture restricts growth perpendicular to the suture and causes compensatory growth in parallel directions.

737658.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the PAX6 gene cause congenital aniridia and the related WAGR spectrum syndrome. Because PAX6 is a master regulator of eye development, such mutations lead to iris hypoplasia, foveal/aplasia and optic-nerve malformations, resulting in severe visual impairment or blindness as a prominent clinical feature of the syndrome.

195246.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the THAP1 gene (primary dystonia type 6, DYT6) produce an autosomal-dominant form of early-onset dystonia that frequently involves the cranial muscles. Patients commonly develop cranio-cervical manifestations such as blepharospasm, along with oromandibular and laryngeal dystonia, making THAP1 mutation the established genetic association with blepharospasm in this disorder.

888242.long_answer: The disorder described is a syndromic form of aniridia in which loss-of-function mutations or 11p13 deletions involving the PAX6 gene abolish iris development and, through effects on brain and kidney morphogenesis, produce cerebellar ataxia, psychomotor retardation, and renal abnormalities. Hence, PAX6 is the gene whose alteration underlies this constellation of findings.

916634.long_answer: Paroxysmal nonkinesigenic dyskinesia is caused by mutations in the PNKD (formerly MR-1) gene. Molecular mapping places PNKD on the long arm of human chromosome 2 (region 2q31-q36). Therefore, the gene responsible for this disorder resides on chromosome 2.

694088.long_answer: Spanish clinicians showed that the very severe hyperostotic bone disorder they observed (later named sclerosteosis) was distinct from van Buchem disease. Molecular studies demonstrated that this disorder is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the SOST gene, which encodes the Wnt-signalling inhibitor sclerostin. Thus, mutation of SOST – not the regulatory deletion that underlies van Buchem disease – causes the disease the Spanish doctors distinguished.

497315.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in TTC37 are the classical cause of tricho-hepato-enteric (THES) syndrome.  Independent reports have shown that other recessive TTC37 mutations can present primarily with brittle, sulfur-deficient hair and the diagnostic features of non-photosensitive trichothiodystrophy, linking the same gene to this form of trichothiodystrophy as well.

914972.short_answer: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
914972.long_answer: The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), a component of the U.S. NIH, funds and coordinates research initiatives aimed at understanding the causes, mechanisms, and potential therapies for myopathies, which are classified among neuromuscular diseases.

855898.long_answer: Cardiomyopathic neutral lipid storage disease (neutral lipid storage disease with myopathy) is produced by pathogenic variants in the PNPLA2 gene, which encodes adipose-triglyceride lipase (ATGL). The PNPLA2 gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 11 (11p15.5), so chromosome 11 carries the causal gene for this disorder.

897355.long_answer: Classic (type-I) lissencephaly is most commonly caused by mutations or deletions in the LIS1 gene, officially named PAFAH1B1, which is located on chromosome 17p13.3. LIS1 encodes a regulator of the dynein motor complex that is essential for proper neuronal migration during cortical development; haploinsufficiency disrupts this process, producing the smooth-brain phenotype characteristic of lissencephaly and Miller–Dieker syndrome.

860801.long_answer: Sandhoff disease results from mutations in the HEXB gene, which encodes the β-subunit common to both β-hexosaminidase A and B. HEXB is located on human chromosome 5 (5q13.3); hence, chromosome 5 carries the gene whose defect causes the combined deficiency of β-hexosaminidases A and B.

822586.long_answer: Morquio A syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA) is caused by loss-of-function variants in the GALNS gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase. The GALNS gene is located on chromosome 16 (cytogenetic band 16q24.3), not on chromosome 4. Therefore the statement that the causative gene malfunction occurs on chromosome 4 is incorrect.

725290.long_answer: Foix–Chavany–Marie (opercular) syndrome causes bilateral loss of voluntary control over the bulbar musculature, including the muscles of facial expression that are supplied by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). Expressive (Broca’s) aphasia most often results from an inferior frontal-gyrus (Broca’s area) lesion that also involves the adjacent primary motor cortex for the lower face; consequently the corticobulbar fibres to cranial nerve VII are disrupted, producing weakness of the facial muscles used in speech. Thus impairment of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) is a feature common to both conditions.

435752.long_answer: The most common X-linked recessive form of ectodermal dysplasia is hypohidrotic/anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, which is caused by pathogenic mutations in the EDA gene (ectodysplasin A) located on the X chromosome. EDA encodes a signaling protein essential for the development of ectoderm-derived structures such as hair, teeth, and sweat glands; loss-of-function variants disrupt this pathway, producing the classic triad of sparse hair, absent or reduced sweating, and abnormal dentition.

338171.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked VMA21 gene cause X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy (XMEA). VMA21 encodes an endoplasmic-reticulum assembly chaperone that is indispensable for correct assembly of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (V-ATPase). When VMA21 is defective, V-ATPase fails to assemble properly, lysosomal acidification is compromised, and muscle fibers accumulate autophagic vacuoles, producing the hallmark excessive autophagy seen in the disease.

812672.long_answer: Hydralazine is primarily metabolized by N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2). The NAT2 gene, whose polymorphisms determine whether an individual is a slow or fast acetylator of hydralazine, is located on the short arm of human chromosome 8 (band 8p22). Hence, chromosome 8 carries the gene that governs hydralazine metabolism.

922375.long_answer: Mutations in any of the genes encoding components of the glycine cleavage system (e.g., GLDC, AMT, GCSH) cause non-ketotic hyperglycinemia. Affected individuals inherit two pathogenic alleles—one from each carrier parent—demonstrating classic autosomal recessive inheritance.

804007.long_answer: The most common form of Batten disease is the juvenile form (juvenile neuronal ceroid-lipofuscinosis, or CLN3 disease). This form is caused by pathogenic variants in the CLN3 gene. The CLN3 gene is located on chromosome 16 (specifically 16p12.1), not on chromosome 20. Therefore, chromosome 20 does not contain the gene responsible for the most common form of Batten disease.

220375.long_answer: Variegate porphyria is caused by mutations in the PPOX gene, which encodes the enzyme protoporphyrinogen oxidase. The human PPOX gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 1 (cytogenetic band 1q22). Defects in this chromosome-1 gene reduce enzyme activity, leading to the biochemical accumulation of porphyrin precursors characteristic of variegate porphyria.

759393.long_answer: Acute kidney injury can arise from post-renal obstruction produced by severe urinary retention. Passing a urethral (Foley) catheter—bladder catheterization—rapidly decompresses the over-distended bladder, re-establishes urine flow, and thereby relieves the obstruction that is compromising renal function.

659488.long_answer: Molybdenum cofactor is required for the function of xanthine oxidase (also called xanthine dehydrogenase). When the cofactor is missing, the enzyme is completely inactive. Xanthine oxidase normally catalyzes the final steps of purine degradation—converting hypoxanthine → xanthine and xanthine → uric acid—so loss of its activity is the reason purine catabolism and uric-acid homeostasis are disturbed in molybdenum cofactor deficiency.

711214.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the MAN2B1 gene, which is mapped to chromosome 19p13.1-p13.2, cause the lysosomal storage disorder alpha-mannosidosis. Individuals with alpha-mannosidosis develop progressive skeletal-muscle involvement that often produces proximal muscle weakness and a characteristic waddling (myopathic) gait, linking the mutation in MAN2B1 to the described clinical picture.

103221.long_answer: The first gene shown to cause Adams–Oliver syndrome is ARHGAP31, which is located at cytogenetic band 3q13.31 on human chromosome 3; pathogenic mutations in ARHGAP31 lead to the characteristic scalp and limb defects of the disorder.

384152.long_answer: Sengers syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the AGK gene (acylglycerol kinase, mitochondrial). AGK encodes the mitochondrial lipid kinase acylglycerol kinase, which phosphorylates mono- and diacylglycerols to lysophosphatidic and phosphatidic acids—key intermediates in cardiolipin biosynthesis. Disrupted cardiolipin metabolism impairs mitochondrial energy production and leads to cardiomyopathy, linking AGK to cardiovascular disease and establishing it as the gene responsible for Sengers syndrome.

391734.long_answer: The first recognized outbreak of rickettsialpox was documented in 1946 among residents of the Kew Gardens neighborhood in the borough of Queens, New York City. Epidemiologic investigation by Dr. Robert Huebner traced the febrile, vesicular illness to mites (Liponyssoides sanguineus) carried by house mice in apartment buildings there, establishing Kew Gardens as the locus of the initial rickettsialpox outbreak.

413877.long_answer: Hereditary myopathy with exercise intolerance (a mitochondrial myopathy presenting as lifelong exercise intolerance) is caused by mutations in the ISCU gene, which lies on chromosome 12q24. ISCU encodes the scaffold protein needed for iron–sulfur-cluster assembly in mitochondrial respiratory-chain enzymes; defective ISCU impairs complexes I, II and III, producing the characteristic exercise-intolerant myopathy.

802575.long_answer: Börjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the PHF6 gene located on the X chromosome. Because males are hemizygous for the X chromosome, a single mutated PHF6 allele produces the full clinical picture, while heterozygous females are typically unaffected or only mildly affected depending on X-inactivation. This pattern of transmission is therefore classified as X-linked recessive.

640842.long_answer: Stocco dos Santos syndrome is the original description of camptodactyly-arthropathy-coxa vara-pericarditis (CACP) syndrome. The disorder results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the PRG4 (lubricin) gene, which was mapped to the chromosomal locus 1q25–q31. Hence, the camptodactyly seen in Stocco dos Santos syndrome is linked to the 1q25–q31 region of chromosome 1.

170805.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the AK2 gene (adenylate kinase 2) produce reticular dysgenesis, the most severe form of severe combined immunodeficiency. AK2 deficiency blocks both myeloid and lymphoid hematopoiesis, leading to agranulocytosis and lymphopenia, and also disrupts inner-ear development, resulting in congenital sensorineural deafness.

856726.long_answer: The X-linked form of congenital zonular (lamellar) cataract accompanied by nystagmus is produced by pathogenic variants in the NDP gene on Xp11.3, which encodes the signaling protein norrin. Mutations in NDP explain both the ocular phenotype and the X-linked pattern of inheritance observed in affected families.

153170.long_answer: Familial multiple intestinal atresia results from recessive mutations in the TTC7A gene (tetratricopeptide repeat domain 7A). TTC7A is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 2 at band 2p16.3, establishing chromosome 2 as the chromosomal location of the disease-causing gene.

643945.long_answer: Absence of fingerprints-congenital milia syndrome (also called adermatoglyphia) is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the skin-specific isoform of the SMARCAD1 gene. SMARCAD1 is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 4 (4q22.3). Thus, the responsible gene resides on chromosome 4.

358053.long_answer: Gunther disease (congenital erythropoietic porphyria) is caused by autosomal-recessive mutations in the UROS gene, which encodes uroporphyrinogen III synthase. The UROS gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 10 (10q25.2-q26.3), making chromosome 10 the chromosomal location responsible for this disorder.

308266.long_answer: The USH2A gene is mutated in Usher syndrome type II. It encodes the trans-membrane protein usherin, which is essential for the proper development and long-term maintenance of stereocilia in inner-ear hair cells and of photoreceptor cells in the retina. Loss-of-function variants in USH2A disrupt these structures, leading to the characteristic hearing impairment and progressive retinitis pigmentosa seen in the disorder.

316826.long_answer: Worth syndrome (endosteal hyperostosis) results from mutations in the LRP5 gene. LRP5 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 11 (region 11q13), so the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 11.

408729.long_answer: Isolated microphthalmia type 1 (MCOP1) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the homeobox transcription factor gene VSX2 (also known as CHX10). The VSX2/CHX10 gene is mapped to the 14q24.3 cytogenetic band, placing it on human chromosome 14.

733016.long_answer: The common juvenile form of Batten disease (juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis) is caused by pathogenic variants in the CLN3 gene. The human CLN3 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 16p12.1 on chromosome 16, making this chromosome the locus for the gene underlying the most prevalent form of Batten disease.

905268.long_answer: Mutations in the RPE65 gene, which is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (band 1p31), are a well-established cause of Leber congenital amaurosis. This chromosomal location was determined through linkage and positional cloning studies, and the gene’s role has been confirmed by successful gene-replacement therapies that restore vision in affected individuals.

966824.long_answer: The Wilms tumor protein is encoded by the WT1 gene, which is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 11 (11p13). This chromosomal location was identified through linkage and cytogenetic studies of patients with Wilms tumor and related syndromes, firmly establishing chromosome 11 as the site of the WT1 gene.

841452.long_answer: Fetal (prenatal) ultrasound can visualize characteristic skeletal abnormalities—such as bowing, fractures, and cortical thickening—caused by autosomal-dominant COL1A1 pathogenic variants (e.g., in osteogenesis imperfecta or Caffey disease). Therefore, prenatal ultrasonography is the key diagnostic tool used to identify affected pregnancies.

578179.long_answer: Pseudoachondroplasia is an autosomal-dominant skeletal dysplasia produced by pathogenic variants in the COMP (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein) gene. The COMP gene is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 19 (region 19p13.1-p12), so chromosome 19 is the chromosomal location responsible for the disorder.

158815.long_answer: WAGR syndrome results from a contiguous-gene deletion at band 11p13 on chromosome 11 that removes or disrupts the WT1 and PAX6 genes. Loss of these genes produces the characteristic features—Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and intellectual disability—linking the disorder specifically to chromosome 11.

699070.long_answer: Most cases of Alagille syndrome result from pathogenic variants or deletions in the JAG1 gene, which is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 20 (band 20p12). Mutations in this chromosome-20-encoded gene disrupt JAG1–NOTCH signaling, leading to the characteristic multisystem features of Alagille syndrome.

569226.long_answer: Kenji Bandō wrote the story that became the Japanese film and novel “Taiyō no Uta” (Midnight Sun), in which the male protagonist falls in love with Kaoru Amane, a girl suffering from xeroderma pigmentosum—a DNA-repair disorder that makes exposure to ultraviolet light potentially lethal. The plot revolves around her need to avoid sunlight and the romance that develops in spite of this medical condition.

853682.long_answer: The gene C4orf26 (Chromosome 4 open reading frame 26), whose loss-of-function mutations cause Kohlschütter–Tönz syndrome, is physically located on human chromosome 4 (band 4q21). Hence chromosome 4 harbors this disease-associated gene.

674071.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in KIF11 (kinesin family member 11) are known to cause the syndrome of microcephaly with or without chorioretinopathy, lymphedema, and mental retardation (MCLMR). A characteristic neuroimaging finding in affected patients is microlissencephaly—a markedly reduced brain size with a simplified or nearly smooth cortical pattern—together with congenital peripheral lymphedema. Thus, a pathogenic KIF11 mutation is the established genetic cause of this rare form of microlissencephaly accompanied by congenital lymphedema.

665042.long_answer: Heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in the PTPN11 gene (coding for the SHP-2 tyrosine-phosphatase) are the most frequent cause of Noonan syndrome, a condition whose cardinal clinical features include proportionate short stature and characteristic craniofacial dysmorphisms such as a broad forehead, hypertelorism, down-slanting palpebral fissures and low-set ears.

646579.long_answer: The major Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility gene is APOE (apolipoprotein E). The ε4 allele of APOE markedly increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, and this gene is located on chromosome 19q13.2. Hence, chromosome 19 harbors the principal genetic locus most strongly linked to Alzheimer’s susceptibility in the general population.

898063.long_answer: The glypican-1 gene (GPC1), whose variation has been implicated in susceptibility to biliary atresia, is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q37).

926968.long_answer: Mutations in the FOXC2 gene, which encodes a forkhead-box transcription factor, cause lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome. A hallmark of this condition is distichiasis—a congenital double row of eyelashes—making FOXC2 the gene most clearly associated with this clinical feature.

850980.long_answer: Macroglossia seen in α-mannosidosis is caused by deficiency of lysosomal α-mannosidase encoded by the MAN2B1 gene. MAN2B1 is located on chromosome 19 (region 19p13–q13); therefore, chromosome 19 contains the gene responsible for this mannosidosis-related form of macroglossia.

688450.long_answer: A gain-of-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene (most commonly the p.G380R substitution) underlies achondroplasia, the prototypic skeletal dysplasia characterized by rhizomelic shortening of the long bones—including marked shortening of the femur—due to impaired endochondral ossification at the growth plates.

885314.long_answer: Lafora disease (progressive myoclonic epilepsy type 2) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in two genes: EPM2A, which encodes the dual-specificity phosphatase laforin, and NHLRC1 (also called EPM2B), which encodes the E3 ubiquitin-ligase malin. Defects in either gene disrupt glycogen metabolism, leading to accumulation of insoluble polyglucosan (Lafora) bodies in neurons and other tissues, producing the characteristic neurodegeneration and myoclonic seizures of Lafora disease.

198944.long_answer: Gliosarcoma, a rare variant of glioblastoma containing both glial and sarcomatous components, is documented to metastasize extracranially (e.g., to lung, liver, bone) more often than other cerebral gliomas. The sarcomatous element is believed to confer greater vascular invasiveness, which underlies its higher propensity for systemic spread compared with typical gliomas confined largely to the central nervous system.

272987.long_answer: The gene most commonly implicated in hereditary spastic paraplegia that alters endoplasmic reticulum morphology is ATL1 (atlastin-1, SPG3A). ATL1 encodes a dynamin-like GTPase that mediates homotypic fusion of ER tubules; mutations disturb ER network structure and cause the early-onset, autosomal-dominant form of HSP. The ATL1 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 14 (region 14q22.1), so chromosome 14 carries this disease-linked locus.

559118.long_answer: The nuclear-encoded gene COX20 (also known as FAM36A) produces the COX20 protein, an inner-mitochondrial-membrane assembly factor essential for the biogenesis and stabilization of cytochrome c oxidase subunit II (COX2). The human COX20 gene is located on Chromosome 1 (band 1q44), so Chromosome 1 contains the gene responsible for this function.

944483.long_answer: The autosomal-dominant, hereditary form of macular dystrophy known as Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy / malattia Leventinese is produced by a missense mutation (classically p.R345W) in the EFEMP1 gene, which encodes the extracellular-matrix protein fibulin-3. Mutant EFEMP1 accumulates beneath the retinal pigment epithelium, forming drusen that progress to macular dystrophy.

333057.long_answer: Mutations in the NTRK1 gene, which encodes the high-affinity receptor (TrkA) for nerve growth factor (NGF), cause Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy type IV (congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis). Loss-of-function variants impair NGF signaling required for survival and differentiation of sensory and autonomic neurons, leading to the characteristic neuropathy.

651510.long_answer: Familial Mediterranean fever is caused by mutations in the MEFV gene, which encodes the inflammation-regulating protein pyrin. The MEFV gene is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 16 (16p13.3); defects here lead to the recurrent peritoneal inflammation characteristic of the disease.

382650.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the IRF6 gene cause Van der Woude syndrome, an autosomal-dominant disorder whose cardinal features include cleft lip and/or cleft palate (malformations of the palate) and lower-lip pits. IRF6 encodes a transcription factor essential for epithelial differentiation during craniofacial development; when mutated, it disrupts palatogenesis, producing the characteristic palatal anomalies seen in the syndrome.

743228.long_answer: Swiss ophthalmologist Adolphe Franceschetti was the first to describe the constellation of optic-nerve coloboma (papillary dysplasia) and renal malformations that later became known as Papillorenal or renal-coloboma syndrome. Molecular studies have since shown that many patients with this syndrome carry heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the transcription-factor gene PAX2, confirming the genetic basis of the disorder he originally delineated.

767984.long_answer: Tuberous sclerosis complex arises from mutations in either the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Mutations in TSC2, located on human chromosome 16p13.3, are consistently associated with a more severe clinical phenotype than mutations in TSC1 on chromosome 9. Hence, chromosome 16 harbors the gene whose defects produce the more severe form of tuberous sclerosis.

273648.long_answer: Fumarase (fumarate hydratase) deficiency results from pathogenic variants in the FH gene. The FH gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 1q42.1 on human chromosome 1, so chromosome 1 is the chromosomal location responsible for the disorder.

475488.long_answer:
Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is most frequently caused by pathogenic variants in genes such as CYP1B1, LTBP2, TEK, FOXC1, and PITX2. By contrast, the only gene that has been conclusively linked, by numerous independent studies, to Peters-plus syndrome is B3GLCT (formerly B3GALTL), an autosomal-recessive glycosyltransferase gene. Pathogenic B3GLCT variants produce the full Peters-plus phenotype (Peters anomaly with short stature, brachydactyly, developmental delay, craniofacial anomalies, etc.).

No peer-reviewed reports or databases (e.g., OMIM, ClinVar, HGMD) document B3GLCT mutations causing isolated primary congenital glaucoma, nor do genes classically mutated in PCG (CYP1B1, LTBP2, TEK, FOXC1, PITX2, MYOC) produce Peters-plus syndrome. Therefore, according to established genetic evidence, there is currently no mutation known to be shared between primary congenital glaucoma and Peters-plus syndrome.

290619.long_answer: Hereditary haemochromatosis, an iron-overload disorder that can disturb thermoregulation, is most commonly caused by mutations in the HFE gene. The HFE gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 6 (6p21.3-p22). Consequently, chromosome 6 carries the gene responsible for this iron-related thermoregulatory condition.

704823.long_answer: In primary hyperparathyroidism, excess parathyroid hormone causes hypercalcemia and marked hypercalciuria. The high urinary calcium fosters the formation of calcium-containing renal calculi (nephrolithiasis). Recurrent or large kidney stones can obstruct the urinary tract, cause infection, and progressively damage renal parenchyma, ultimately leading to chronic kidney disease and renal failure. Thus, nephrolithiasis is a common and clinically significant complication of primary hyperparathyroidism that can progress to kidney failure if untreated.

668547.long_answer: In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, one possible pancreatic tumor is a glucagonoma. This tumor arises from pancreatic alpha cells, which normally secrete the hormone glucagon. Excess glucagon stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, opposing insulin action and producing marked hyperglycemia. Therefore, the alpha cell is the pancreatic cell type whose hormone secretion can lead to hyperglycemia in MEN 1 patients.

832671.long_answer: Juvenile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (Batten disease, JNCL) is caused by mutations in the CLN3 gene. The CLN3 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 16p12.1 on human chromosome 16, establishing chromosome 16 as the chromosomal location responsible for JNCL.

196149.long_answer: Erythrokeratodermia variabilis is caused by mutations in connexin genes (e.g., GJB3/Connexin-31 and GJB4/Connexin-30.3) that encode gap-junction proteins highly expressed in epidermal keratinocytes. The defective connexins impair intercellular communication among these keratinocytes, leading to the characteristic transient erythema and hyperkeratotic plaques of the disease.

615171.long_answer: Northern epilepsy syndrome (also known as Finnish progressive epilepsy with mental retardation or EPMR) is produced by recessive mutations in the CLN8 gene, which is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 8 (region 8p23.3).

152431.long_answer: Beta thalassemia results from mutations in the beta-globin (HBB) gene, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 11 (region 11p15.5). Alterations in this gene disrupt β-globin chain production, leading to the characteristic imbalance of globin chains that underlies the clinical manifestations of beta thalassemia.

176253.long_answer: NCSTN (nicastrin), PSEN1 (presenilin-1), and PSENEN (PEN-2) encode core components of the γ-secretase complex. Loss-of-function mutations in any of these subunits impair γ-secretase activity, disrupt Notch signaling in follicular epithelium, and are a well-established genetic cause of familial hidradenitis suppurativa.

432386.long_answer: The reported Primrose syndrome patient had congenital cryptorchidism (an undescended testis), a well-established risk factor that predisposes germ cells to malignant transformation and thus likely contributed to the development of his testicular tumor.

640712.long_answer: Hypochondroplasia is caused by activating mutations in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, which regulates bone growth during embryonic development. FGFR3 is localized to the short arm of human chromosome 4 (4p16.3); therefore, chromosome 4 harbors the gene whose alteration leads to hypochondroplasia.

572079.long_answer: Canavan disease, a leukodystrophy that characteristically presents with megalencephaly (macrocephaly), is caused by pathogenic variants in the ASPA gene located on human chromosome 17 (17p13.2). Mutations here impair aspartoacylase activity, leading to spongiform white-matter degeneration and the clinical picture of macrocephaly-associated leukodystrophy.

929142.long_answer: ATR-16 (α-thalassemia/mental-retardation) syndrome is produced by large deletions on chromosome 16p13.3 that remove the α-globin gene cluster. The critical genes lost for the haematological phenotype are the two closely linked α-globin genes, HBA1 and HBA2; their absence abolishes α-globin synthesis, producing the α-thalassemia component of the syndrome.

395418.long_answer: Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11) results from pathogenic variants in the SPG11 gene (encoding the protein spatacsin). Cytogenetic mapping places SPG11 on the long arm of human chromosome 15 (15q21.1), establishing chromosome 15 as the locus responsible for this hereditary spastic paraplegia subtype.

227531.long_answer: Craniometaphyseal dysplasia exists in two genetic forms. The autosomal-dominant form is linked to ANKH on chromosome 5 and is generally milder. The autosomal-recessive form is clinically much more severe, often causing extreme skull bone overgrowth with optic-canal narrowing and consequent visual impairment. Linkage studies have mapped this recessive, severe form to the locus on chromosome 6q21–q22.

161779.long_answer: A Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews analysis concluded that conjunctival autograft surgery was significantly less likely to show pterygium recurrence at 6 months than amniotic membrane transplantation, highlighting lower risk ratios for recurrence in the autograft group.

508819.long_answer: Adult-onset autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD), a disorder marked by progressive central nervous system demyelination together with prominent autonomic failure (e.g., orthostatic hypotension, bladder and bowel dysfunction), is produced by a genomic duplication of the LMNB1 gene. The duplicated LMNB1 allele leads to over-expression of the nuclear envelope protein lamin-B1, which disrupts myelin gene regulation, resulting in the characteristic demyelination and autonomic dysfunction.

708802.long_answer: Niemann–Pick disease type C is caused in the great majority of cases by mutations in the NPC1 gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 18 (band 18q11.2). Defects in NPC1 disrupt intracellular cholesterol trafficking, leading to the characteristic lipid accumulation seen in the disorder.

606905.short_answer: Mutations in GALNT3, FGF23, and KL (Klotho)
606905.long_answer: The peri-articular, tumor-like form of calcinosis cutis—known as tumoral calcinosis and also encountered as a complication in patients on chronic renal dialysis—has been linked to loss-of-function mutations in three phosphate-regulating genes: GALNT3, FGF23, and KL (Klotho). These mutations disrupt the FGF23-mediated pathway that maintains phosphate homeostasis, leading to hyperphosphatemia and massive calcium-phosphate deposition around joints.

328554.long_answer: Schinzel–Giedion syndrome is caused by de-novo pathogenic variants in the SETBP1 gene, which is located on the long arm of chromosome 18 (18q12.3). Because SETBP1 resides on an autosome, it is not present on either human sex chromosome (X or Y).

957103.long_answer: The Fragile X mental-retardation 1 (FMR1) gene that causes X-linked intellectual disability resides on the X chromosome, while the huntingtin (HTT) gene responsible for Huntington’s disease is located on chromosome 4 (locus 4p16.3).

308837.long_answer: Spastic paraplegia autosomal dominant type 42 (SPG42) is caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC33A1 gene, which encodes the acetyl-CoA transporter 1. The SLC33A1 gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 3 at band q25.33; therefore, the gene responsible for SPG42 resides on chromosome 3.

154679.long_answer: The ABO gene, located at 9q34 on human chromosome 9, encodes the glycosyl-transferases that determine ABO blood groups. Individuals with blood group O (a result of a specific ABO allele) show markedly reduced Plasmodium falciparum rosetting of infected erythrocytes, diminishing microvascular obstruction and thereby lowering the risk of severe malaria. Hence, the chromosomal location relevant to this rosetting-reducing gene is chromosome 9.

598235.long_answer: The Old Kingdom governor Harkhuf, whose tomb inscription records several expeditions to Nubia, famously returned with a living pygmy (dwarf) for Pharaoh Pepi II. His autobiography at Qubbet el-Hawa describes the mission and the king’s delight, making Harkhuf the official historically linked to bringing a pygmy—stature sometimes associated with microcephaly—from Nubia to Egypt.

484402.long_answer: Loss of the copper-dependent enzyme tyrosinase stops the conversion of tyrosine to DOPA-melanin, producing oculocutaneous albinism. Without melanin, the skin lacks pigment, so underlying blood vessels give it a pink-reddish tint and the skin becomes extremely sensitive to sunlight and other cutaneous insults.

148155.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the OSGEP gene, which encodes the catalytic subunit of the KEOPS complex responsible for N6-threonyl-carbamoylation (t6A) of adenosine-37 in ANN-type tRNAs, have been repeatedly identified in patients with Galloway–Mowat syndrome. Loss-of-function mutations impair t6A modification, leading to the neuro-renal manifestations characteristic of this disorder.

342587.long_answer: Meleda disease (autosomal-recessive palmoplantar keratoderma) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLURP1 gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 8 (region 8q24). Hence, the responsible gene resides on chromosome 8.

607762.long_answer: Choriocarcinoma is a highly vascular malignant trophoblastic tumor that aggressively invades uterine tissue and blood vessels. This invasion frequently produces profuse vaginal bleeding, which can be severe enough to cause significant blood loss and resultant hypovolemia.

636201.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the transcription-factor gene SALL1 cause Townes-Brocks syndrome, whose core features include external ear anomalies such as pre-auricular pits or tags and a high frequency of renal malformations. Unlike branchio-oto-renal (BOR) syndrome, clinically significant hearing loss is typically absent or mild, so the presence of preauricular pits with renal disease but no hearing impairment points to a pathogenic SALL1 mutation.

855971.long_answer: Acyl-CoA oxidase deficiency (also called pseudoneonatal adrenoleukodystrophy) is caused by pathogenic variants in the ACOX1 gene, which encodes peroxisomal straight-chain acyl-CoA oxidase 1—the first enzyme of the peroxisomal β-oxidation pathway. Loss of ACOX1 activity blocks degradation of very-long-chain fatty acids, leading to their pathological accumulation.

936449.long_answer: Among patients with inflammatory bowel disease, a very common extraintestinal complication is iron-deficiency anemia. Chronic intestinal bleeding and impaired iron absorption lead to iron depletion, resulting in reduced hemoglobin synthesis and anemia, which manifests outside the gastrointestinal tract.

284452.long_answer: László Seitelberger, a Hungarian-born neurologist and neuropathologist, was one of the first investigators to describe and analyse infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (later linked to PLA2G6 mutations). In the early literature this childhood neurodegenerative disorder was frequently mistaken for a form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis because both conditions show intracellular autofluorescent storage material. Seitelberger’s clinicopathological studies were pivotal in recognising it as a distinct disease, separating it from the NCLs.

574969.long_answer: The inherited form of triphalangeal thumb maps to the 7q36 region of chromosome 7. Mutations or duplications in the ZRS regulatory element within the LMBR1 gene on this chromosome alter Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling during limb development, producing a thumb with three phalanges that often necessitates corrective plastic surgery.

887116.long_answer: Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder that can manifest as coronary vasospasm and variant (Prinzmetal) angina, is caused by pathogenic mutations in the GLA gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme α-galactosidase A. Loss-of-function mutations in GLA lead to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in vascular smooth-muscle and endothelial cells, predisposing affected patients to the vasospastic chest pain characteristic of variant angina.

933413.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the NOG gene, which encodes the bone morphogenetic protein antagonist noggin, cause disorders such as stapes ankylosis with broad thumbs and toes/multiple synostosis syndrome. These conditions present with congenital, non-progressive conductive hearing loss due to stapes fixation together with characteristic skeletal deformities (digital broadening, joint fusions, other bone abnormalities).

815179.long_answer: According to the case reports catalogued in the dysmorphology and OMIM literature, the combination of congenital distichiasis with structural congenital heart defects and mixed peripheral vascular malformations has been documented in only two individual patients. No additional patients or families have been reported since those original descriptions, making the total number of published cases two.

716696.long_answer: Tangier disease results from loss-of-function mutations in the ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) gene. The ABCA1 gene resides on chromosome 9q31; defects in this transporter impair cholesterol efflux from cells, leading to the markedly low HDL levels characteristic of Tangier disease.

531165.long_answer: Myxoid liposarcomas are commonly driven by the t(12;16)(q13;p11) translocation that fuses the FUS gene on chromosome 16p11 with the DDIT3 gene on chromosome 12q13. Thus, the FUS gene resides on chromosome 16.

394032.long_answer: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita often involves severe, rigid deformities of the feet; congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) occurs in the majority of affected infants and is therefore regarded as a common birth defect associated with arthrogryposis.

825091.long_answer: After a traumatic brain injury, excessive glutamatergic signalling can cause hyperactivity of neurons—particularly excitatory cortical and hippocampal pyramidal cells. This sustained neuronal overexcitation produces abnormal synchronous firing and network hyperexcitability, a well-established mechanism that can progress to post-traumatic epilepsy.

205244.long_answer: Pendred syndrome, in which children typically progress to profound sensorineural hearing loss by about 10 years of age, is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the SLC26A4 gene (encoding the anion transporter pendrin).

738222.long_answer: The human GIF gene encodes gastric intrinsic factor, the glycoprotein that binds vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the duodenum and carries it to the ileum for absorption. Crystal structures of intrinsic factor–B12 complexes have been solved and deposited in the Protein Data Bank, confirming the gene-to-protein relationship.

301586.long_answer: Mutations in the SRD5A2 gene, which encodes the type-2 5-α-reductase enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT), cause 5-α-reductase deficiency. Affected 46,XY individuals are under-virilized at birth and may present with predominantly female external genitalia, a condition that older literature labeled “male pseudohermaphroditism.” Thus, loss-of-function mutations in SRD5A2 underlie the disorder historically referred to by that term.

526495.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the TUBA1A gene, located on chromosome 12q13, disrupt α-tubulin function and neuronal microtubule dynamics. This impairs neuronal migration during cortical development and produces the tubulinopathy form of lissencephaly (often called LIS3). Hence, TUBA1A mutations on chromosome 12 are a well-established genetic cause of lissencephaly.

972964.long_answer: The key negative regulator of prolactin release is dopamine acting through the pituitary D2 dopamine receptor. The gene encoding this receptor (DRD2), which governs dopamine-mediated inhibition of prolactin secretion, is located on human chromosome 11 (band 11q22-q23).

144569.long_answer: Abdallat–Davis–Farrage syndrome has been documented in siblings born to non-affected, consanguineous parents, with males and females equally affected. This segregation pattern—affected children of healthy carrier parents and no vertical transmission—establishes that the disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

232679.long_answer: The spleen normally resides high in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen, tucked beneath the left hemidiaphragm and protected by the 9th–11th ribs. In Felty’s syndrome—characterized by rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia, and splenomegaly—the organ enlarges in this same left upper quadrant location.

654919.long_answer: Mutations in the OTC (ornithine transcarbamylase) gene disrupt the urea cycle enzyme ornithine transcarbamylase, preventing efficient conversion of ammonia to urea. This enzymatic block causes toxic accumulation of ammonia in the bloodstream, the hallmark of the most common inherited urea-cycle disorder, ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

743047.long_answer: Fryns-Aftimos syndrome is caused by a single pathogenic variant present in only one of the two ACTB alleles. Reported patients harbor de-novo or dominantly inherited heterozygous mutations in ACTB; no homozygous or compound-heterozygous cases have been documented. Hence, the disease-causing ACTB mutation is heterozygous.

208919.long_answer: Sporadic inclusion body myositis is an acquired, inflammatory myopathy (with endomysial T-cell infiltrates), whereas hereditary inclusion body myopathies are genetically inherited, non-inflammatory muscle disorders; the key distinction is the presence of immune-mediated inflammation in IBM versus purely genetic (inherited) causation in hIBM.

183487.long_answer: Mutations in the CAPN3 gene, located at 15q15 on human chromosome 15, cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A (LGMD2A). CAPN3 encodes the skeletal-muscle–specific protease calpain-3, and loss-of-function variants impair muscle fiber maintenance, producing the characteristic proximal muscle weakness of this LGMD subtype. Hence, the critical LGMD-linked gene resides on chromosome 15.

215780.long_answer: Conditions that impair fat absorption—such as cholestatic liver disease, cystic fibrosis, or biliary atresia—can lead to vitamin E deficiency. Lack of vitamin E allows oxidative damage to long-axon neurons and posterior column pathways, frequently manifesting as peripheral neuropathy (loss of vibration/position sense, distal weakness, paresthesias). Thus, peripheral neuropathy is a well-recognized neurological complication of vitamin E deficiency arising from these malabsorptive disorders.

850246.long_answer: Mutations in the OAT gene, which encodes ornithine aminotransferase, cause gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. Loss of this enzyme blocks normal ornithine metabolism, producing marked hyper-ornithinemia in blood and leading to progressive retinal degeneration that culminates in blindness.

888513.long_answer: The first and most widely cited autosomal-dominant locus for hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG3A/ATL1) was mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 14 (14q22-q24).
