The MITF gene is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 3 (cytogenetic band 3p13-p14). Therefore, the causative gene for Tietz syndrome resides on chromosome 3.

999462.long_answer: Congenital contractural arachnodactyly (Beals syndrome) is produced by pathogenic variants in the FBN2 gene, which encodes fibrillin-2. FBN2 is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 5 (5q23-q31). Mutations in this chromosomal locus can cause the skeletal features of CCA and, in some patients, progressive aortic root dilatation.

987454.long_answer: Achondroplasia, a common form of disproportionate dwarfism that shows no clinically meaningful response to growth-hormone therapy, is caused by activating mutations in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene. The mutant FGFR3 receptor constitutively suppresses chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral bone growth at the growth plate, so adding exogenous growth hormone cannot correct the underlying signaling defect, rendering the condition GH-insensitive.

777071.long_answer: Uncombable Hair Syndrome type 2 (UHS2) is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the TGM3 gene, which encodes epidermal transglutaminase 3. The TGM3 gene is located at cytogenetic band 20q11.23, so the chromosomal locus involved in UHS2 is chromosome 20.

467373.long_answer: Homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the PTF1A gene disrupt development of the hindbrain’s GABAergic lineage; as a result, the cerebellar anlage fails to form, producing near-complete cerebellar agenesis. Several patients with PTF1A mutations have been described whose brains developed almost entirely without a cerebellum, confirming that defects in PTF1A can cause this condition.

302779.long_answer: Uromodulin kidney disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the UMOD gene, which encodes the uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall) protein. The UMOD gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 16 at cytogenetic band 16p12.3; therefore, chromosome 16 is the chromosome that carries the disease-causing gene.

691307.long_answer: Hitchhiker’s thumbs are a classic clinical sign of diastrophic dysplasia, an autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia. Diastrophic dysplasia is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC26A2 gene (formerly called DTDST), which encodes a cartilage sulfate transporter essential for proper sulfation of proteoglycans in developing cartilage. Defective SLC26A2 disrupts cartilage matrix formation, producing the characteristic limb shortening, ‘cauliflower ear,’ and the hyperextended, abducted ‘hitchhiker’ thumbs seen in affected individuals.

819737.long_answer: Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease can be caused by loss-of-function mutations in the STAT1 gene. STAT1 mediates IFN-γ signalling through tyrosine phosphorylation and subsequent dimerization and nuclear translocation; defective phosphorylation blocks this pathway and predisposes to mycobacterial infection. The human STAT1 gene is located on chromosome 2 (band 2q32.2), making chromosome 2 the chromosome that carries this MSMD-associated, phosphorylation-dependent gene.

798914.long_answer: Erythropoietic protoporphyria results from partial deficiency of the enzyme ferrochelatase. The ferrochelatase enzyme is encoded by the FECH gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 18 (18q21). Mutations in this gene reduce ferrochelatase activity, leading to the accumulation of protoporphyrin and the clinical manifestations of the disorder.

391819.long_answer: Athabaskan brainstem dysgenesis syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HOXA1 gene, which maps to cytogenetic band 7p15.2 on human chromosome 7. Therefore, the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 7.

125976.long_answer: Mutations in the IQCB1 gene (also called NPHP5) cause Senior–Løken syndrome, a ciliopathy that presents with retinal degeneration leading to progressive blindness and nephronophthisis that progresses to renal failure. The ciliary protein encoded by IQCB1 is required for photoreceptor outer-segment integrity and renal tubular function; loss-of-function variants therefore produce the combined phenotype of degenerative blindness and renal dysfunction.

986447.long_answer: The gene encoding T-cell leukemia homeobox protein 3 (TLX3, also known as HOX11L2) is located on the long arm of human chromosome 5 (band 5q35). Chromosomal translocations involving 5q35—such as t(5;14)(q35;q32)—up-regulate TLX3 expression and are a recurrent molecular lesion in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

467583.long_answer: Alpha-thalassemia results from deletions or other mutations in the α-globin genes HBA1 and HBA2, which are arranged in tandem within the α-globin gene cluster on chromosome 16 (band 16p13.3). Disruption of these chromosome-16 genes impairs α-globin chain production, leading to the clinical spectrum of alpha-thalassemia.

453171.long_answer: In 2016 a new, corticosteroid-responsive autoimmune meningo-encephalo-myelitis was delineated and termed ‘autoimmune GFAP astrocytopathy’. The disease is marked by serum and cerebrospinal-fluid immunoglobulin G that targets the intracellular filament protein glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Detection of anti-GFAP IgG reliably identifies this autoimmune form of myelitis and differentiates it from aquaporin-4 or MOG antibody-associated syndromes.

871734.long_answer: Yersinia pestis enhances its virulence by using its Pla protease to convert human plasminogen into plasmin, promoting tissue invasion and systemic spread. The human plasminogen protein is encoded by the PLG gene, which is located on chromosome 6 (band 6q26–q27). Hence, the relevant human gene resides on chromosome 6.

423508.long_answer: Mohr–Tranebjærg syndrome is an X-linked recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the TIMM8A (DDP1) gene. TIMM8A is situated at cytogenetic band Xq22.1 on the human X chromosome; therefore, the disease-causing gene resides on the X chromosome.

262530.long_answer: Sarcosinemia is caused by inherited deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme sarcosine dehydrogenase, encoded by the SARDH gene. Cytogenetic and molecular mapping studies place SARDH on the long arm of human chromosome 9 (region 9q33-q34). Hence, the gene responsible for sarcosinemia is located on chromosome 9.

656524.long_answer: The description refers to Ménétrier disease, a hypertrophic gastropathy marked by massive foveolar (mucus-secreting) cell hyperplasia that creates thick gastric folds and excessive mucus with protein-losing enteropathy. The disease is driven by overexpression of transforming growth factor-α, which activates the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). Targeting this pathway with the monoclonal antibody cetuximab, an EGFR inhibitor, is recommended as first-line therapy because it directly counteracts the underlying EGFR-mediated mucous cell proliferation and can induce symptomatic and histologic remission.

789393.long_answer: Deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1) causes ‘wet’ beriberi, a clinical syndrome characterized by high-output heart failure, peripheral edema, and marked cardiac enlargement that can mimic or progress to a dilated cardiomyopathy. Restoration of thiamine reverses the myocardial dysfunction, confirming the causal link between vitamin B1 deficiency and the enlarged, failing heart.

823018.long_answer: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is caused by mutations in the COL7A1 gene, which encodes type VII collagen forming anchoring fibrils at the dermal-epidermal junction. The COL7A1 locus is situated on human chromosome 3 at band 3p21.3, so chromosome 3 carries the gene responsible for this skin disorder.

407393.long_answer: Congenital disorders of glycosylation arise from defects in the enzymes that add or trim oligosaccharide chains on newly synthesized proteins. These post-translational glycosylation steps—including modification of N-linked glycans—take place in the Golgi apparatus, making this organelle central to the process that is impaired in such disorders.

114281.long_answer: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type II D (PHAII-D) is caused by pathogenic variants in the CUL3 gene. The CUL3 locus is situated on the long arm of human chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q36). Therefore, chromosome 2 carries the gene responsible for the PHAII-D subtype.

388441.long_answer: Cenegermin-bkbj, marketed as Oxervate, is the first FDA-approved treatment for neurotrophic keratitis. One of the common causes of neurotrophic keratitis is herpes zoster ophthalmicus, the ocular manifestation of varicella zoster virus infection. Cenegermin is a recombinant human nerve growth factor that restores corneal innervation and promotes epithelial healing, directly addressing the nerve damage produced by VZV-related disease.

275113.long_answer: Thanatophoric dysplasia, a lethal congenital skeletal dysplasia whose radiographs show a characteristic 'moth-eaten' or irregular, poorly ossified appearance of the fetal long bones, is produced by activating mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3). This transmembrane tyrosine-kinase receptor normally restrains endochondral bone growth; its constitutive activation disturbs cartilage and bone development, giving rise to the distinctive radiologic pattern.

918210.long_answer: Hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is most often caused by autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in the CSF2RB gene, which encodes the β-chain of the GM-CSF receptor. CSF2RB is located on chromosome 22q12, so chromosome 22 carries the gene whose mutation produces the hereditary form of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

813139.long_answer: The congenital absence of fingernails seen in Cooks syndrome is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in the RSPO4 (R-spondin-4) gene, which is located on chromosome 20p13. Disruption of RSPO4 interferes with Wnt–β-catenin signalling that is essential for nail matrix development, producing the anonychia characteristic of this syndrome.

793802.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis is the most common life-limiting autosomal recessive disorder in individuals of European descent. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 7 (7q31.2).

727296.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the SAG (S-antigen, visual arrestin) gene cause Oguchi disease, a form of congenital stationary night blindness. Arrestin terminates activated rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors; when SAG is mutated, rod phototransduction cannot shut off properly, leading to impaired dark adaptation and night-time visual impairment while cone function is largely spared.

721270.long_answer: Schindler disease is caused by mutations in the NAGA gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme α-N-acetylgalactosaminidase. Cytogenetic mapping and sequence data place the NAGA gene on human chromosome 22 (band 22q13.2). Therefore, the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 22.

150692.long_answer: The gene TREM2, which encodes the Triggering Receptor Expressed on Myeloid cells-2 found on monocytes (and microglia), carries rare variants such as R47H that markedly increase the risk of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease. The TREM2 gene is located on human chromosome 6 (region 6p21.1).

701257.long_answer: Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis is caused by recessive mutations in the ANTXR2 (also called CMG2) gene. Molecular mapping shows that ANTXR2 is located at cytogenetic band 4q21 on human chromosome 4; therefore, chromosome 4 carries the gene responsible for the disorder.

335097.long_answer: Hermann Werner Siemens (1891–1969) was a German dermatologist who described several distinct dermatoses—including the form of epidermolysis now called ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens—and in 1926 detailed the X-linked, anhidrotic type of ectodermal dysplasia. His work clarified the hereditary nature and clinical spectrum of hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, earning the disorder its eponym Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome.

253028.long_answer: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) results from heterozygous mutations in one of several genes encoding pancreatic β-cell transcription factors or enzymes (e.g., HNF1A, GCK). These mutations are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, so a single mutated allele inherited from an affected parent is sufficient to cause the disease and it typically appears in successive generations.

982347.long_answer: Oxidative metabolism of fats and carbohydrates generates large amounts of carbon dioxide (CO₂). When CO₂ dissolves in water within body fluids it forms carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), the principal volatile acid in the body. Because carbonic acid is in equilibrium with CO₂, it is eliminated by ventilation; failure to expel it causes CO₂ retention and a rise in H₂CO₃ concentration, producing respiratory acidosis.

883833.long_answer: Inherited Factor X deficiency is caused by mutations in the F10 gene, which encodes coagulation factor X. The F10 gene is mapped to chromosome 13 at band 13q34, so the genetic locus responsible for the disorder resides on chromosome 13.

610297.long_answer: Severe caloric and protein restriction in anorexia nervosa increases vagal tone and weakens myocardial function, producing marked sinus bradycardia. The slow heart rate lowers cardiac output and cerebral perfusion, so patients may experience dizziness or frank syncope as a consequence of this cardiac complication.

303896.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or microdeletions of the NSD1 gene on chromosome 5q35 cause Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism). This genetic disorder is characterized by marked prenatal and postnatal overgrowth, macrocephaly, and developmental delay/intellectual disability, establishing NSD1 mutation as the molecular basis for excessive physical growth with cognitive impairment.

693907.long_answer: Recessive mutations in the COL11A2 gene disrupt the α-2 chain of type XI collagen, leading to otospondylomegaepiphyseal dysplasia (OSMED). This disorder is characterized by severe sensorineural hearing loss together with skeletal abnormalities such as enlarged epiphyses and spinal involvement, establishing COL11A2 mutations as the causative factor.

622219.long_answer: The congenital motor neuron disorder appearing at birth in children—classically exemplified by Werdnig-Hoffmann disease (spinal muscular atrophy type I)—results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the SMN1 gene. Because two defective alleles are required, the condition follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

142513.long_answer: The FGFR2 gene encodes fibroblast growth factor receptor 2, a receptor-tyrosine kinase that regulates osteoblast proliferation and differentiation during craniofacial morphogenesis. Pathogenic variants in FGFR2 disrupt signaling at the cranial sutures, leading to premature suture fusion and craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert, Crouzon, and Pfeiffer, highlighting its central role in craniofacial development.

658380.long_answer: Ataxia–telangiectasia results from loss-of-function mutations in the ATM gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 11q22.3 on human chromosome 11; therefore, chromosome 11 carries the gene responsible for the disease.

578715.long_answer: Weeks to months after chickenpox, varicella-zoster virus can infect and inflame the walls of large intracranial arteries. This post-varicella arteriopathy (varicella cerebral vasculopathy) narrows or occludes the vessels, predisposing children to ischemic stroke. It is one of the best-documented and relatively common late neurological complications of varicella infection.

881537.long_answer: Achondroplasia—the type of dwarfism portrayed in Willow—is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3). The activating FGFR3 mutation inhibits chondrocyte proliferation in growth plates, producing the characteristic short-limb dwarfism seen in the character played by Warwick Davis.

903340.long_answer: COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3 encode the α-chains of type IX collagen, a collagen that binds to and stabilizes type II collagen fibrils in hyaline cartilage (including articular and growth-plate cartilage). Mutations in these genes therefore disrupt the structure and function of hyaline cartilage, leading to the skeletal disorder multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.

858068.long_answer: The gene that encodes microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP)—mutations of which produce a form of familial hypobetalipoproteinemia/abetalipoproteinemia—is located on human chromosome 4 (cytogenetic region 4q24-q25). Pathogenic variants in this chromosome-4 MTTP locus impair lipid transfer in the endoplasmic reticulum, leading to markedly reduced plasma apolipoprotein-B–containing lipoproteins and the hypobetalipoproteinemia phenotype.

525850.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ERCC2 gene, which encodes the XPD helicase component of the TFIIH complex, cripple nucleotide-excision repair. This defect produces the photosensitive skin disorder xeroderma pigmentosum and, in many patients, a combined phenotype marked by progressive neurodegeneration and intellectual disability (e.g., the XP/TTD or XP/CS overlap syndromes). Hence an ERCC2/XPD mutation is the recognized genetic cause of the syndrome that couples xeroderma pigmentosum with worsening cognitive impairment.

646300.long_answer: Pulmonary agenesis is the complete absence of a lung, including its bronchus and vasculature, whereas pulmonary hypoplasia refers to a lung that is present but markedly underdeveloped, containing reduced airways, parenchyma, and vessels.

927513.long_answer: Mitochondrial Complex I deficiency is most commonly linked to pathogenic variants in the nuclear-encoded NDUFV1 gene, which codes for the 51-kDa flavoprotein subunit of Complex I. The NDUFV1 gene is located on human chromosome 11 at cytogenetic band 11q13. Mutations in this locus impair NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase activity, leading to the clinical spectrum of Complex I deficiency.

502756.long_answer: Mutations in the IRF6 gene (Interferon Regulatory Factor 6) cause Popliteal Pterygium Syndrome, characterized by popliteal webbing, and the same gene is the principal genetic cause of Van der Woude syndrome. Thus, IRF6 is the shared gene whose mutation links both conditions.

255650.long_answer: Fumarase deficiency is caused by mutations in the FH gene (fumarate hydratase). Cytogenetic mapping shows that FH lies at 1q42.1 on human chromosome 1, making chromosome 1 the locus for the gene responsible for this disorder.

136615.long_answer: Porokeratosis that manifests as numerous small papular lesions on the palms and/or soles—punctate palmoplantar porokeratosis—has been linked to heterozygous mutations in two mevalonate-pathway genes: MVK (mevalonate kinase) and MVD (mevalonate diphosphate decarboxylase). Pathogenic variants in either gene disrupt cholesterol/isoprenoid biosynthesis, producing the characteristic papular keratotic lesions of this porokeratosis subtype.

387202.long_answer: Crigler–Najjar syndrome arises from inherited deficiency or complete absence of the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1), which normally conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid. Without functional UGT1A1, bilirubin cannot be converted to its water-soluble (conjugated) form, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates to very high levels, producing the characteristic severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia of the disorder.

659319.long_answer: In the United States the most frequent reason for an enlarged (goitrous) thyroid is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, also called chronic autoimmune/lymphocytic thyroiditis. Ascher’s syndrome often includes a nontoxic, euthyroid goiter, and in the U.S. this enlargement is most commonly attributable to Hashimoto’s autoimmune destruction and accompanying lymphoid infiltration of the gland.

575062.long_answer: The most common form of leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD-I) is caused by mutations in the ITGB2 gene, which encodes the β2-integrin subunit CD18 that is essential for leukocyte adhesion and migration. The ITGB2 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 21 (cytogenetic band 21q22.3). Hence, chromosome 21 does indeed contain the gene whose defects produce the classic, common form of leukocyte adhesion deficiency.

717101.long_answer: Beta-thalassemia results from mutations in the HBB gene, which encodes the β-globin subunit of hemoglobin. The entire β-globin gene cluster, including HBB, is located on the short arm of human chromosome 11 (region 11p15.4). Therefore, chromosome 11 is the chromosome that carries the gene whose defects cause beta thalassemia.

900028.long_answer: The human SRP54 gene encodes the 54-kDa subunit of the signal recognition particle, a key protein that directs nascent polypeptides to the endoplasmic reticulum during co-translational targeting. Cytogenetic mapping places SRP54 on chromosome 14 (band 14q13), so chromosome 14 is the chromosome that carries the gene for this ER-targeting protein.

213017.long_answer: Activating mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR3) gene cause thanatophoric dysplasia, a lethal skeletal dysplasia. Affected fetuses have markedly shortened limbs, narrow thorax and pulmonary hypoplasia, so the condition frequently results in stillbirth or death in the early neonatal period.

854757.long_answer: Worth syndrome (also known as Worth-type autosomal-dominant endosteal hyperostosis) has been linked to activating (gain-of-function) mutations in the LRP5 gene.  The LRP5 gene is located on chromosome 11 (cytogenetic location 11q13.4), not on chromosome 21.  No gene on chromosome 21 has been shown to cause Worth syndrome according to the current genetic and clinical literature.  Therefore the statement that chromosome 21 contains the gene that causes Worth syndrome is incorrect.

114621.long_answer: Malouf syndrome (dilated cardiomyopathy with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) is produced by pathogenic variants in the LMNA gene, which encodes lamin A/C. The LMNA gene is located on human chromosome 1 (band 1q22). Because lamin defects impair connective-tissue integrity, affected individuals can show joint laxity and skin hyperextensibility resembling Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Hence, the gene responsible for Malouf syndrome resides on chromosome 1.

710549.long_answer: Berlin’s edema (commotio retinae) is characterized by transient whitening of the outer retina after blunt ocular trauma. Fluorescein angiography in this condition typically shows normal retinal vascular filling and, at most, a blocked or mottled background choroidal fluorescence caused by the opaque retina. This fluorescence pattern is a masking or blocking phenomenon rather than a sign of dye leakage or specific tissue staining. Consequently, the presence or absence of choroidal fluorescence on fluorescein angiography does not correlate with the degree of photoreceptor or other retinal cell damage, nor does it predict functional visual outcome. Modern imaging (e.g., optical coherence tomography) is required to evaluate the true extent of outer retinal disruption. Therefore, choroidal fluorescence in Berlin’s edema is not an indicator of the extent of retinal cell damage.

346402.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the LRP5 gene cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome. This single-gene disorder is characterized by very low bone density (severe juvenile osteoporosis) and congenital or early-onset retinal dysplasia leading to blindness, showing that LRP5 is crucial for both skeletal mass acquisition and normal retinal vascular development.

841746.long_answer: In northern European populations the prevalent form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD2I) is produced by a founder mutation (c.826C>A) in the FKRP gene. FKRP is mapped to cytogenetic band 19q13.3, so chromosome 19 is the chromosome that contains the gene most commonly mutated in this region.

512359.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the MYO5A gene (encoding the motor protein myosin-Va) cause Griscelli syndrome type 1 / Elejalde neuroectodermal melanolysosomal disease. This disorder is characterized by primary central-nervous-system dysfunction together with only moderate skin pigment dilution and scalp hair that appears light-colored with a distinctive metallic, silvery sheen. Hence, MYO5A is the gene associated with this CNS disease phenotype.

777454.long_answer: Ewing's sarcoma and peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor are now regarded as morphologic variants within the Ewing sarcoma family of tumors. They share the characteristic EWSR1-FLI1 (t(11;22)(q24;q12)) and related gene fusions, identical immunohistochemical profiles, and common cell of origin, differing only in the extent of neural differentiation. Thus, they represent the same biological entity rather than distinct diseases.

363408.long_answer: In medical genetics, a ʻsyndromeʼ refers to a distinct, recurring combination of characteristic signs and symptoms. Microphthalmia that presents together with additional, consistent abnormalities is therefore described as part of a syndromic picture—i.e., it occurs within a defined syndrome such as CHARGE or Lenz microphthalmia syndrome.

804830.long_answer: In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), pathogenic autoantibodies inhibit the plasma metalloprotease ADAMTS13 (von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease). Loss of ADAMTS13 activity prevents normal cleavage of ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers, causing widespread platelet-rich microthrombi. This mechanism underlies the blood disorder and can disseminate, affecting multiple organs.

176176.long_answer: Pseudoachondroplasia is an autosomal-dominant osteochondrodysplasia produced by pathogenic variants in the COMP (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein) gene on chromosome 19p13.1. Mutant COMP misfolds and accumulates in the rough endoplasmic reticulum of growth-plate chondrocytes, triggering cellular stress and premature chondrocyte death, which impairs endochondral bone growth and leads to the characteristic short-limb dwarfism of pseudoachondroplasia.

883061.long_answer: The syndrome described is Aagenaes syndrome (lymphoedema-cholestasis syndrome), characterized by congenital hypoplasia of lymphatic vessels with recurrent neonatal/infantile cholestasis. Linkage studies have mapped the responsible autosomal-recessive locus (LCS1) to the long arm of human chromosome 15 (15q), establishing chromosome 15 as the location of the gene associated with this condition.

766298.long_answer: Fine–Lubinsky syndrome has been shown to result from biallelic loss-of-function variants in CWC27, the gene encoding a spliceosome-associated protein. Individuals with pathogenic CWC27 variants present with the cardinal features of the syndrome – ocular anomalies (microphthalmia, coloboma, high myopia or retinal dystrophy), sensorineural hearing impairment, marked speech and developmental delay, and intellectual disability – establishing CWC27 as the causative gene.

514861.long_answer: The most common form of Weill–Marchesani syndrome is produced by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene (fibrillin-1). FBN1 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 15 (15q21.1). Mutations in this gene disrupt the microfibrillar architecture of connective tissue, giving rise to the characteristic short stature, brachydactyly and microspherophakia seen in Weill–Marchesani syndrome.

324498.long_answer: Homozygous or compound-heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the RSPO2 gene (R-spondin-2), located at cytogenetic band 8q23.1 on human chromosome 8, are known to cause tetra-amelia syndrome that is frequently accompanied by complete lung (pulmonary) agenesis. RSPO2 is a key modulator of Wnt/β-catenin signalling during limb and lung bud development; its disruption abolishes limb formation and arrests early lung morphogenesis, producing the characteristic tetra-amelia with lung agenesis phenotype.

698782.long_answer: Molecular studies have shown that micro-deletions or pathogenic variants involving the HNF1B gene at cytogenetic band 17q12 are present in a proportion of patients with the classical Eagle-Barrett (Prune belly) syndrome. Because HNF1B is located on human chromosome 17, this chromosome is considered the chromosomal site of the gene associated with Prune belly syndrome.

427216.long_answer: Werner syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the WRN gene. WRN encodes a RecQ family DNA helicase/exonuclease that participates in DNA replication, recombination, and repair, and it physically interacts with RNA polymerase-associated factors during transcription-coupled DNA repair. Therefore, mutation of the WRN gene links Werner syndrome to cellular processes that involve RNA polymerase.

633429.long_answer: Mutations in the MECP2 gene cause Rett syndrome, a well-characterized neurodevelopmental disorder whose core clinical features include global developmental delay and moderate-to-severe intellectual disability. MECP2 encodes methyl-CpG-binding protein 2, a key regulator of gene expression in neurons; loss-of-function variants disrupt neuronal maturation and synaptic function, leading to the cognitive and developmental deficits observed in affected individuals.

218090.long_answer: Curry–Jones syndrome is produced by a recurrent, post-zygotic activating mutation in the SMO gene (Smoothened, frizzled class receptor). The SMO locus is situated at 7q32.1 on human chromosome 7; hence the causative gene for Curry–Jones syndrome is located on chromosome 7.

754446.long_answer: Joubert syndrome is genetically heterogeneous, and several causative genes have been identified on different chromosomes. Among them, the CEP290 gene (responsible for Joubert syndrome type 5) is located on chromosome 12q21.3, and the TCTN2 gene (another Joubert-associated gene) is located on chromosome 12q24.31. Therefore, at least two well-established Joubert-syndrome genes reside on chromosome 12, making the statement correct.

223436.long_answer: Howel–Evans syndrome (tylosis with oesophageal cancer) is caused by mutations in the RHBDF2 gene (encoding iRhom2). iRhom2 is known to bind the pro-apoptotic protein Bcl-2-interacting killer (BIK). The RHBDF2 gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 17 (17q25.1), so chromosome 17 carries the gene that both interacts with BIK and is implicated in Howel–Evans syndrome.

864923.long_answer: Tangier disease results from loss-of-function mutations in the ABCA1 gene (ATP-binding cassette transporter A1). The ABCA1 locus is situated on the long arm of human chromosome 9 (9q31), so chromosome 9 is the chromosomal location responsible for the HDL deficiency characteristic of Tangier disease.

720733.long_answer: The form of thalassemia most widespread in Pakistan is β-thalassemia. This disease results from mutations in the β-globin (HBB) gene, which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 11 (11p15.5). Therefore, chromosome 11 carries the gene whose defects lead to the prevalent type of thalassemia in that population.

982706.long_answer: Activating mutations in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor-3) gene are the well-established cause of achondroplasia, a classic skeletal dysplasia. The mutant FGFR3 protein constitutively inhibits chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate, leading to shortened long bones and characteristic dwarfism. Achondroplasia is therefore a skeletal disorder squarely within the domain of medical genetics.

599135.long_answer: Chédiak–Higashi syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder produced by loss-of-function mutations in the LYST (lysosomal trafficking regulator) gene. The LYST gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 1 at band 1q42.1-q42.2; therefore, chromosome 1 carries the genetic defect responsible for the syndrome.

701290.long_answer: Miyoshi myopathy (also called Miyoshi distal myopathy) is caused by recessive mutations in the DYSF gene that encodes the membrane-repair protein dysferlin. The DYSF gene is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 2 at band p13 (chromosomal locus 2p13), and defects at this locus lead to the characteristic distal muscle weakness of Miyoshi myopathy.

668369.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the DLL3 gene (encoding the Delta-like 3 ligand of the Notch pathway) cause spondylocostal dysostosis type 1, a congenital disorder of vertebral segmentation. The disturbed Notch signalling impairs normal formation of somites, producing malformed and fused vertebrae and ribs that manifest clinically as progressive, often severe spinal curvature (scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis).

719467.long_answer: Morquio syndrome type IVB (Morquio B) is produced by pathogenic variants in the GLB1 gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme β-galactosidase. Loss of enzyme activity causes keratan-sulfate storage and skeletal dysplasia, and affected patients frequently develop pronounced spinal deformities such as scoliosis.

302376.long_answer: Excessive urinary excretion of orotic acid (orotic aciduria) results from an inherited deficiency of uridine-5′-monophosphate (UMP) synthase, the bifunctional enzyme that normally converts orotate to UMP via its orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidine-5′-phosphate decarboxylase activities. When UMP synthase is absent or defective, orotate accumulates and is spilled into the urine, producing the characteristic orotic aciduria phenotype.

601989.long_answer: The SFTPB gene on human chromosome 2 (locus 2p11.2) encodes surfactant protein B, a hydrophobic component of pulmonary surfactant that is essential for lowering surface tension at the air–liquid interface in the alveoli, thereby preventing alveolar collapse and facilitating normal lung function.

195407.long_answer: Deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme (α-1,4-→-α-1,6-glucan trans-glycosylase) causes glycogen-storage disease type IV (Andersen disease). In this disorder an abnormally long, poorly branched glycogen—often termed “amylopectin-like” polymer—accumulates in skeletal and cardiac muscle as well as liver. Because these insoluble polyglucosan bodies adopt an amyloid-like, β-pleated sheet conformation, the disease is classically linked to the structure of beta sheets.

564458.long_answer: Fazio–Londe disease is caused by recessive mutations in the riboflavin transporter gene SLC52A3 (formerly C20orf54). This gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 20 (20p13), making chromosome 20 the chromosomal location associated with the disorder.

176311.long_answer: Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis (Haberland syndrome) presents with porencephalic brain cysts together with characteristic facial skin tags and other ectomesodermal anomalies. Molecular studies have shown that this disorder is caused by activating, somatic (mosaic) mutations in the fibroblast growth-factor receptor-1 gene (FGFR1), making FGFR1 mutation the established genetic association with this clinical picture.

504848.long_answer: Mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the connective-tissue protein fibrillin-1, cause Marfan syndrome. This disorder often produces progressive scoliosis and other spine deformities, so affected individuals are routinely followed with periodic examinations and imaging to detect and manage spinal irregularities.

257420.long_answer: In autism spectrum disorder—a neurological condition in which atypical sodium-channel function can lead to reduced sensitivity to the local anaesthetic lidocaine—patients frequently experience debilitating sensory overload (hyper-reactivity to sound, light, touch, etc.). Structured occupational therapy that incorporates sensory-integration techniques is an evidence-based intervention used to modulate sensory input, teach coping strategies, and thereby lessen sensory overload in these individuals.

171460.long_answer: Familial Amyloidosis, Finnish Type is produced by missense mutations in the GSN gene that encodes the actin-modifying protein gelsolin. The GSN gene is mapped to chromosome 9q34, so the disease-causing mutation is associated with chromosome 9.

543623.long_answer: Fragile X syndrome is caused by expansion of CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene, which is situated at band Xq27.3 of the X chromosome; therefore, the gene responsible for the disorder resides on the X chromosome.

820940.long_answer: Field studies in West Africa have shown that the straw-coloured fruit bat, Eidolon helvum, frequently carries IgG antibodies that react with Zaire ebolavirus antigens, indicating previous asymptomatic infection and implicating this species as a natural host of the virus that causes Ebola virus disease.

134057.long_answer:
Prosopagnosia ("face blindness") is primarily a perceptual-recognition disorder: affected individuals have difficulty perceiving and identifying faces because cortical regions that analyse facial structure (e.g., the fusiform face area and occipital face area) are damaged or function abnormally. Once a face is correctly perceived and encoded by another route (for example, by verbal description), episodic memory for that information is generally normal.

Prosopamnesia (sometimes misspelled “prosoamnesia”) is different: perceptual analysis of faces is intact, but the specific ability to encode newly seen faces into long-term memory is impaired. Patients can perceive that a stimulus is a face and can describe its features, yet they fail to form or store a durable memory of that face.

Thus, prosopagnosia does not disrupt memory encoding in the same way; its core deficit lies earlier (visual analysis/recognition), whereas prosopamnesia’s deficit lies at the stage of encoding faces into memory. Therefore, the two conditions affect different cognitive processes, and the statement that they affect memory encoding in the same way is not supported by scientific evidence.

667298.long_answer: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in the CHD7 gene cause CHARGE syndrome. This syndrome typically presents with severe sensorineural hearing loss from inner-ear malformations, ocular colobomas leading to vision impairment, and brain anomalies such as hypoplasia or agenesis of the corpus callosum. Thus, mutation of CHD7 is the well-established genetic cause of the disorder displaying these combined features.

218205.long_answer: Gray platelet syndrome is a rare inherited disorder marked by a marked reduction or absence of α-granules in blood platelets. The disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NBEAL2 gene, which encodes Neurobeachin-like protein 2, a protein essential for the biogenesis and retention of platelet α-granules.

698625.long_answer: Oto-faciocervical syndrome type 2 (OFCS2) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PAX1 gene, which is located on chromosome 20p11.2. Disruption of this paired-box transcription factor impairs branchial arch and skeletal development, leading to the characteristic ear, facial and cervical anomalies seen in this form of the syndrome.

928278.long_answer: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a treatment for major depressive disorder that intentionally induces therapeutic seizures. During ECT, the patient is anesthetized with an ultra-short-acting barbiturate such as methohexital, which exerts its effect by potentiating the GABA-A receptor—enhancing inhibitory chloride influx to produce rapid unconsciousness.

502537.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the membrane-associated guanylate kinase (MAGUK) scaffold genes DLG3 (SAP102) and CASK cause X-linked intellectual disability. Both of these MAGUK genes are located on the X chromosome (DLG3 at Xq13.1 and CASK at Xp11.4), making the X chromosome the genomic site implicated in MAGUK-related intellectual disability.

933451.long_answer: Dent’s disease is an X-linked recessive renal tubular disorder most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CLCN5 gene (encoding the ClC-5 chloride channel). CLCN5 is located at Xp11.22 on the human X chromosome; therefore the gene responsible for Dent’s disease resides on chromosome X.

379692.long_answer: Sarcosinemia results from mutations in the SARDH gene (sarcosine dehydrogenase) located on human chromosome 9q34. Loss-of-function variants in both alleles of SARDH are required to produce the enzyme deficiency, so the disorder follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

720301.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked NHS gene (Nance-Horan syndrome gene) cause Nance-Horan syndrome, an ocular–dental disorder characterized by dense bilateral congenital cataracts and microcornea. These ocular anomalies appear at birth, markedly reduce visual acuity, and are the hallmark of the syndrome, firmly linking NHS mutations to congenital cataract–microcornea–associated visual impairment.

367642.long_answer: In juvenile idiopathic arthritis, a positive ANA test identifies children—especially young girls with oligoarticular onset—who are at markedly increased risk for developing chronic, asymptomatic anterior uveitis. ANA positivity therefore guides ophthalmologic screening intervals rather than reflecting joint disease severity.

229323.long_answer: The Hereditary Hearing Loss Homepage is the curated database that assigns and displays the unique DFN (DFNA/DFNB/DFNX) numbers used worldwide to identify each gene or chromosomal locus known to cause nonsyndromic deafness.

480347.long_answer: The FERMT1 gene (also called KIND1, encoding kindlin-1) maps to cytogenetic band 20p12.3 on chromosome 20. Pathogenic variants in this gene cause the autosomal-recessive skin disorder Kindler syndrome, confirming its chromosomal location.

740231.long_answer: Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI) is the primary database for curated information on mouse genes, alleles, phenotypes and their associations with human diseases. It includes entries for the murine Suox gene and disease models annotated to sulfite oxidase deficiency, making it the appropriate resource for this query.

287843.long_answer: OMIM entry 300600 does not correspond to a xeroderma-pigmentosum–type disorder or any other syndrome whose hallmark is a defect in repairing ultraviolet-induced DNA lesions. Instead, 300600 refers to an X-linked disorder whose molecular defect is in a pathway unrelated to the nucleotide-excision repair (NER) machinery that removes UV-generated photoproducts. Conditions that are classically UV-repair–deficient, such as xeroderma pigmentosum or the photosensitive forms of trichothiodystrophy and Cockayne syndrome, are catalogued under different OMIM numbers in the 27-8-xxx series. Consequently, OMIM 300600 is not about defective DNA repair of UV damage.

991927.long_answer: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the SLC22A5 gene, which encodes the OCTN2 carnitine transporter. Because disease manifests only when both alleles are defective, the disorder follows an autosomal-recessive pattern of inheritance.

644656.long_answer: Aldosterone, the mineralocorticoid produced by the adrenal cortex, is released when angiotensin II rises. Angiotensin II both stimulates aldosterone secretion and promotes renal potassium (K⁺) excretion; aldosterone then further enhances kaliuresis in the distal nephron. Thus the hormone whose secretion is stimulated by a compound that also causes potassium excretion is aldosterone.

616763.long_answer: Lafora disease is a progressive myoclonic epilepsy caused by pathogenic variants in two known genes: EPM2A, which encodes the dual-specificity phosphatase laforin, and NHLRC1 (also called EPM2B), which encodes the E3-ubiquitin ligase malin. Mutations in EPM2A are a well-established cause of the disease. In contrast, the SHH (Sonic Hedgehog) gene is not implicated in Lafora disease; it is a developmental morphogen best known for its roles in embryogenesis and patterning of the central nervous system. There is no evidence in the medical or genetic literature linking SHH mutations or dysregulation to Lafora disease. Therefore, while EPM2A is associated with Lafora disease, SHH is not, making the statement incorrect.

652294.long_answer: Glutathione-synthetase deficiency results from pathogenic variants in the GSS gene, which is located on chromosome 20q11.23. Chromosome 20 is one of the 22 non-sex chromosomes, making the disorder autosomal (and inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner).

983852.long_answer: The National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), one of the National Institutes of Health, funds and conducts research on bone and skeletal development. Its mission explicitly includes studying congenital skeletal disorders such as brachydactyly to identify the genes and molecular pathways that cause abnormal digit formation.

902859.long_answer: The three fibrinogen genes—FGA (alpha chain), FGB (beta chain) and FGG (gamma chain)—are clustered on human chromosome 4 (region 4q31-q32). These genes encode the polypeptide chains that assemble into fibrinogen, the precursor of the fibrin clot. Mutations or deletions in any of these chromosome-4 genes can lead to bleeding disorders such as congenital hypofibrinogenemia, and altered fibrinogen levels contribute to coagulopathies like disseminated intravascular coagulation.

170129.long_answer: A rare, autosomal-dominant form of multiple sclerosis characterized by tumefactive lesions, including Baló’s concentric sclerosis, has been linked to a missense mutation (p.Arg415Gln) in the NR1H3 gene, which encodes the nuclear receptor LXR-α. This NR1H3 mutation segregates with the disease in affected families, distinguishing this MS subtype from the common polygenic forms.

993801.long_answer: The ERLIN2 gene, whose mutations cause the autosomal-recessive form of hereditary spastic paraplegia designated SPG18, is located on human chromosome 8 (cytogenetic band 8p11.23).

421042.long_answer: Neurofibromatosis type II is caused by pathogenic variants in the NF2 tumor-suppressor gene that encodes the protein merlin (schwannomin). The NF2 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 22 (cytogenetic band 22q12.2), not on chromosome 21. Therefore, the statement that the gene responsible for tumor formation in neurofibromatosis type II is found on chromosome 21 is incorrect.

698989.long_answer: The MYO7A gene, whose mutations are a well-established cause of Usher syndrome type I (specifically the USH1B subtype), is located on human chromosome 11 (band 11q13.5).

249007.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the GJA1 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein Connexin-43 and maps to chromosome 6q22-q24, are responsible for the syndrome classically known as oculo-dento-digital dysplasia. This disorder presents with characteristic facial dysmorphisms together with digital and skeletal (osseous) anomalies and can include cardiac conduction defects, fitting the description of a syndrome with cardiac, digital and osseous anomalies plus facial dysmorphisms located on the long arm of chromosome 6.

643264.long_answer: Endomyocardial fibrosis is regarded as the most frequent worldwide cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy. The dense fibrous tissue that lines the ventricular endocardium can extend onto the papillary muscles and valve leaflets, particularly on the right side of the heart, producing tricuspid (and sometimes pulmonary) valve regurgitation or stenosis. Thus it both explains the restrictive ventricular physiology and the characteristic right-sided cardiac valve disease.

213796.long_answer: Parkes Weber syndrome is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the RASA1 gene, which underlies the capillary malformations called port-wine stains in the disorder. The RASA1 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 5q13.3, so the relevant gene resides on human chromosome 5.

375218.long_answer: The triad of ichthyosis follicularis, congenital alopecia and (often) photophobia defines IFAP syndrome, an X-linked disorder. Multiple studies have shown that missense or splice-site mutations in the MBTPS2 gene, which encodes the membrane-bound transcription factor peptidase, site 2, are responsible for this syndrome. Loss of MBTPS2 protease activity disrupts sterol-regulated transcriptional pathways in skin and hair follicles, producing the combined phenotype of ichthyosis follicularis and alopecia.

673359.long_answer: Turrón is a traditional Spanish-Mediterranean nougat confection made from honey, sugar, egg whites and large amounts of roasted tree nuts—usually almonds or hazelnuts. Almonds and other tree nuts are among the eight major food allergens and can elicit IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reactions, including life-threatening anaphylaxis, in susceptible individuals. Because turrón routinely contains these nuts, it poses a recognized allergenic risk.

546258.long_answer: Uniparental disomy (UPD) occurs when the two homologous copies of a chromosome are inherited from a single parent instead of one copy from each parent. Because both alleles derive from the same parent, any recessive mutation present on that chromosome can become homozygous, leading to recessive genetic conditions, and parent-of-origin (imprinting) effects may also arise.

114210.long_answer: The hereditary condition is Brugada syndrome, an autosomal-dominant cardiac channelopathy that manifests on ECG as right (occasionally left) bundle branch block with ST-segment elevation in the right pre-cordial leads and predisposes to lethal ventricular arrhythmias. No medication has been shown to reliably prevent sudden cardiac death in these patients; implantation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is the only therapy that has conclusively been proven to reduce mortality.

732973.long_answer: The measles (rubeola) virus can persist in the central nervous system and years later cause sub-acute sclerosing panencephalitis, a relentlessly progressive inflammatory degeneration of the brain. During the acute infection it can also infect the myocardium, producing viral myocarditis that may progress to dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure. Thus the same virus is linked both to progressive brain inflammation and to potentially fatal cardiac failure.

242217.long_answer: Fanconi anemia results from mutations in the Fanconi anemia (FA) gene network, whose proteins assemble in the nucleus to repair DNA inter-strand cross-links via the FA–BRCA pathway. The defective step occurs within the nuclear DNA repair machinery, so the organelle central to this impaired process is the nucleus.

551143.long_answer: Kaufman oculocerebrofacial syndrome results from autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in the UBE3B gene (ubiquitin-protein ligase E3B). The UBE3B locus is mapped to cytogenetic band 12q24 on human chromosome 12; therefore, chromosome 12 contains the gene responsible for this syndrome.

875702.long_answer: Schmitt-Gillenwater-Kelly (radial hypoplasia–hypospadias) syndrome has been shown to segregate in an X-linked pattern, and linkage studies have mapped the responsible locus to the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq). Therefore, the gene that potentially causes the radial hypoplasia characteristic of this syndrome is located on the human X chromosome.

389003.long_answer: Diencephalic syndrome is classically produced by low-grade gliomas that arise in the hypothalamic/optic-chiasmatic region of the brain. Tumors centered in the hypothalamus disrupt its regulatory functions, leading to the characteristic failure to thrive, hyperactivity, and emaciation seen in this syndrome.

322484.long_answer: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative opportunistic bacterium that commonly causes superficial skin infections such as ‘hot-tub’ folliculitis and ecthyma gangrenosum. Fluoroquinolones, particularly ciprofloxacin, have potent anti-pseudomonal activity and are frequently prescribed when systemic therapy is required, making P. aeruginosa the bacterium whose skin infections are effectively treated with ciprofloxacin.

817718.long_answer: Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the DHCR7 gene, which encodes 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase. DHCR7 is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 11 (region 11q13.4). Mutations in this chromosome-11 gene disrupt cholesterol biosynthesis, producing the clinical features of the syndrome, including congenital ptosis.

377888.long_answer: Mutations in the ASS1 gene (argininosuccinate synthetase 1) block the conversion of citrulline to argininosuccinate in the urea cycle, producing classic citrullinemia type I. This enzymatic defect causes citrulline to accumulate in the blood, leading to the characteristic elevation seen in this urea-cycle disorder.

582650.long_answer: The inherited Roberts/SC-phocomelia syndrome, which presents with phocomelia together with visceral anomalies including renal dysplasia, is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the ESCO2 gene located on chromosome 8p21. Therefore, the genetic form of the syndrome is linked to chromosome 8.

523651.long_answer: Biallelic mutations in the DCAF17 gene (formerly C2orf37) cause Woodhouse-Sakati syndrome. This autosomal-recessive disorder is characterized by progressive childhood-onset alopecia and distinct MRI evidence of iron deposition in the basal ganglia, linking the DCAF17 mutation to both brain iron accumulation and early hair thinning.

913596.long_answer: Prolonged thrombin time is the key screening test for fibrinogen disorders such as congenital afibrinogenemia or dysfibrinogenemia. The fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, and FGG) that cause these bleeding disorders are clustered together on the long arm of human chromosome 4 (4q). Hence, the gene associated with the thrombin-time bleeding disorder resides on chromosome 4.

609049.long_answer: Rendered animal by-product known as meat-and-bone meal (MBM) is commonly added to cattle rations and is also sold as an organic phosphate-rich fertilizer for crops and gardens. If the MBM is prepared from carcasses of animals carrying the misfolded prion protein (PrP^Sc), those prions can survive rendering, contaminate the meal, and, when ingested by cattle, initiate Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE). Thus MBM is a recognized potential source of prion transmission to cattle.

581693.long_answer: Lujan–Fryns syndrome is an X-linked intellectual-developmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the MED12 gene. MED12 is located at cytogenetic band Xq13.3 on the human X chromosome, establishing that the causative gene resides on the X chromosome.

541597.long_answer: Over 90 % of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) cases are due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The enzyme 21-hydroxylase is encoded by the CYP21A2 gene, and pathogenic variants in this gene are commonly inherited in an autosomal-recessive, compound heterozygous manner—each allele carrying a different CYP21A2 mutation that together cause the classic or non-classic CAH phenotype.

579245.long_answer: Mutations in the ABCD1 gene on the X chromosome (locus Xq28) cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. ABCD1 encodes the adrenoleukodystrophy protein (ALDP), an ATP-binding cassette peroxisomal membrane transporter responsible for importing very-long-chain fatty acids into peroxisomes. Defective ALDP impairs peroxisomal β-oxidation, leading to the characteristic neurodegenerative and adrenal manifestations of the X-linked disorder.

215065.long_answer: The enzyme-coding gene responsible for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is situated on the long arm of the human X chromosome (region Xq28). Because the G6PD gene is X-linked, males who inherit a mutant X chromosome manifest the deficiency. (By contrast, the point mutation that produces sickle cell disease lies in the β-globin gene on chromosome 11.)

740070.long_answer: Sly syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type VII) is caused by mutations in the GUSB gene that encodes the lysosomal enzyme β-glucuronidase; the human GUSB gene is located on chromosome 7 (region 7q11).

474276.long_answer: Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the cathepsin C (CTSC) gene. The CTSC gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 11 at band q14, so chromosome 11 carries the gene responsible for this syndrome.

168281.long_answer: The non-photosensitive (non–UV-sensitive) form of trichothiodystrophy, designated ‘trichothiodystrophy non-photosensitive 1’, is caused by pathogenic variants in the TTDN1 gene (also known as MPLKIP/C7orf11). Mutations in TTDN1 differentiate this congenital/birth-defect variant of TTD from the photosensitive forms that involve DNA-repair genes such as ERCC2 (XPD) or ERCC3 (XPB).

679648.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type 0 results from loss-of-function mutations in the liver glycogen synthase gene, GYS2. Cytogenetic mapping places GYS2 at 12p12.2 on the short arm of chromosome 12; therefore, the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 12.

117663.long_answer: A missense or other pathogenic mutation in the ACADM gene abolishes the activity of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD). MCAD is the mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first step of β-oxidation for medium-chain fatty acids and acts only on fatty acyl groups bound to coenzyme A. Loss of ACADM function therefore produces MCAD deficiency, the classic disorder of fatty-acid oxidation that manifests with fasting-induced hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.

317285.long_answer: The EYA1 gene, located on human chromosome 8q13.3, is frequently mutated in branchio-oto-renal (BOR) syndrome. BOR-associated renal anomalies commonly include multicystic dysplastic kidney. Thus, mutations in EYA1 on chromosome 8 are a known genetic cause of multicystic dysplastic kidney.

193347.long_answer: Malignant hyperthermia is most frequently caused by pathogenic variants in the RYR1 gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel. Mutations in RYR1 lead to excessive sarcoplasmic Ca²⁺ release when patients are exposed to triggering anesthetics or succinylcholine, producing the hypermetabolic crisis characteristic of the disorder. Over 60-70 % of genetically confirmed malignant hyperthermia cases harbor RYR1 mutations, making this gene the primary target for preventive genetic testing.

433325.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ATR (ataxia-telangiectasia and Rad3-related) gene cause Seckel syndrome type 1. Seckel syndrome presents with severe microcephaly and proportionate primordial dwarfism—core clinical features that closely resemble those seen in Microcephalic primordial dwarfism, Montreal type—making the ATR mutation the established genetic change linked to a disorder with overlapping symptoms.

951434.long_answer: A genetic defect in the lactase enzyme (β-galactosidase), which normally splits lactose into glucose and galactose in the small-intestinal brush border, prevents proper lactose digestion. Undigested lactose reaches the colon, causing osmotic diarrhea, bloating, and gas—clinical features collectively termed lactose intolerance, the characteristic sugar-malabsorption disorder arising from lactase deficiency.

192756.long_answer: Proconvertin is coagulation factor VII, encoded by the F7 gene. The F7 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 13 at band q34, so chromosome 13 contains the gene that produces proconvertin.

354506.long_answer: The inborn error of GABA degradation most often encountered is succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency. Mutations in the ALDH5A1 gene, which encodes this enzyme, cause the disorder. ALDH5A1 is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 6 (6p22.3), so chromosome 6 contains the gene whose defect leads to the enzymatic block in the GABA catabolic pathway.

239420.long_answer: An autosomal-dominant, early-onset form of Alzheimer disease (AD4) was first traced to several large ‘Volga German’ families. The condition is produced by pathogenic mutations in the PSEN2 (presenilin-2) gene—most famously the N141I substitution—establishing PSEN2 mutation as the causal genetic defect described in these German families.

188450.long_answer: The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene—the gene in which pathogenic variants cause cystic fibrosis—is located on the long arm of chromosome 7 at position 7q31.2. It is not found on chromosome 2. This chromosomal assignment has been firmly established since the late 1980s through linkage analysis and subsequent sequencing studies, and it remains a cornerstone fact in human genetics.

602992.long_answer: Sandhoff disease, a GM2 gangliosidosis caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HEXB gene encoding the β-subunit of β-hexosaminidase, has been explored for substrate-reduction therapy. Miglustat (N-butyl-deoxynojirimycin), an iminosugar that inhibits glucosylceramide synthase and thereby lowers glycosphingolipid accumulation, has been administered in pre-clinical models and compassionate-use/clinical studies of Sandhoff patients to slow neurologic deterioration.

625417.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the DCAF17 gene (formerly C2orf37) cause Woodhouse-Sakati syndrome, an autosomal-recessive disorder whose name begins with “W.” The syndrome’s core clinical features include progressive diffuse hair thinning/alopecia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, along with other endocrine and neurological manifestations, firmly linking DCAF17 mutations to this presentation.

284265.long_answer: Huntington’s disease results from a CAG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the HTT (huntingtin) gene, which is located on the short arm (4p16.3) of human chromosome 4.

509913.long_answer: Folliculitis decalvans is a chronic neutrophilic cicatricial alopecia in which cultures of pustules and crusted lesions almost invariably grow Staphylococcus aureus. The frequent isolation of this bacterium and clinical improvement with antistaphylococcal antibiotics support its key role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

660967.long_answer: Miyoshi myopathy (also called Miyoshi distal myopathy) is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the DYSF gene, which encodes dysferlin. The DYSF gene is located on chromosome 2p13—not on chromosome 4.  Rarer Miyoshi-like phenotypes can be produced by mutations in other genes such as ANO5 (chromosome 11p14.3) and CAV3 (chromosome 3p25), but none of the currently recognized genes responsible for Miyoshi myopathy reside on chromosome 4.  Therefore, the assertion that the chromosomal locus of the gene involved in Miyoshi myopathy is on chromosome 4 is not supported by established genetic evidence.

613416.long_answer: A well-known genetic cause of aplasia cutis congenita is the telomeric deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p16.3), responsible for Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome. This 4p deletion disrupts genes critical for craniofacial and skin development, and affected infants characteristically present with midline scalp defects (aplasia cutis) along with the syndrome’s facial and developmental features.

645534.long_answer: Missense mutations in the FGFR2 (fibroblast growth factor receptor-2) gene are the classic cause of syndromic craniosynostosis disorders such as Crouzon and Apert syndromes, in which the cranial sutures fuse prematurely during development, leading to early closure of skull bones.

465459.long_answer: In urticarial vasculitis, the patient shows wheal-like, ‘urticarial’ plaques that persist for longer than ordinary urticaria. Biopsy of these fixed lesions reveals a leukocytoclastic small-vessel vasculitis rather than the dermal edema of simple urticaria, hence the name urticarial vasculitis.

679596.long_answer: The X-linked recessive form of cutis laxa is produced by mutations in genes (e.g., ATP7A) that lie on the X chromosome; all X-linked recessive disorders, by definition, involve genes located on this chromosome.

719682.long_answer: The hormone follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) binds to FSH receptors on Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules. This activation drives Sertoli-cell proliferation and supplies the trophic support required for spermatogenesis, making Sertoli cells the primary testicular cells stimulated by FSH.

815484.long_answer: Cystinosis is caused by mutations in the CTNS gene, which encodes the lysosomal cystine transporter cystinosin. The CTNS gene is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 17 at band 17p13, so chromosome 17 is the locus responsible for cystinosis.

182767.long_answer: Benign familial neonatal seizures (BFNS) have been linked to a paracentric inversion on chromosome 20q13 that disrupts the KC​NQ2 potassium-channel gene. This inversion at 20q13.3 was the first cytogenetic abnormality identified in BFNS families and established chromosome 20 as the critical locus for the disorder.

301765.long_answer: Neurofibromatosis type II is produced by pathogenic mutations in the NF2 tumor-suppressor gene, located at band q12 on chromosome 22. Many disease-causing variants occur in intronic regions, disrupting normal splicing and expression of the NF2 gene product (merlin), which underlies the development of schwannomas, meningiomas and other NF2 manifestations.

397249.long_answer: Alpha-thalassemia results from deletions or mutations of the two tandem α-globin genes, HBA1 and HBA2, which are located on the short arm of human chromosome 16 (region 16p13.3). Defective expression of these chromosome 16 genes reduces α-globin chain production, producing the characteristic alpha-thalassemia phenotypes.

144315.long_answer: Hemophilia A is the most common hereditary blood-clotting (coagulation) disorder. It is caused by mutations in the factor VIII gene (F8), which is located at band q28 of the human X chromosome. Thus, the gene responsible for the disorder resides on the X chromosome.

232372.long_answer: Acute intermittent porphyria—classified among the porphyrias, a group of blood/heme disorders—arises when activity of the heme-biosynthetic enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase (also called hydroxymethylbilane synthase) is diminished or inhibited. This enzymatic block leads to accumulation of neurotoxic precursors and can produce severe neuro-psychiatric symptoms. Quetiapine is one of the atypical antipsychotics considered safe and effective for treating these psychiatric manifestations in patients with acute intermittent porphyria.

772297.long_answer: Most patients who develop a syrinx do so because of a Chiari type I malformation, in which herniation of the cerebellar tonsils obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow at the foramen magnum. This CSF blockage creates hydrodynamic pressure waves that enlarge the central canal, forming a syringomyelia cavity. Decompression of the Chiari malformation is therefore the neurosurgical procedure most often performed to treat syringomyelia.

996336.long_answer: Worth syndrome (endosteal hyperostosis) is produced by gain-of-function mutations in the LRP5 gene. LRP5 is located at cytogenetic band 11q13.4 on human chromosome 11; alterations at this locus elevate Wnt signaling in osteoblasts, leading to the markedly increased bone density that characterizes the disorder.

985589.long_answer: The disorder is xeroderma pigmentosum (XP). OMIM entry 278700 describes XP, a recessive condition in which mutations in genes of the nucleotide-excision repair pathway greatly reduce the ability to repair ultraviolet-induced DNA damage, causing extreme sun sensitivity and a high incidence of skin cancers.

724842.long_answer: Mutations in the CENPJ gene, which encodes a centrosomal protein necessary for centriole formation and overall centrosome function, cause a form of Seckel syndrome. The CENPJ gene is situated on the long arm of human chromosome 13 (13q12.2), making chromosome 13 the chromosomal location relevant to this Seckel-syndrome-associated, centrosome-related gene.

272408.long_answer: ANCA-associated vasculitis is defined by the presence of circulating anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) that bind specific neutrophil granule antigens—primarily proteinase-3 (PR3) or myeloperoxidase (MPO). These antibodies drive a pauci-immune, necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that includes granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

270623.long_answer: The lymphoma in question is mantle-cell lymphoma, which arises from naïve B-cells that occupy the mantle zone (the concentric collar of small lymphocytes surrounding the germinal center) of a lymphatic nodule. Castleman disease shows prominent expansion of this same mantle zone and can be a benign lymphoproliferative process, highlighting the anatomic relationship.

356431.long_answer: The first gene shown to confer risk for Tourette syndrome is SLITRK1, identified through a chromosomal inversion and mutation screening in affected families. SLITRK1 is situated at cytogenetic band 13q31 on human chromosome 13, so the Tourette-associated gene resides on chromosome 13.

282773.long_answer: Obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) has been documented as a comorbid psychiatric condition in both pica and Kleine–Levin syndrome (KLS). Pica is sometimes viewed as part of the OCD spectrum because the repetitive, non-nutritive eating behavior is often driven by intrusive urges and relieved by the act of ingestion. Likewise, clinical reports of KLS describe patients who, between or during hypersomnolent episodes, exhibit pronounced obsessive thoughts and compulsive rituals characteristic of OCD. Therefore, OCD is the mental disorder that can co-occur with both pica and Kleine–Levin syndrome.

351286.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the KIF7 gene cause acrocallosal syndrome. This ciliopathy is classically characterized by agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum together with pre- or postaxial polydactyly, macrocephaly, and developmental delay. KIF7 encodes a kinesin that regulates Sonic Hedgehog signaling during embryonic brain and limb development, explaining the concurrence of callosal and digit malformations.

884972.long_answer: The rheumatic disease that chiefly targets the spinal column—ankylosing spondylitis—is strongly linked to the HLA-B27 allele and other MHC class I genes. All of these immune-related genes lie within the major histocompatibility complex on the short arm of chromosome 6 (6p21), making chromosome 6 the locus that harbors the key genetic determinants of this upper-spinal rheumatic condition.

282544.long_answer: In the Mediterranean region, inherited hemoglobinopathies such as β-thalassemia and other chronic hemolytic anemias are common in children. These disorders produce persistent anemia and increased erythropoietic drive, which stimulate secondary (reactive) thrombocythemia. Consequently, pediatric patients from Mediterranean countries frequently present with hemolytic anemia and thalassemia as underlying causes of elevated platelet counts.

884019.long_answer: The disorder with multiple enchondromas and cavernous hemangiomas is Maffucci syndrome. Over 70–80 % of affected individuals harbor post-zygotic, mosaic missense mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase genes IDH1 (most often p.R132C/H) or, less commonly, IDH2 (p.R172S/G). These gain-of-function mutations lead to accumulation of the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, driving the abnormal cartilage and vascular tumors characteristic of the syndrome.

714560.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the ACAT1 gene, which encodes mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA (β-ketothiolase), cause β-ketothiolase deficiency. This inborn error of isoleucine and ketone-body catabolism leads to recurrent severe ketoacidotic attacks; during these episodes patients often develop neurologic signs such as seizures/convulsions because of the profound metabolic acidosis and accumulation of organic acids.

301165.long_answer: Many genetic birth-defect syndromes arise from a single mutated gene or chromosomal abnormality that has pleiotropic effects—i.e., it simultaneously disturbs the development of several different organs or tissues. This ‘one gene, many phenotypes’ property explains why affected individuals often present with multiple, seemingly unrelated congenital anomalies characteristic of the syndrome.

775049.long_answer: The most common form of ovarian cancer is high-grade serous carcinoma, and virtually all of these tumors harbor mutations in the TP53 tumor-suppressor gene. The human TP53 gene is located on chromosome 17 (region 17p13), so chromosome 17 contains the gene most directly linked to the predominant type of ovarian cancer.

636556.long_answer: Topical corticosteroids are first-line anti-inflammatory treatments for atopic dermatitis, but chronic or excessive use can inhibit collagen synthesis and reduce dermal matrix production, producing cutaneous atrophy—clinically recognized as skin thinning.

380316.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the MYH3 gene, which encodes embryonic myosin heavy chain 3, cause distal arthrogryposis type 2A (Freeman-Sheldon syndrome). This disorder combines multiple congenital limb contractures (arthrogryposis) with marked craniofacial abnormalities such as microstomia, puckered lips (“whistling face”), and a small chin, establishing MYH3 mutation as the genetic basis of an arthrogryposis form that involves craniofacial anomalies.

660270.long_answer: Somatic activating mutations in the PIK3CA gene underlie the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS). This spectrum includes Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome, CLOVES syndrome, macrodactyly, and other segmental overgrowth disorders. The mutant PIK3CA hyper-activates the PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling pathway, driving abnormal vascular and tissue overgrowth characteristic of these conditions.

753900.long_answer: The most common congenital foot abnormality that produces a pigeon-toed (in-toeing) appearance is metatarsus adductus. This deformity is produced by medial deviation of the forefoot at the tarsometatarsal joints, involving the metatarsal bones, which angle inward toward the midline while the hind-foot remains neutral.

549581.long_answer: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) most commonly results from inactivating mutations in the CASR gene, which encodes the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid and renal tubular cells. Loss-of-function CASR mutations raise the set-point for calcium sensing, leading to lifelong mild hypercalcemia with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion—the hallmark of FHH.

279274.long_answer: Primary ciliary dyskinesia can result from mutations in the NME8 gene, also known as TXNDC3 because it encodes thioredoxin domain-containing protein 3. The NME8/TXNDC3 gene is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 7 (region 7p14.1), so chromosome 7 harbours the gene in question.

646559.long_answer: Infantile free sialic acid storage disease (also called infantile sialic acid storage disease or Salla disease) is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the SLC17A5 gene, which encodes the lysosomal membrane sialic-acid transporter (sialin). The SLC17A5 gene is located on chromosome 6 (region 6q14-q15), not on chromosome 20. Therefore, chromosome 20 does not contain the gene responsible for this disorder.

496504.long_answer: The first family reported with Metaphyseal dysostosis-intellectual disability-conductive deafness syndrome consisted of two affected siblings whose clinically normal parents both came from the same small village in northern Flanders, Belgium. This shared Belgian origin was highlighted in the original description of the syndrome.

499476.long_answer: The key gene historically named AML1 (now RUNX1), whose mutations and translocations are tightly linked to acute myeloid leukemia, is located at band q22 of human chromosome 21.

713571.long_answer: The muscle that extends the big toe (extensor hallucis longus) is innervated by the deep fibular (peroneal) nerve, a branch of the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve. The sciatic nerve arises from the sacral plexus (roots L4–S3). Thus, the sacral plexus is the nerve plexus that provides the motor innervation enabling extension of the hallux.

681898.long_answer: Truncating mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes type II collagen, cause spondyloperipheral dysplasia. This skeletal dysplasia presents with marked platyspondyly (flattened vertebral bodies) together with brachydactyly (shortened digits), establishing COL2A1 mutation as the underlying genetic defect.

786341.long_answer: Succinate – a key intermediate of the citric (tricarboxylic) acid cycle – acts as an extracellular signalling molecule that binds to and activates the G-protein-coupled succinate receptor-1, SUCNR1 (also known as GPR91). Disruption of the SUCNR1 locus in X-chromosome rearrangements has been reported in families with X-linked intellectual disability, linking this receptor to the disorder. Hence, the receptor activated by the citric-acid-cycle compound and associated with X-linked intellectual disability is SUCNR1 (GPR91).

743964.long_answer: Mutations responsible for Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency are detected by amplifying the CPT2 gene with PCR and performing direct DNA sequencing (e.g., Sanger sequencing or next-generation sequence analysis). Sequencing reveals single-nucleotide substitutions, small insertions, or deletions across the CPT2 coding region and splice sites, enabling definitive identification of pathogenic variants.

647155.long_answer: A point mutation (classically A8344G) in the mitochondrial MT-TK gene, which encodes tRNA-Lys, causes the syndrome MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibers). This multisystem mitochondrial disorder is characteristically marked by stimulus-sensitive myoclonic seizures, along with ataxia and myopathy, linking the MT-TK mutation directly to a disease whose core symptom is myoclonic epilepsy.

838359.long_answer: Human cytomegalovirus (HHV-5) is a well-known cause of CMV interstitial pneumonitis/pneumonia in immunocompromised or transplanted patients. The infection produces diffuse inflammation in the lung parenchyma, targeting the alveolar walls and epithelial cells. Thus, the lung structure chiefly affected by this HHV-5–associated disease is the pulmonary alveoli.

645252.short_answer: Acrocyanosis is symptom-free; peripheral cyanosis shows dyspnea
645252.long_answer: In acrocyanosis the bluish discoloration of hands and feet occurs without accompanying systemic symptoms—patients are not short of breath and feel otherwise well. Peripheral cyanosis, by contrast, reflects systemic arterial desaturation or poor circulation and therefore is typically accompanied by hypoxic symptoms such as breathlessness (dyspnea), tachypnea or other signs of cardiorespiratory distress.

257050.long_answer: Trish Cook is the author of the young-adult novel "Midnight Sun," whose teenage protagonist, Katie Price, has xeroderma pigmentosum (XP). XP is a rare inherited defect in nucleotide-excision DNA repair that makes skin cells unable to repair UV-induced damage, so affected individuals must avoid sunlight—an essential element of the book’s plot.

601556.long_answer: Mutations in the MMP20 gene, which encodes the enamel protease enamelysin responsible for degrading enamel matrix proteins during the secretory stage of amelogenesis, cause an autosomal-recessive form of amelogenesis imperfecta. The human MMP20 gene is located on chromosome 11q22.3, so chromosome 11 is the chromosome whose alteration can lead to this enamel defect.

318525.long_answer: Pfeiffer syndrome is an autosomal-dominant craniosynostosis disorder produced by activating mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor genes FGFR1 or FGFR2.
