Premature fusion of cranial sutures creates shallow orbits, leading to marked ocular proptosis (exophthalmos), along with the characteristic broad thumbs and great toes seen in this condition.

227338.long_answer: Sonoda syndrome was originally reported by Dr. Yoshimasa Sonoda in patients from Kagoshima Prefecture in southern Japan; the first clinical description appeared in observations of several unrelated children from that prefecture, establishing the eponymous syndrome.

291423.long_answer: Leiner’s disease, a rare disorder presenting in early infancy with severe generalized seborrheic dermatitis, diarrhoea and recurrent systemic infections, has been linked to a hereditary deficiency of complement component C5. Absence or marked reduction of C5 impairs the formation of the membrane-attack complex and opsonisation, predisposing affected infants to widespread cutaneous inflammation and serious infections.

394493.long_answer: Staphylococcus species (e.g., S. aureus, S. saprophyticus) can ascend the urethra, causing urethritis and other urinary-tract infections. Because the urethra is a component of the urinary and reproductive tracts, such infections involve and can compromise the genitourinary system as a whole.

769075.long_answer: Paralytic strabismus arises when the motor supply to the extra-ocular muscles is impaired. These muscles are innervated by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III), trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV), and abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI); damage to any of these three nerves can therefore produce a paralytic deviation of the eyes.

167282.long_answer: The congenital limb-reduction pattern now called femur-fibula-ulna (FFU) syndrome was first described as a distinct clinical entity by Daentl and co-workers in 1970, when they reported infants showing the characteristic simultaneous hypoplasia or absence of the femur, fibula and ulna. Their publication introduced and defined the syndrome in the medical literature.

583887.long_answer: Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 48 (SPG48) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the AP5Z1 gene, which encodes the ζ-subunit of the adaptor protein complex-5 (AP-5). Defective AP5Z1 impairs endosomal membrane trafficking, leading to axonal degeneration characteristic of SPG48.

362476.long_answer: Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome presents with craniosynostosis together with cerebriform (gyrate) thickening of the skin. All confirmed cases harbor recurrent activating missense mutations (e.g., Ser372Cys, Tyr375Cys) in the FGFR2 gene, which encodes fibroblast growth factor receptor 2. The gain-of-function alterations in FGFR2 disrupt normal signaling during cranial suture and skin development, leading to premature suture fusion (craniosynostosis) and the characteristic cutis gyrata.

105644.long_answer: In several families with autosomal-dominant benign familial neonatal seizures (also called benign familial neonatal convulsions), the disorder segregates with a paracentric inversion of human chromosome 5 [inv(5)(p15q11-q13)]. This chromosomal rearrangement alters a locus required for normal neonatal neuronal excitability, producing the transient seizure phenotype.

789857.long_answer: In Bell's palsy, paralysis of the facial nerve can prevent complete eyelid closure, leading to corneal exposure, dryness, and keratitis. The medical specialty that evaluates and manages these eye-related complications—including lubricating therapy, protective measures, and possible surgical interventions—is ophthalmology.

534344.long_answer: Mutations in the CDMP1 gene—also known as GDF5, encoding cartilage-derived morphogenetic protein-1—cause Grebe-type chondrodysplasia, a skeletal dysplasia marked by severely shortened and malformed bones of the arms and legs. Loss-of-function variants disrupt BMP signaling crucial for limb skeletal patterning, leading to the characteristic limb malformations.

830206.long_answer: Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome is an X-linked syndromic intellectual-disability disorder that has been shown to result from loss-of-function mutations in the CUL4B gene on Xq24. Pathogenic variants in CUL4B, which encodes the cullin-4B scaffold of an E3 ubiquitin-ligase complex, were identified in multiple families originally described with the Smith–Fineman–Myers phenotype, establishing CUL4B mutation as the molecular cause of the syndrome.

527185.long_answer: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) results from mutations in the ABCD1 gene on the X chromosome. The defect lowers peroxisomal long-chain fatty acyl-CoA synthetase/transport activity, so very-long-chain fatty acids cannot be efficiently converted to their CoA esters and β-oxidised. Accumulation of these fatty acids in the adrenal cortex and central white matter produces the characteristic neurologic and adrenal manifestations of the disorder.

861512.long_answer: The commonest form, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type 1, results from inactivating mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor (CASR) gene, which is located on chromosome 3q (region 3q21–3q24). Hence chromosome 3 is the chromosomal locus classically associated with this disorder.

525335.long_answer: Paget disease of bone is a metabolic bone disorder that is common in people of European descent but very uncommon in individuals of African ancestry in the United States. The principal susceptibility gene linked to this disease is SQSTM1 (sequestosome-1), which is located at cytogenetic band 5q35. Thus, the relevant human chromosome harboring the gene is chromosome 5.

723309.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the CC2D2A gene, which encodes a ciliary transition-zone protein and is well known for causing Meckel syndrome type 6 and Joubert syndrome type 9, have also been documented to produce a clinical picture of syndromic microphthalmia (designated MCOPS6 in OMIM). Thus, CC2D2A mutations link the ciliopathy spectrum of Meckel/Joubert syndromes with syndromic microphthalmia.

571244.long_answer: Vascular dementia is a frequent neuro-psychiatric disorder that can follow cerebellar degeneration produced by repeated or focal cerebrovascular insults. Ischaemic or haemorrhagic injury to the brain’s blood vessels, including those supplying the cerebellum, leads to neuronal loss and atrophy; the resulting multi-infarct damage manifests clinically as cognitive decline and behavioural or psychiatric symptoms that define vascular dementia.

332612.long_answer: Neutrophil elastase proteolytically cleaves and thereby inactivates the serpin antithrombin. The gene that encodes neutrophil elastase (ELANE, formerly ELA2) is located on human chromosome 19 (19p13.3), making chromosome 19 the chromosomal site of the enzyme that can inactivate antithrombin.

206180.long_answer: Juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN3 disease/Batten disease) is primarily caused by pathogenic variants in the CLN3 gene. The CLN3 gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 16 (16p12.1), making chromosome 16 the chromosome most commonly associated with this neurodegenerative disorder.

911035.long_answer: Isolated autosomal-recessive woolly hair is most commonly produced by loss-of-function mutations in the LIPH (lipase H) gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 3 (3q27). Hence, the responsible gene resides on chromosome 3.

331454.long_answer: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I results from a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase, encoded by the IDUA gene. The human IDUA gene is located on chromosome 4 at band 4p16.3; hence, chromosome 4 carries the gene whose loss of function causes this disorder.

825263.long_answer: Across multiple large cohorts, synovial sarcoma patients who harbour the canonical SS18-SSX1 or SS18-SSX2 fusion have an aggregate five-year overall survival of roughly 60 %. Detailed analyses show ~40 % for the SS18-SSX1 subtype and ~70 % for SS18-SSX2, but when the two fusion types are considered together—as is typical in clinical summaries—the accepted five-year survival rate converges on about sixty percent.

521595.long_answer: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency results from loss-of-function mutations in the carnitine transporter gene SLC22A5 (also called OCTN2). SLC22A5 is mapped to cytogenetic region 5q31 on human chromosome 5, so chromosome 5 harbors the gene responsible for the disorder.

960936.long_answer: Systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone are frequently prescribed to control the inflammatory and eosinophilic manifestations of Kimura’s disease. Because prednisone is a potent glucocorticoid, chronic or high-dose use can produce iatrogenic Cushing syndrome—the form of Cushing syndrome that results from prolonged exposure to exogenous glucocorticoids.

525529.long_answer: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) is the mitochondrial urea-cycle enzyme that catalyzes the first step—combining ammonia, CO₂ and ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate. A deficiency of CPS-I blocks this reaction, preventing conversion of toxic ammonia into urea and producing the disorder termed carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency with severe hyperammonemia.

288105.long_answer: The 18th-dynasty pharaoh Akhenaten (Amenhotep IV) has been proposed by medical historians to have had homocystinuria, an inborn error of methionine metabolism. Homocystinuria leads to excessive urinary excretion of homocysteine and produces a tall, slender, Marfanoid body habitus with ocular findings such as severe myopia—traits that some scholars believe are reflected in Amarna-period depictions of Akhenaten’s physique.

663611.long_answer: Huntington’s disease is caused by expansion of CAG repeats in the HTT (huntingtin) gene, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 4 at band p16.3.

875028.long_answer: Sandhoff disease results from mutations in the HEXB gene, which encodes the common β-subunit of β-hexosaminidases A and B. The HEXB gene is located on human chromosome 5 (region 5q13.3); therefore, chromosome 5 carries the defect that causes the combined deficiency of these enzymes in Sandhoff disease.

141340.long_answer: The LDL receptor (LDLR) gene, whose mutations produce familial hypercholesterolemia, is located at 19p13.2 on chromosome 19. The same chromosome also harbors genes such as INSR (insulin receptor) that are implicated in diabetes, linking chromosome 19 to both conditions.

887476.long_answer: Mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes the α1 chain of type II collagen, cause achondrogenesis type II (Langer-Saldino form). Because COL2A1 produces the major cartilage-specific collagen, its defects place this lethal skeletal dysplasia within the spectrum of type II collagen disorders.

694103.long_answer: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the APRT gene. The APRT gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 16 (cytogenetic band 16q24.3), so chromosome 16 carries the gene responsible for this hereditary metabolic disorder.

180324.long_answer: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) arises from mutations in either TSC1 or TSC2. Clinical studies consistently show that mutations in TSC2 produce an earlier onset and more severe neurological and systemic manifestations than TSC1 mutations. The TSC2 gene is located on chromosome 16p13.3, so chromosome 16 carries the gene whose disruption is linked to the more severe form of the disorder.

176116.long_answer: Camurati–Engelmann disease is caused by activating mutations in the TGFB1 (transforming growth factor-β1) gene. TGFB1 is located on the long arm of chromosome 19 (19q13.1-q13.3), establishing chromosome 19 as the chromosomal site implicated in this skeletal dysplasia.

682210.long_answer: Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC25A20 gene, which encodes the mitochondrial carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase. The SLC25A20 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 3p21 on human chromosome 3, so the disorder-causing gene resides on chromosome 3.

429372.long_answer: The Jackson Laboratory, located in Bar Harbor, Maine, is the research institute that successfully isolated the ALMS1 gene responsible for the rare genetic disorder Alström syndrome. This laboratory is internationally recognized for mouse genetics and human genomics research, and its Maine campus was the site where the Alström syndrome gene was identified.

173482.long_answer: Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD) frequently results from loss-of-function mutations in the IFN-γ receptor 1 gene (IFNGR1). The IFNGR1 locus is situated at band 6q23.3 on human chromosome 6; mutations here impair IFN-γ signalling, compromising macrophage activation and conferring the characteristic vulnerability to weakly virulent mycobacteria.

216295.long_answer: Dentin dysplasia type II is produced by mutations in the DSPP (dentin sialophosphoprotein) gene, which is located on chromosome 4 at band q21.3. Thus, the causative gene mutation resides on chromosome 4.

595125.long_answer: Familial eosinophilia has been genetically mapped to the 5q31–q33 region of chromosome 5, which harbours the cytokine gene cluster encoding IL-3, IL-5 and GM-CSF. Overexpression of these cytokines can drive marked eosinophilia, and rearrangements involving this chromosomal region (e.g., t(5;14) bringing IL-3 next to T-cell receptor genes) are also seen in certain T-cell lymphomas with eosinophilia, linking chromosome 5 to both familial eosinophilia and lymphoma development.

417993.long_answer: Bazex–Dupré–Christol syndrome is an X-linked dominantly inherited disorder. The causal gene, ACTRT1, maps to the long arm of the X chromosome in the Xq24–q25 region.

329497.long_answer: The most common inherited disorder of lipid metabolism affecting skeletal muscle is carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT II) deficiency. The CPT2 gene, which encodes the CPT II enzyme, is mapped to chromosome 1 (band 1p32). Hence, chromosome 1 contains the gene responsible for this enzyme.

260137.long_answer: Autosomal-dominant congenital cataract-microcornea syndrome has been mapped to missense mutations in the CRYAA gene, which encodes the αA-crystallin lens protein. Families carrying the R116H or similar CRYAA mutations present with bilateral congenital cataracts and marked microcornea while showing no facial or systemic dysmorphic features, establishing CRYAA mutation as the cause of this specific clinical picture.

235158.long_answer: White sponge nevus is produced by pathogenic variants in the keratin genes KRT4 and KRT13. KRT4 maps to chromosome 12q13, while KRT13 maps to chromosome 17q21. Hence, the responsible genes reside on human chromosomes 12 and 17.

865040.long_answer: Chédiak–Higashi syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LYST gene (Lysosomal Trafficking Regulator, also called CHS1). The LYST gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 1 (band 1q42.1–q42.2), not on chromosome 7. Therefore, human chromosome 7 does not contain the gene responsible for Chédiak–Higashi syndrome.

144935.long_answer: Haim–Munk syndrome is produced by autosomal-recessive mutations in the CTSC gene, which encodes the lysosomal protease cathepsin C. Genetic mapping and sequencing studies have placed CTSC on the long arm of human chromosome 11 (region 11q14-q15). Thus, chromosome 11 carries the gene whose defects cause Haim–Munk syndrome.

572239.long_answer: Mutations in the SPTLC1 gene, which encodes a subunit of serine-palmitoyltransferase—the key enzyme initiating sphingolipid biosynthesis—cause the HSAN I subtype known as HSN1A. These missense mutations alter enzyme specificity, leading to accumulation of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids and the sensory–autonomic neuropathy phenotype.

780208.long_answer: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is produced by inactivating mutations in the CASR gene, which encodes the calcium-sensing receptor. Loss-of-function of this receptor makes parathyroid and renal tubular cells less sensitive to extracellular calcium, so higher serum calcium levels are required to suppress parathyroid hormone secretion and limit renal reabsorption, leading to persistent hypercalcemia.

570627.long_answer: Mutations in the PAX3 gene cause Waardenburg syndrome types 1 and 3, a congenital disorder characterized by sensorineural hearing loss along with pigmentary abnormalities of the hair, skin, and eyes. The presence of congenital hearing loss is a hallmark clinical feature linking PAX3 to this syndromic condition.

658049.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the FOXC2 gene (encoding the forkhead box C2 transcription factor) cause lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome. A cardinal feature of this condition is distichiasis, the presence of a second row of eyelashes arising from Meibomian glands. FOXC2 is therefore the gene classically associated with the skin/ocular finding of a double row of eyelashes.

695018.long_answer: Cavernous sinus thrombosis usually originates from a septic infection of the face, nose, or paranasal sinuses. The same bacteria can track along venous channels into the cranial cavity, spreading beyond the cavernous sinus to the meninges. This intracranial spread can precipitate acute bacterial meningitis, an aggressive and potentially fatal inflammation of the leptomeninges, making meningitis the key life-threatening complication of the infection that causes cavernous sinus thrombosis.

382117.long_answer: Congenital hypothyroidism is one of the most common and completely preventable causes of intellectual disability. Newborns lacking thyroid hormone develop lethargy, feeding difficulties, and metabolic slowing; without early thyroxine replacement this progresses to failure to thrive and permanent cognitive impairment. Routine neonatal screening and prompt treatment avert both growth failure and intellectual disability.

904579.long_answer: Type 2 Congenital Generalized Lipodystrophy is caused by pathogenic variants in the BSCL2 (seipin) gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 11 (11q12-11q13).

718992.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the OTX2 homeobox gene, a key regulator of early anterior neural plate development, can abolish formation of the prosencephalon. Homozygous or severe loss-of-function mutations have been reported to produce the lethal malformation termed aprosencephaly (from Greek a- ‘without’ + prosencephalon ‘embryonic forebrain’), in which the forebrain fails to form. Thus, OTX2 mutation is a recognized genetic cause of the condition whose name literally means ‘without embryonic forebrain’.

586060.long_answer: In infants with a cleft palate, the oral and nasal cavities are not fully separated, making it hard to generate the negative pressure needed for effective sucking. Milk or food therefore pools in the oropharynx and can reflux into the nasal cavity or airway, predisposing the infant to aspiration of feeds. Repeated aspiration of these oral contents is a well-recognized cause of aspiration pneumonia, making feeding difficulties one of the most common and clinically important complications of cleft palate.

533435.long_answer: Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) is a strong mitogen for fibroblasts, endothelial cells and other mesenchymal-derived cells. By driving cell proliferation and extracellular-matrix production, PDGF promotes tissue hyperplasia. In the conjunctiva, PDGF-induced fibroblast proliferation contributes to the papillary and epithelial hyperplasia that characterises disorders such as vernal keratoconjunctivitis.

499862.long_answer: The rare autosomal-recessive syndrome ‘veno-occlusive disease with immunodeficiency’ (VODI) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SP110 gene, which encodes the SP110 nuclear body protein. Defective SP110 disrupts immune regulation and hepatic sinusoidal endothelial integrity, leading to the hereditary form of hepatic veno-occlusive disease.

465442.long_answer: The RUNX1 (also termed AML1) gene, whose disruption in the t(8;21)(q22;q22) translocation is a hallmark of acute myeloid leukemia, is located on human chromosome 21 at band 21q22.

211003.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked OFD1 gene cause Orofaciodigital syndrome type 1, a disorder marked by congenital malformations of the face (hypertelorism, cleft lip), the oral cavity (lobulated or cleft tongue, oral frenula), and the digits (polydactyly, brachydactyly, syndactyly).

211816.long_answer: Tay-Sachs disease presents in early infancy with progressive neuro-degeneration, including tremors and myoclonic jerks. The disorder is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme β-hexosaminidase A, leading to accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons and consequent neurologic symptoms.

141889.long_answer: Mutations in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7, are well established as the cause of inherited primary erythromelalgia—a rare vascular pain syndrome marked by episodic redness, warmth, and severe burning pain in the limbs. Gain-of-function SCN9A variants increase NaV1.7 channel activity, heightening nociceptor excitability and producing the characteristic extremity vasodilation and intense pain.

438791.long_answer: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is a chronic keratinization disorder that produces well-demarcated, reddish-orange (salmon-colored) scaly patches and thickened skin on the palms and soles. Although most cases are sporadic, certain forms (notably Type V) are inherited in an autosomal-dominant pattern due to pathogenic variants in the CARD14 gene, so the disease can run in families.

387280.long_answer: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 6 is caused by mutations in the RARS2 gene, which encodes the mitochondrial arginyl-tRNA synthetase required for mitochondrial protein synthesis and respiratory-chain function. The RARS2 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 6 (band 6q22.1), making chromosome 6 the chromosome that carries this mitochondrial-function gene associated with pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

177267.long_answer: Chorea acanthocytosis is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the VPS13A (also called CHAC) gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 9q21 on human chromosome 9. Therefore, the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 9.

234536.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome is caused by mutations in the NBN (NBS1) gene. Cytogenetic mapping places NBN at 8q21.3 on human chromosome 8, establishing chromosome 8 as the location of the disease-causing gene.

950274.long_answer: In malonic aciduria, deficiency of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase causes intracellular accumulation of malonyl-CoA. Malonyl-CoA is a well-established allosteric inhibitor of the mitochondrial outer-membrane enzyme carnitine palmitoyl-transferase I (CPT I), which controls entry of long-chain acyl-CoA into mitochondria for β-oxidation. Thus, the fatty-acid-oxidation enzyme inhibited by the accumulating molecule is CPT I.

860302.long_answer: Alpha thalassemia results from deletions or mutations in the duplicated alpha-globin genes (HBA1 and HBA2), both of which are clustered on the short arm of chromosome 16 (16p13.3). Defects in these genes reduce or abolish alpha-globin chain production, producing the clinical spectrum of alpha thalassemia.

972520.long_answer: Variants in the STOX1 gene, which is located on chromosome 10q22, have been shown to segregate with familial cases of pre-eclampsia and increase disease risk. This chromosomal location is therefore specifically associated with a genetic influence on the development of pre-eclampsia.

811710.long_answer: Werner syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the WRN gene, which encodes a RecQ family DNA helicase involved in genome stability. The WRN gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 8 (band 8p12); its mutation leads to premature aging features and a markedly increased risk of multiple cancers.

743400.long_answer: The protein AF9, encoded by the MLLT3 gene, physically interacts with the corepressor BCOR and is a well-known fusion partner of KMT2A in the t(9;11)(p22;q23) translocation that drives acute myeloid leukemia. The MLLT3 gene is located on human chromosome 9 (band 9p22), so chromosome 9 is the chromosome that contains this gene.

868401.long_answer: Benign hereditary chorea is most often produced by pathogenic variants in the NKX2-1 (thyroid transcription factor-1) gene, which has been mapped to the 14q13 region. This places the causative gene on human chromosome 14.

919924.long_answer: Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are concentrically layered basophilic inclusions found within enlarged foamy macrophages called von Hansemann cells. These macrophages are the hallmark of malakoplakia, a chronic granulomatous condition that can manifest clinically as an ulcerative lesion. Identification of von Hansemann cells containing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies is therefore diagnostic for this disease.

613756.long_answer: Mutations in the PHOX2B gene (most often poly-alanine repeat expansions) cause congenital central hypoventilation syndrome. The same hypoventilation syndrome can also be acquired after severe brainstem trauma or other neurologic injury, linking PHOX2B mutation to a condition that may likewise appear following serious brain injury.

313181.long_answer: Triple-A (Allgrove) syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AAAS gene, which encodes the nuclear-pore protein ALADIN. Cytogenetic mapping places the AAAS gene at 12q13, meaning it resides on human chromosome 12.

304450.long_answer: MKRN3 (Makorin RING finger protein 3) is located in the Prader-Willi critical region on chromosome 15q11-q13, inherited from the paternal allele. Loss-of-function variants in MKRN3 are a well-established genetic cause of familial and sporadic central precocious puberty. It is therefore not situated on chromosome 16, so the statement is incorrect.

944919.long_answer: For therapeutic bone-marrow transplantation, marrow is most commonly harvested from the posterior iliac crest of the pelvis. This site provides a large, easily accessible volume of marrow with minimal morbidity, making it the standard donor site for treating conditions such as Myhre syndrome that may benefit from marrow-derived stem-cell therapy.

584405.long_answer: A pathogenic variant in the TSC2 gene (encoding tuberin) causes tuberous sclerosis complex. Brain and systemic MRI is the standard imaging test used to identify the cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and other characteristic lesions that establish and monitor the diagnosis of this disease.

533330.long_answer: Primary infection with influenza virus damages the respiratory epithelium and impairs mucociliary clearance, creating an environment in which Streptococcus pneumoniae can more easily colonize the lower airways. This viral-induced disruption of host defenses is a well-documented predisposing factor for secondary bacterial pneumonia caused by S. pneumoniae.

985249.long_answer: Conditions that acutely affect the dominant temporal lobe—most famously herpes simplex encephalitis, which presents with severe confusion and delirium—often damage the posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area). Lesions here produce a fluent-receptive language deficit called Wernicke’s aphasia, so the same pathological process that causes delirium can simultaneously lead to this specific type of aphasia.

487470.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the MYH9 gene, encoding non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA, cause MYH9-related disorders such as May-Hegglin anomaly. These conditions are typified by macrothrombocytopenia with markedly giant platelets, making MYH9 mutation a well-established genetic cause of a giant platelet disorder.

854354.long_answer: Absent pulmonary valve syndrome frequently occurs in patients with the 22q11.2 microdeletion (the same deletion seen in DiGeorge/velocardio-facial syndrome). Thus, the pathogenic microdeletion is on human chromosome 22.

115626.long_answer: Feingold syndrome type 1 is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the MYCN gene, which is located on chromosome 2p24.1. A smaller subset of cases (type 2) result from deletions encompassing the MIR17HG micro-RNA cluster on chromosome 13q31.3. No form of Feingold syndrome has been linked to a gene on chromosome 3. Therefore, the statement that the gene responsible for Feingold syndrome is located on chromosome 3 is incorrect.

414384.long_answer: Paroxysmal nonkinesigenic dyskinesia (PNKD) is caused by pathogenic variants in the PNKD gene (also called MR-1). Cytogenetic mapping places PNKD at 2q31, so the responsible gene is located on human chromosome 2. Clonazepam is frequently used to reduce the frequency and severity of PNKD attacks, linking the clinical treatment to the chromosome-2–encoded gene.

851720.long_answer: Hand–foot–genital syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HOXA13 homeobox gene. The entire HOXA gene cluster, including HOXA13, is located on the short arm of human chromosome 7 (region 7p15.2). Thus, chromosome 7 is the chromosome that carries the gene responsible for this syndrome.

168466.long_answer: Marek’s disease virus is an alphaherpesvirus of chickens. The closely related human alphaherpesvirus is Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), which has historically been implicated in the etiology of cervical cancer. Thus, HSV-2 is the virus that links cervical cancer risk with a virus related to Marek’s disease virus.

575606.long_answer: The skeletal disorder with severe dwarfism and the pathognomonic lace-like pattern of bone (Dyggve-Melchior-Clausen/Smith-McCort dysplasia) is produced by mutations in the DYM gene, which is located on human chromosome 18q21. Thus, chromosome 18 carries the gene responsible for this radiographically distinctive disease.

767378.long_answer: Aromatase deficiency is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CYP19A1 gene, which encodes the aromatase enzyme responsible for converting androgens to estrogens. The CYP19A1 gene is located on chromosome 15 (region 15q21.2); therefore, mutations on chromosome 15 can lead to aromatase deficiency.

378601.long_answer: The CRLF1 gene, which encodes cytokine receptor-like factor 1, maps to the short arm of human chromosome 19 (cytogenetic band 19p13).

908521.long_answer: Mutation of the LDL receptor (LDLR) gene causes familial hypercholesterolaemia, a disorder characterised by markedly elevated LDL cholesterol and a greatly increased risk of premature myocardial infarction. Myocardial infarction can be recognised biochemically by the classic “flipped pattern” of lactate dehydrogenase isoenzymes (LDH-1 > LDH-2). Thus the gene mutation linked to the condition diagnosed with this LDH pattern is in the LDLR gene.

463448.long_answer: Farber lipogranulomatosis presents as a granulomatous panniculitis rich in histiocytes. It results from an inherited deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid ceramidase (ASAH1), causing ceramide to accumulate in macrophages/histiocytes and produce the characteristic subcutaneous nodules.

604990.long_answer: In urea-cycle disorders the liver cannot convert ammonia to urea, so plasma ammonia rises (hyperammonemia). Persistently high ammonia drives skeletal-muscle proteolysis—muscle tissue converts amino-nitrogen into glutamine to help clear ammonia—so chronic hyperammonemia both characterizes the disorder and leads to progressive muscle loss.

377776.long_answer: Acalculous cholecystitis frequently arises in critically ill patients; extensive thermal (severe) burns are a classic precipitating factor because the associated hypovolemia and gallbladder ischemia lead to inflammation without gallstones. Thus, the same severe burn injury that causes cutaneous burns can also precipitate cholecystitis.

527361.long_answer: The cluster of findings—ichthyosis together with intellectual disability, growth retardation (dwarfism), and renal dysfunction—occurs in the X-p22.3 contiguous-gene deletion syndrome; because the causal genes lie on the X chromosome, the condition is transmitted in an X-linked recessive manner, affecting almost exclusively hemizygous males while female carriers are usually asymptomatic or mildly affected.

486789.long_answer: Mutations in the FERMT1 gene (also called KIND1) cause Kindler syndrome, an autosomal-recessive disorder characterised by acral, fluid-filled skin blisters in infancy and progressive poikiloderma. Because kindlin-1 is required for integrin-mediated adhesion in intestinal as well as epidermal epithelium, patients frequently develop gastrointestinal involvement such as colitis, strictures or bleeding. Thus, a FERMT1 mutation links the combination of gastrointestinal disease and cutaneous blistering.

111593.long_answer: Gingival (mucosal) bleeding is a classic manifestation of von Willebrand disease, which results from quantitative or qualitative deficiency of the von Willebrand factor. The von Willebrand factor gene (VWF) is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 12 (12p13.3); mutations in this gene are responsible for the deficiency and the associated bleeding tendency.

952246.long_answer: Activating germ-line mutations in the RET proto-oncogene cause Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B, a syndrome characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, and a marfanoid body habitus. RET encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase; constitutive activation drives the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma while also producing the connective-tissue and skeletal features that give the Marfanoid appearance.

458318.long_answer: Pathogenic mutations in the MECP2 gene cause Rett syndrome, a well-characterized neurodevelopmental disorder. Affected individuals initially have normal early development, then regress and develop motor impairment, intellectual disability, stereotypic hand movements, and progressive neuromuscular signs. Spasticity and hypertonia are common clinical features of Rett syndrome, directly linking MECP2 mutations to neurodevelopmental disease accompanied by spasticity.

518694.long_answer: Autosomal-dominant hereditary gingival fibromatosis is most often caused by heterozygous mutations in the SOS1 gene (Son-of-Sevenless homolog 1). SOS1 encodes a RAS guanine-nucleotide exchange factor; gain-of-function variants heighten RAS/MAPK signalling in gingival fibroblasts, driving excessive collagen deposition and the characteristic fibromatous overgrowth of the gingiva.

559000.long_answer: The BRCA1 tumour-suppressor gene, located on human chromosome 17q21, forms functional complexes with the ATM serine/threonine kinase after DNA damage. ATM phosphorylates BRCA1 and the two proteins cooperate in homologous-recombination repair of double-strand DNA breaks. Because the interacting gene (BRCA1) resides on chromosome 17, that is the chromosome containing the gene that works with ATM in double-strand break repair.

372241.long_answer: Familial isolated vitamin E deficiency (also called ataxia with vitamin E deficiency) results from loss-of-function mutations in the TTPA gene, which encodes the α-tocopherol transfer protein responsible for distributing vitamin E to tissues. The TTPA gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 8q13, meaning it resides on human chromosome 8. Therefore, chromosome 8 contains the gene whose mutation causes this disorder.

714563.long_answer: The majority of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia cases carry pathogenic variants in the COMP (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein) gene. COMP is located at cytogenetic band 19p13.11 on human chromosome 19; therefore, chromosome 19 harbors the gene most frequently mutated in this disorder.

154391.long_answer: Abetalipoproteinemia results from mutations in the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein gene (MTTP), which is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 4 (4q24). Defects in MTTP impair assembly and secretion of apolipoprotein-B–containing lipoproteins, producing the characteristic absence of plasma LDL and chylomicrons seen in the disorder.

503992.long_answer: Spondyloenchondrodysplasia is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the ACP5 gene, which encodes tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP). The ACP5 gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 19 (19p13), so chromosome 19 harbors the causative gene for this disorder.

943515.long_answer: In hypopituitarism the pituitary fails to secrete adequate ACTH, so the adrenal cortex is under-stimulated and cortisol production falls. This ACTH-deficiency state produces a form of adrenal failure that clinically resembles Addison’s disease and is therefore termed secondary Addison’s disease, or secondary adrenal insufficiency.

597619.long_answer: EEM syndrome (Ectodermal dysplasia-Ectrodactyly-Macular dystrophy) is produced by pathogenic variants in the CDH3 gene, which encodes P-cadherin. The CDH3 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 16q22.1 on human chromosome 16; therefore, this chromosome harbors the causative gene for EEM syndrome.

425704.long_answer: In infants or children whose dextro-Transposition of the great arteries is not corrected, chronic hypoxemia and ventricular pressure overload predispose the myocardium to malignant ventricular arrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation, which can precipitate sudden cardiac arrest.

724695.long_answer: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors commonly harbor inactivating mutations or loss of the DAXX gene. DAXX encodes the death-domain associated protein, first characterized for its binding to the Fas death receptor complex and its ability to modulate apoptotic signaling. Thus, DAXX is both frequently altered in PanNETs and directly involved in apoptosis regulation.

800779.long_answer: Mutations in the GIF gene, which encodes gastric intrinsic factor, abolish or greatly reduce production of intrinsic factor. Without intrinsic factor the ileum cannot take up the vitamin B12-intrinsic-factor complex, so dietary vitamin B12 is not absorbed. The ensuing cobalamin deficiency blocks the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, causing accumulation of methylmalonic acid and clinical methylmalonic acidemia.

738331.long_answer: Fatal familial insomnia is a prion disease caused by a point mutation (most commonly D178N coupled with methionine at codon 129) in the PRNP gene, which encodes the prion protein. The PRNP gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 20 (20p13), making chromosome 20 the chromosome that carries the pathogenic mutation responsible for this disorder.

982140.long_answer: Filippi syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CKAP2L gene, which is situated on the long arm of chromosome 2 (region 2q).

397427.long_answer: Hyperkalemia is defined as an elevated serum potassium concentration and is, by definition, an electrolyte imbalance. Potassium plays a critical role in establishing the resting membrane potential of cardiac myocytes. When extracellular potassium becomes markedly elevated, it impairs normal cardiac conduction, producing electrocardiographic changes such as peaked T-waves, PR-interval prolongation, QRS widening, and eventual ‘sine-wave’ morphology. Without prompt treatment, these electrophysiologic disturbances can degenerate into life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, or progress to asystole. Therefore, hyperkalemia is indeed an electrolyte imbalance capable of precipitating ventricular fibrillation.

488543.long_answer: Mutations in the FGFR2 gene cause Apert syndrome, a postnatally diagnosable craniosynostosis disorder characterized by craniofacial abnormalities and complex syndactyly of the hands and feet. Missense mutations in FGFR2 (e.g., Ser252Trp or Pro253Arg) activate the fibroblast growth-factor receptor 2, leading to premature suture fusion, facial dysmorphology, and fused digits.

203386.long_answer: Mutations—most commonly poly-alanine expansions—in the HOXD13 homeobox gene disrupt normal anterior–posterior patterning of the limb bud, producing synpolydactyly (webbing plus extra digits). Several Turkish families with this inherited limb malformation have been reported, firmly linking HOXD13 to the condition.

736288.long_answer: Most cases of osteogenesis imperfecta result from mutations in the COL1A1 gene, which encodes the α1 chain of type I collagen. COL1A1 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 17 (17q21–q22). Defects in this collagen gene disrupt normal bone matrix formation, producing the brittle-bone phenotype characteristic of osteogenesis imperfecta.

972815.long_answer: Renal agenesis has been linked to loss-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene; RET resides on the long arm of human chromosome 10 (10q11.2). Defective RET signalling blocks ureteric-bud outgrowth, causing failure of kidney formation, which establishes chromosome 10 as the chromosomal location associated with renal agenesis.

845647.long_answer: In adults the spinal cord ends at the L1–L2 vertebral level; the lumbar vertebral canal therefore contains only the lumbosacral nerve-root bundle called the cauda equina. Consequently, paraplegia arising from lesions of the lumbar vertebrae results from compression or injury of the cauda equina rather than the spinal cord itself.

569557.long_answer: In bubonic plague, Yersinia pestis bacteria spread via the lymphatic system and replicate in regional lymph nodes, causing them to become markedly swollen and tender; thus, the lymph nodes are the primary site affected.

436434.long_answer: Filter-feeding mussels readily bioaccumulate algal neurotoxins such as saxitoxin and domoic acid produced during harmful dinoflagellate or diatom blooms. When these popular delicacy shellfish are eaten by humans, the stored toxins can provoke paralytic or amnesic shellfish poisoning, making mussels a well-known source of shellfish poisoning outbreaks.

705523.long_answer: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare, progressive, fatal neurologic disease that occurs years after an initial measles infection. It results from persistent, defective measles virus in the brain and most often presents in children, adolescents, or young adults with cognitive decline, myoclonus, and progressive encephalitis.

121953.long_answer: CDG syndrome type 1t is caused by mutations in the PGM1 (phosphoglucomutase-1) gene. PGM1 is located on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (cytogenetic band 1p). Pathogenic variants in this chromosome-1 gene disrupt the interconversion of glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, reducing the supply of UDP-glucose/UDP-galactose needed for N-glycan biosynthesis and resulting in the CDG-It phenotype.

905635.long_answer: The gene most strongly linked to ankylosing spondylitis is the HLA-B gene, specifically the HLA-B27 allele. HLA-B lies in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region on the short arm of human chromosome 6 (locus 6p21.3). Carrying the HLA-B27 variant on chromosome 6 markedly increases the risk of developing ankylosing spondylitis.

942455.long_answer: Mutation of the SOD1 gene (encoding superoxide dismutase-1) is classically linked to familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a neurodegenerative disorder that produces degeneration of corticospinal (upper motor) neurons as well as lower motor neurons.

891044.long_answer: Congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (CIPA) is almost invariably caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NTRK1 gene, which encodes the high-affinity nerve growth factor (NGF) receptor TrkA. Defective TrkA signaling disrupts the survival and differentiation of nociceptive sensory neurons and sympathetic neurons controlling sweating, producing absence of pain perception and impaired sweating characteristic of the disorder.

574214.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signalling gene disrupts normal rotation and fusion of the ventral pancreatic bud during embryogenesis, producing an annular pancreas. This congenital malformation can encircle and obstruct the second part of the duodenum, leading to duodenal stenosis or complete duodenal atresia.

378001.long_answer: Alpha-mannosidosis is caused by pathogenic variants in the MAN2B1 gene, which encodes lysosomal α-mannosidase. The MAN2B1 locus is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 19 (region 19p13.2). Mutations on this chromosome disrupt lysosomal degradation of mannose-rich oligosaccharides, leading to the multisystem disorder that can include psychosis.

497392.long_answer: Missense mutations in the FLNA gene (filamin-A) on chromosome Xq28 cause Melnick-Needles syndrome, an X-linked dominant form of osteochondrodysplasia. Affected individuals show distinctive craniofacial abnormalities such as exophthalmos, micrognathia, and malar hypoplasia, fitting the described inheritance pattern and phenotype.

644924.long_answer: The STOX1 gene, located at 10q22 on human chromosome 10, acts as a transcriptional regulator that increases expression and alternative splicing of FLT1, thereby elevating soluble Flt-1 (sFLT1) levels. Elevated sFLT1 is a key pathogenic factor in pre-eclampsia, so the chromosome carrying the STOX1 gene—and hence linked to sFLT1 upregulation—is chromosome 10.

716904.long_answer: Autosomal dominant nanophthalmos has been linked to mutations in the TMEM98 gene. Cytogenetic mapping places TMEM98 at 17q11.2 on human chromosome 17, making chromosome 17 the locus for the gene responsible for the dominantly inherited form of this disorder.

237160.long_answer: The split hand/split foot malformation type 3 (SHFM3), which results from a tandem duplication of the 10q24 region, is classically transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion. Affected individuals need only one copy of the duplicated segment to manifest the disorder, although expressivity is variable and penetrance can be reduced.

148648.long_answer: Duplications involving the short arm (Xp) of the X chromosome—particularly regions such as Xp11.22–Xp11.23—are a recognized cause of X-linked intellectual disability, because they increase dosage of X-linked genes crucial for neurodevelopment.

600052.long_answer: WAGR syndrome results from a contiguous-gene deletion at 11p13 on chromosome 11 that removes the WT1 gene; loss of WT1 disrupts urogenital development, leading to the characteristic genitourinary anomalies seen in the syndrome.

969723.long_answer: Roberts syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in the ESCO2 gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 8p21.1 on human chromosome 8. Therefore, the gene responsible for Roberts syndrome is located on chromosome 8.

711731.long_answer: Type II focal facial dermal dysplasia has been shown to result from loss-of-function mutations in the TWIST2 gene. TWIST2 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q37). Thus the gene responsible for the disorder resides on chromosome 2.

144206.long_answer: Palaeopathological studies of the theropod Allosaurus (notably the specimen MOR 693, “Big Al,” of the species Allosaurus fragilis) revealed pronounced exostosis—abnormal bony overgrowth—on several proximal caudal (tail) vertebrae. This documented pathology demonstrates that the genus Allosaurus includes a species exhibiting exostosis in its tail vertebrae.

361826.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the NBN (formerly NBS1) gene, which encodes the DNA-damage–response protein nibrin. The NBN gene is located at cytogenetic band 8q21 on human chromosome 8; therefore the causative gene resides on chromosome 8.

717088.long_answer: Heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in the mechanosensitive ion-channel gene PIEZO2 cause Distal Arthrogryposis type 3 (Gordon syndrome). This syndrome is characterized clinically by congenital contractures of the hands and feet (a form of arthrogryposis) together with craniofacial anomalies such as cleft palate. The link between PIEZO2 mutations and these specific contracture-cleft palate features is now well established in human genetics literature.

864306.long_answer: The disorder ‘leprechaunism’ (Donohue syndrome), named after the mythical Irish leprechaun, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the insulin receptor gene (INSR). The INSR gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 19 (19p13.2), so the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 19.

466064.long_answer: Tyrosinemia (types I, II, and III) results from biallelic mutations in the FAH, TAT, or HPD genes, respectively. Because pathogenic variants must be present on both alleles for disease to manifest, the disorder follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

585147.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the TCOF1 gene account for the large majority of Treacher-Collins (mandibulofacial dysostosis) cases. This craniofacial syndrome is characterized by hypoplasia of the zygomatic and mandibular bones, external and middle-ear malformations, and consequent conductive hearing loss. Thus, TCOF1 is the gene most frequently linked to a craniofacial syndrome that includes hearing loss.

342020.long_answer: Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene (encoding neuropathy target esterase). PNPLA6 is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 19 (19p13.2). Mutations in this chromosome-19 gene produce the triad that includes cerebellar ataxia, establishing chromosome 19 as the chromosomal location associated with the ataxia seen in the syndrome.

255159.long_answer: The Andalusian physician–surgeon Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (Albucasis) of Córdoba, writing in the 10th–11th century in his surgical compendium ‘Al-Tasrif’, gave the earliest recorded description of children born with fused fingers or toes, identifying syndactyly as a congenital (birth) anomaly.

530744.long_answer: Feingold syndrome is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the MYCN gene. MYCN is located on the short arm of human chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2p24), so chromosome 2 carries the gene responsible for the disorder.

253624.long_answer: Gardner's syndrome is a phenotypic variant of familial adenomatous polyposis that results from germ-line mutations in the APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) tumor-suppressor gene. The human APC gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 5 at band 5q21-q22; therefore, chromosome 5 carries the gene whose mutation causes Gardner’s syndrome.

489470.long_answer: Spinocerebellar ataxia-14 (SCA14) is caused by pathogenic variants in the PRKCG gene, which encodes the γ-isoform of protein kinase C. In humans, the PRKCG gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 19 (cytogenetic band 19q13.42). Therefore, chromosome 19 is the chromosome that contains the gene associated with SCA14.

614237.long_answer: Finnish-type PEHO syndrome (Progressive Encephalopathy with Edema, Hypsarrhythmia and Optic atrophy) is caused by a founder missense mutation (c.92G>C; p.Arg31Pro) in the ZNHIT3 gene. Loss of normal ZNHIT3 function disrupts neuronal development and leads to early-onset epileptic seizures characteristic of the disorder.

443226.long_answer: Classic Refsum disease is most commonly caused by biallelic mutations in the PHYH gene, which encodes phytanoyl-CoA 2-hydroxylase. Loss of this peroxisomal enzyme leads to accumulation of phytanic acid, producing clinical features such as peripheral neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, and the cutaneous manifestation ichthyosis, a form of hyperkeratosis. Thus, a PHYH gene mutation is the defect that links Refsum disease to the hyperkeratotic skin condition.

142532.long_answer: Cross syndrome (also called Mohr-Cross or orofaciodigital syndrome type IV) was first delineated in 1973, when Cross and co-workers published the original report describing patients with the characteristic constellation of orofacial, digital and systemic anomalies that now define the disorder.

436007.long_answer: When a cerebral cavernous malformation forms in the temporal lobe—particularly in medial temporal structures such as the hippocampus—it can compress the surrounding cortical tissue. This compression irritates the seizure-generating networks of the temporal cortex, often producing recurrent, potentially dangerous epileptic seizures.

360300.long_answer: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type II (LAD-II) results from mutations in the SLC35C1 gene, which encodes the Golgi GDP-fucose transporter required for fucosylation of selectin ligands. The SLC35C1 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 11 (region 11q12-q13), so defects on chromosome 11 give rise to LAD-II.

433180.long_answer: The CPS1 gene, whose mutation causes carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I deficiency, is located on chromosome 2 (band 2q35-q37). Chromosome 2 is one of the numbered autosomes, so the disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion.

602748.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the PAX2 gene have been reported in some patients who manifest the ‘morning-glory’ optic-disc anomaly. This congenital optic-nerve malformation was first described in 1970 by the German ophthalmologist Hans-Walter Kindler, who named it after the resemblance of the excavated disc to the morning-glory flower.

812169.long_answer: Danon disease, an autophagic vacuolar myopathy transmitted in an X-linked dominant fashion, is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the LAMP2 gene. LAMP2 encodes lysosome-associated membrane protein-2; its deficiency blocks normal autophagosome–lysosome fusion, causing accumulation of autophagic vacuoles in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Hemizygous males are severely affected, while heterozygous females manifest variable disease, consistent with X-linked dominant inheritance.

821690.long_answer: 5α-Reductase 2 deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the SRD5A2 gene, which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 2 (band 2p23). Mutations in SRD5A2 impair conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, leading to undervirilization and intersex traits in affected 46,XY individuals.

801145.long_answer: Listeria monocytogenes, a Gram-positive bacterium that can lead to fulminant sepsis, neonatal meningitis, and brain-stem encephalitis, gains access to the central nervous system partly by retrograde axonal spread through the trigeminal (fifth cranial) nerve from the oropharyngeal mucosa to the brain-stem. Hence, the cranial nerve specifically associated with this bacterium’s CNS invasion is the trigeminal nerve.

719555.long_answer: A broad, web-like neck that stretches laterally to the shoulders (pterygium colli) is a classic dysmorphic feature of both Turner syndrome (45,X or variants) and Noonan syndrome (an autosomal-dominant RAS-MAPK pathway disorder). In each condition the webbed neck arises from prenatal lymphatic maldevelopment (cystic hygroma), making these two syndromes the well-established associations.

864624.long_answer: The HELLS gene (helicase, lymphoid specific; also known as LSH/SMARCA6) is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 10 (band q23.33). Pathogenic variants in HELLS on chromosome 10 cause Immunodeficiency–centromeric instability–facial anomalies (ICF) syndrome type 4, linking this chromosomal location to the disorder.

329668.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type Ib is produced by deficiency of the microsomal enzyme/transport protein glucose-6-phosphate translocase (encoded by SLC37A4). Loss of this translocase prevents transfer of glucose-6-phosphate into the endoplasmic reticulum for hydrolysis, causing the typical metabolic derangements of GSD I. Unlike type Ia, the translocase defect also impairs neutrophil function and maturation, leading to chronic neutropenia and recurrent infections that characterize this variant.

501533.long_answer: Haemochromatosis type 3 is caused by pathogenic variants in the TFR2 gene (transferrin receptor 2). The TFR2 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 7q22 on human chromosome 7, making chromosome 7 the chromosomal location associated with this form of hereditary haemochromatosis.

454005.long_answer: Epidemiologic studies report that the autosomal-recessive (infantile) form of osteopetrosis occurs in roughly 1 in 140,000–150,000 live births in Denmark, whereas estimates for the United States are on the order of 1 in 200,000–250,000 live births. Because the Danish incidence is numerically greater (i.e., a higher frequency per population), Denmark has the higher rate of osteopetrosis.

333727.long_answer: Harnaam Kaur is a British social-media personality and body-positivity activist who revealed that she was diagnosed in childhood with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is an endocrine disorder marked by excess androgen production, which frequently causes hirsutism (excess facial and body hair), along with acne, irregular periods and other metabolic or reproductive symptoms. Kaur’s PCOS-related hirsutism is the reason she famously grew and keeps her beard.

130688.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the IFT80 gene cause Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy, a skeletal ciliopathy characterized by a very narrow thorax with short, small ribs. The defective IFT80 protein disrupts intraflagellar transport in chondrocytes, impairing rib and thoracic cage growth and producing the clinically observed small ribcage and restricted chest volume.

107945.long_answer: Achondrogenesis type II (Langer-Saldino), a perinatally lethal skeletal dysplasia that often results in stillbirth, is produced by dominant mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes the α1 chain of type II collagen essential for cartilage and bone development.

960205.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene, which encodes the receptor for glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), impair ureteric-bud outgrowth. Heterozygous RET mutations can give unilateral renal agenesis, while homozygous or more severe loss can cause bilateral renal agenesis; the latter produces severe oligohydramnios and the Potter sequence.

802537.long_answer: Clinical series of girls with the 49,XXXXX (Pentasomy X) karyotype consistently report marked growth deficiency; their stature averages about four standard deviations below the population mean, reflecting pronounced short stature that is characteristic of this aneuploidy.

398937.long_answer: Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas) are treated first-line with dopamine agonists. Bromocriptine, a D2-receptor agonist, suppresses prolactin synthesis and shrinks the tumor, thereby alleviating hyperprolactinemia and preventing hypopituitarism caused by mass effect.

881484.long_answer: Parkes Weber syndrome is most often produced by pathogenic variants in the RASA1 gene (encoding p120-RasGAP). The RASA1 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 5 (5q13.3), so chromosome 5 is the chromosome that carries the gene whose mutation causes this vascular overgrowth disorder.

275032.long_answer: Injected botulinum toxin type A (commonly known as Botox) is an established therapy for reducing focal muscle spasticity in disorders such as spastic cerebral palsy, which presents with lower-limb stiffness and hypertonia similar to the spasticity seen in hereditary spastic paraplegia. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, producing temporary muscle relaxation and improving mobility.

583433.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive hyperammonemia type I is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CPS1 gene, which encodes mitochondrial carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I, the first enzyme of the urea cycle. Deficiency of this enzyme blocks the conversion of ammonia to carbamoyl phosphate, resulting in toxic accumulation of ammonia (hyperammonemia).

797678.long_answer: The syndrome is produced by pathogenic variants in the MED23 gene. MED23 is mapped to band q23.3 on the long arm of human chromosome 6, so chromosome 6 harbours the gene responsible for severe intellectual disability-progressive spastic diplegia syndrome.

324933.long_answer: Hyperlysinemia, the metabolic disorder marked by markedly elevated lysine concentrations in blood, results from loss-of-function mutations in the AASS gene. AASS encodes α-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (lysine-ketoglutarate reductase/saccharopine dehydrogenase), the first two catalytic steps of lysine degradation. Mutations that inactivate AASS block lysine catabolism, causing lysine to accumulate systemically and producing the observed biochemical phenotype.

552423.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome results from pathogenic variants in the FGFR2 gene (fibroblast growth factor receptor 2). FGFR2 is located on the long arm of chromosome 10 at band q26; thus, chromosome 10 harbors the gene whose mutation causes Crouzon syndrome.

297526.long_answer: Tricho–dento–osseous syndrome is produced by autosomal-dominant mutations in the DLX3 homeobox gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 17q21-q22. Therefore, the causative gene resides on human chromosome 17.

609244.long_answer: Pascual-Castroviejo syndrome type 1 (PCSV1) is produced by pathogenic variants in the NR2F1 gene. NR2F1 is mapped to the 5q14.3 region, meaning the responsible gene resides on chromosome 5.

575952.long_answer: Red-cell enolase deficiency in the studied Caucasian families was traced to mutations in the ENO1 (α-enolase) structural gene. Cytogenetic and linkage analyses place ENO1 on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (region 1p36), establishing chromosome 1 as the chromosomal location responsible for this enolase deficiency.

908003.long_answer: The most lethal variant of nemaline myopathy is caused by mutations in the ACTA1 gene, which encodes skeletal-muscle α-actin. Certain ACTA1 mutations produce a prenatal-onset form with absent fetal movements, profound muscle weakness, and respiratory failure at birth, leading to death in utero or shortly after delivery—rendering the condition essentially incompatible with life.

501166.long_answer: Cardiac synovial sarcoma, like its more common soft-tissue counterpart, is characterized by the balanced chromosomal translocation t(X;18)(p11;q11). This rearrangement fuses the SS18 (SYT) gene on chromosome 18 to one of the SSX genes (usually SSX1 or SSX2) on the X chromosome, creating the pathognomonic SS18-SSX fusion oncogene that drives tumorigenesis.

503263.long_answer: Hoyeraal–Hreidarsson syndrome is a severe, telomere-biology disorder and variant of dyskeratosis congenita. Pathogenic germ-line mutations that can be detected by molecular genetic testing have been documented in several telomere-maintenance genes, most commonly the X-linked DKC1 (dyskerin) gene, but also in the telomerase catalytic subunit gene TERT, the telomerase RNA component gene TERC, and the helicase gene RTEL1. These mutations impair telomerase function or telomere elongation, leading to the very short telomeres and multisystem clinical features characteristic of the syndrome.

666619.long_answer: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia is most commonly caused by mutations in the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene. The human APOE gene is located on chromosome 19 at band q13.32, so chromosome 19 is the chromosome that harbors the gene responsible for this disorder.

873325.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the LRP5 gene cause Osteoporosis-Pseudoglioma syndrome, a condition characterized by congenital ocular defects such as microphthalmia (small eyes) and early-onset severe osteoporosis with multiple fractures. The LRP5 protein is a Wnt co-receptor essential for both eye development and regulation of bone mass, so its disruption produces the combined eye–bone phenotype observed in the syndrome.

842230.long_answer: Several species of cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), such as Anabaena, Aphanizomenon and Cylindrospermopsis, biosynthesize the potent neurotoxin saxitoxin. This toxin accumulates in shellfish and, when ingested by humans, blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, producing paralytic shellfish poisoning.

167538.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the NIPBL gene are the principal cause of Cornelia de Lange syndrome. This multisystem developmental disorder is classically marked by severe prenatal growth deficiency, pronounced microcephaly, intellectual disability, and characteristic upper-limb malformations (from shortened forearms to absent digits). Thus, a mutation in NIPBL produces the syndrome that presents with both microcephaly and limb anomalies.

761614.long_answer: Expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene causes Fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited form of intellectual disability. Affected individuals typically show mild-to-moderate intellectual disability along with characteristic facial features and (in males) macro-orchidism, firmly linking FMR1 mutation to a syndrome where mild intellectual disability is a core symptom.

113679.long_answer: The RUNX1 (formerly AML1) gene, situated at band q22 on human chromosome 21, is frequently involved in chromosomal translocations such as t(8;21)(q22;q22). These abnormalities create fusion genes (e.g., RUNX1-RUNX1T1) that disrupt normal hematopoietic regulation and are a well-established cause of acute myeloid leukemia.

142402.long_answer: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) is caused by pathogenic variants in the ABCC6 gene. ABCC6 is located on the short arm of human chromosome 16 (region 16p13.1). Loss-of-function mutations in this gene lead to aberrant calcium and phosphate handling, resulting in pathological mineralization of elastic fibers that can be visualized with an electron microscope. Therefore, the responsible gene resides on chromosome 16.

437725.long_answer: Uncombable Hair Syndrome type 2 (UHS2) is caused by pathogenic variants in the TGM3 gene, which encodes transglutaminase-3. The TGM3 locus is situated on the long arm of human chromosome 20 (20q11.23). Hence, chromosome 20 carries the gene responsible for UHS2.

765103.long_answer: Mutations in the DMD gene, which encodes the dystrophin protein, cause Duchenne (and Becker) muscular dystrophy. Dystrophin is the central scaffold of the dystrophin-associated protein complex (DAPC); loss or alteration of dystrophin disrupts the entire complex, leading to the characteristic muscle degeneration seen in the disease.

385109.long_answer: Hemeralopia (day-blindness) can follow traumatic brain injury when the damage involves the occipital lobe, where the primary visual cortex that interprets photopic (cone-mediated) vision is located. Injury to this part of the brain disrupts normal cone pathway processing, leading to difficulty seeing in bright light.

894780.long_answer: Essential fructosuria is caused by deficiency of hepatic ketohexokinase (fructokinase), encoded by the KHK gene. According to the Human Genome Organization (HUGO) Gene Nomenclature Committee and multiple genomic databases (e.g., NCBI Gene, Ensembl), the KHK gene is located on chromosome 2 at cytogenetic band 2p23.3, not on chromosome 5. Therefore, the statement that chromosome 5 contains the KHK gene linked to essential fructosuria is incorrect.

746403.long_answer: Chorea-acanthocytosis is an autosomal-recessive neurodegenerative disease in which peripheral-blood smears show numerous acanthocytes. The disorder is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the VPS13A gene (also called the chorein gene), which encodes the chorein protein essential for membrane trafficking; its absence leads to the characteristic red-cell spiculated (acanthocytic) morphology.

657989.long_answer: The keratin 2e (KRT2) mutation on chromosome 12 causes superficial epidermolytic ichthyosis, historically called ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens. This disorder was first described in 1937 by the German dermatologist Hermann Werner Siemens, after whom the condition is named.

422433.long_answer: Benign fasciculation syndrome (BFS) and neuromyotonia are now viewed as different points along the same peripheral nerve hyperexcitability spectrum. Both disorders arise from spontaneous, repetitive discharges of motor axons; BFS produces isolated fasciculations without weakness, while neuromyotonia represents the more severe end with continuous muscle fiber activity (myokymia, cramps, stiffness) and can be associated with VGKC-complex antibodies. Thus, BFS is essentially the mildest clinical expression of the same pathophysiological process that, when more intense, manifests as neuromyotonia.

443190.long_answer: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis (HGF) is most often caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SOS1 gene (Son-of-Sevenless homolog 1). Pathogenic variants in SOS1 lead to constitutive activation of Ras/MAPK signaling in gingival fibroblasts, driving the excessive collagen deposition and gingival tissue overgrowth characteristic of this inherited fibromatosis.

508405.long_answer: The COL1A1 gene, located on human chromosome 17q21.33, encodes the α1 chain of type I collagen. Pathogenic variants in COL1A1 are the classic cause of osteogenesis imperfecta and have also been reported in families displaying an atypical, marfanoid phenotype that mimics features of Marfan syndrome. Thus, the chromosome harbouring the gene implicated in both osteogenesis imperfecta and atypical Marfan presentations is chromosome 17.

585875.long_answer: Deficiency of phosphoglucomutase 1 (PGM1) causes a condition now classified both as glycogen-storage disease type XIV and as a congenital disorder of glycosylation (PGM1-CDG). PGM1 catalyzes the interconversion of glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, a key step in glycogenolysis; the same reaction provides activated sugar precursors (UDP-glucose/galactose) required for protein N- and O-glycosylation. Loss of PGM1 therefore disrupts both glycogen breakdown and glycoprotein synthesis, accounting for the combined clinical phenotype.

658922.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the COL6A1 gene (encoding the α1-chain of type VI collagen) cause Bethlem myopathy. This condition often presents with finger and ankle contractures at birth; the contractures may loosen during infancy but characteristically return and progress in later childhood or adulthood. The COL6A1 defect disrupts collagen VI microfibrils in muscle and connective tissue, explaining the relapsing pattern of joint contractures.

375532.long_answer: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency results from pathogenic variants in the SERPINA1 gene. SERPINA1 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 14 (14q32.13), so chromosome 14 carries the gene whose mutations cause this hereditary disorder.

445975.long_answer: The multi-system (autosomal-recessive) form of type I pseudohypoaldosteronism, designated PHA1B, results from loss-of-function mutations in the SCNN1A gene that encodes the α-subunit of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). SCNN1A is located on human chromosome 12 at band 12p13, so chromosome 12 carries the gene responsible for the multi-system form of PHA type I.

724508.long_answer: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the transthyretin (TTR) gene. The human TTR gene is located on chromosome 18 (band 18q12.1), so the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 18.

953155.long_answer: Cardiospondylocarpofacial syndrome is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the MAP3K7 gene (encoding the kinase TAK1). The MAP3K7 locus is situated at cytogenetic band 6q15 on human chromosome 6; therefore, chromosome 6 contains the disease-causing gene.

948708.long_answer: Griscelli syndrome type 1 is an autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by moderate dilution of skin and hair pigmentation together with severe central nervous system dysfunction (developmental delay, seizures, neurodegeneration). The disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the MYO5A gene, which encodes the motor protein myosin Va that is essential for melanosome transport in melanocytes and vesicle transport in neurons. Dysfunction of MYO5A therefore produces both the hypopigmentation and the profound neurologic phenotype seen in this syndrome.

696948.long_answer: Mutations in the DMD gene, which encodes the muscle-stabilizing protein dystrophin, lead to Duchenne muscular dystrophy. This X-linked disorder causes progressive skeletal-muscle degeneration; affected boys usually lose independent ambulation by about 10–12 years of age and thereafter rely on a wheelchair for mobility.

243125.long_answer: Mutations in the HNF1A gene (hepatocyte nuclear factor-1α) cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 3 (MODY 3). This autosomal-dominant disorder impairs transcriptional regulation required for normal pancreatic β-cell function, leading to inadequate insulin production and early-onset hyperglycaemia.

154125.long_answer: The hereditary condition characterized by a double row of eyelashes (distichiasis) and limb swelling (lymphedema) is lymphedema–distichiasis syndrome. This autosomal-dominant disorder is caused by pathogenic variants in the FOXC2 gene, a forkhead family transcription factor crucial for lymphatic and eyelid follicle development. Mutations in FOXC2 disrupt lymphatic valve formation, leading to peripheral lymphedema, and alter eyelid follicle patterning, producing the extra row of lashes.

436133.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) gene. The CFTR gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 7 at position q31.2—not on chromosome 22. This chromosomal location has been firmly established since its discovery in 1989 and is consistently reported in genetic and medical literature. Therefore, the statement that the gene responsible for cystic fibrosis is on chromosome 22 is incorrect.

894462.long_answer: Mutations in the TNFRSF1A gene cause TNF-receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS), an autosomal-dominant autoinflammatory disorder marked by recurrent fevers, rash, serositis and musculoskeletal pain. Inflammatory attacks in TRAPS commonly improve with systemic corticosteroids and symptomatic NSAIDs, making TNFRSF1A mutations the canonical genetic defect linked to a condition treated by these agents.

587426.long_answer: Mutations in the PAX6 gene cause congenital aniridia, a developmental eye disorder characterized by partial or complete absence of the iris, foveal hypoplasia, and other structural defects that lead to reduced visual acuity. Thus, a PAX6 mutation is directly linked to a condition that alters the eye’s structure and impairs vision.

113343.long_answer: In healthy cells, the mitochondrial isoform of malate dehydrogenase (MDH2) occasionally ‘moonlights’: instead of catalysing the normal malate ↔ oxaloacetate reaction, it promiscuously reduces α-ketoglutarate to the on-comer metabolite L-2-hydroxyglutarate (L-2-HG). Under normal circumstances L-2-HG is rapidly reconverted to α-ketoglutarate by L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase (L2HGDH). When L2HGDH is defective, as in L-2-Hydroxyglutaric aciduria, the continual side-production of L-2-HG by mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase leads to its pathological accumulation.

946475.long_answer: Around 90 % of Treacher Collins syndrome cases are due to pathogenic variants in the TCOF1 gene, which is situated on the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q32-q33).

901378.long_answer: Mutations in the PFKM gene, which encodes the muscle isoform of the glycolytic enzyme phosphofructokinase, cause glycogen storage disease type VII (Tarui disease). Loss of phosphofructokinase activity blocks a key glycolytic step, so glucose released from glycogen cannot be effectively broken down in skeletal muscle cells, leading to exercise-induced muscle cramps and other symptoms characteristic of this glycogen storage disorder.

380049.long_answer: Pulmonary hypertension damages and remodels the pulmonary arteries and arterioles. These vessels’ chief role is to convey de-oxygenated blood pumped from the right ventricle to the lung capillary beds, where carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen; in other words, they deliver blood to the alveoli for gas exchange.

769196.long_answer: Mutations in the FGFR2 gene (fibroblast growth factor receptor 2) cause Apert syndrome, an acrocephalosyndactyly condition in which patients characteristically present with severe syndactyly of the hands and feet along with craniosynostosis. Thus, an FGFR2 mutation is classically associated with a condition that includes syndactyly.

860863.long_answer: Mutations in the SPATA7 gene, which lies on chromosome 14q31.3, cause autosomal-recessive retinal dystrophies such as Leber congenital amaurosis type 3 and early-onset retinitis pigmentosa. These disorders lead to severe visual impairment from infancy or childhood, establishing SPATA7 as the chromosome-14 gene whose mutation produces vision-loss disease.

264578.long_answer: Coagulation factor V is the closest human homologue of coagulation factor VIII; its gene (F5) resides on the long arm of chromosome 1 at 1q23. Thus, chromosome 1 contains the gene encoding the protein homologous to factor VIII.

261658.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the PKD1 gene, which encodes polycystin-1, is the commonest cause of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD). While ADPKD is best known for renal cysts, up to ~10–15 % of affected individuals also develop intracranial arachnoid (brain) cysts and other cerebrovascular complications. Thus, a PKD1 mutation produces the disease beginning with 'A' (ADPKD) that can lead to cyst formation on the brain.

351236.long_answer: Kowarski syndrome is an autosomal-recessive form of isolated growth hormone deficiency (IGHD type IB). It is produced by biallelic mutations in the GH1 gene; affected individuals carry the same pathogenic variant on both alleles (homozygosity or compound heterozygosity). Thus, the disease-causing GH1 mutation is associated with a homozygous state.

778264.long_answer: Molecular confirmation of Rosai–Dorfman disease (especially the familial/H-syndrome variant) is obtained by sequencing the SLC29A3 gene; this gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 10 (10q23).

439910.long_answer: The autonomic-nervous-system disorder treated at Sheba Medical Center is Familial Dysautonomia; it is caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the IKBKAP gene (also named ELP1), most commonly the 2507+6 T>C splice-site mutation that reduces IKAP/ELP1 protein and impairs development of autonomic and sensory neurons.

172024.long_answer: Mutations in ATP6V0A2, encoding the a2-subunit of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase, cause autosomal-recessive cutis laxa type II—a connective-tissue disorder that clinically overlaps with wrinkly skin syndrome. Defective ATP6V0A2 impairs Golgi acidification, leading to abnormal protein glycosylation and the characteristic loose, wrinkled skin and other connective-tissue manifestations shared by both conditions.

261663.long_answer: Anchoring fibrils that secure the basement membrane to underlying dermis are composed of type VII collagen. The gene encoding type VII collagen is COL7A1, which is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 3 (region 3p21.3). Hence, the chromosome harboring the gene responsible for anchoring fibrils is chromosome 3.

313748.long_answer: Marked taurine loss in urine (taurinuria) is produced by mutations in the taurine transporter gene SLC6A6. This gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 3, band p25.1, so the disorder is mapped to chromosomal locus 3p25.1.

897286.long_answer: Mutations or homozygous deletions in the SMN1 (survival motor neuron 1) gene on chromosome 5q13 cause spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), a neuromuscular disorder in which degeneration of anterior-horn motor neurons leads to severe, progressive muscle weakness and atrophy that is particularly prominent in the proximal muscles of the legs.
