712661.long_answer: The most frequent form of focal cortical dysplasia (especially type II) is produced by germ-line or somatic mutations in genes such as MTOR, PIK3CA, AKT3, TSC1/2, and DEPDC5. All of these genes converge on and dysregulate the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling cascade, leading to hyperactive mTOR activity that perturbs neuronal growth and cortical lamination. Hence, the disease-causing mutations primarily affect the mTOR signaling pathway.

939250.long_answer: Reactive arthritis shows a strong genetic association with the HLA-B27 class I major histocompatibility complex gene. Up to 70–80 % of patients carry the HLA-B27 allele, and its presence greatly increases susceptibility to this seronegative spondyloarthropathy, highlighting its central role in disease pathogenesis.

342880.long_answer: The first and principal gene identified for Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome is HPS1, which was mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 10 (region 10q23). Mutations in this chromosome-10 gene disrupt formation of lysosome-related organelles, producing the oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding diathesis and pulmonary fibrosis characteristic of the syndrome.

409824.long_answer: Homozygous deletion or other loss-of-function mutations in the SMN1 gene eliminate Survival Motor Neuron protein, producing spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). SMA is an autosomal-recessive neuromuscular disorder that typically presents in early infancy with hypotonia and progressive weakness and is now detectable by newborn screening. Thus, an SMN1 mutation is the causative genetic defect diagnosed in affected infants.

690265.long_answer: Mutations in the FMO3 gene impair the hepatic enzyme flavin-containing mono-oxygenase 3. The resulting enzymatic deficiency prevents conversion of trimethylamine to its odorless N-oxide, causing trimethylaminuria (‘fish-odor syndrome’) characterized by markedly increased body odor.

754382.long_answer: Osteoprotegerin (OPG, TNFRSF11B) is a soluble member of the TNF receptor superfamily that regulates bone remodeling by acting as a decoy receptor for RANKL. Its C-terminal region contains two death-domain-like motifs; these homologous ‘death domains’ mediate disulfide-linked homodimer formation of OPG, a structural feature essential for its high-affinity binding to RANKL and inhibition of osteoclast differentiation.

721109.long_answer: Mutations in the BTD gene (encoding biotinidase) cause biotinidase deficiency. This inherited disorder impairs recycling of the vitamin biotin, leading to neurological features such as seizures and hypotonia. Because the underlying problem is biotin shortage, lifelong oral biotin supplementation effectively treats the condition and prevents further neurologic decline.

552977.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the LDLR (low-density lipoprotein receptor) gene cause familial hypercholesterolaemia. The defective receptor leads to markedly elevated LDL-cholesterol, rapid atherosclerotic plaque development in coronary arteries, and therefore a greatly increased risk of premature myocardial infarction.

218124.long_answer: The combined disorder of infantile convulsions and paroxysmal kinesigenic choreoathetosis (ICCA syndrome) maps to a locus on chromosome 16 (16p11–q12); mutations in the PRRT2 gene within this region are responsible for the phenotype, establishing chromosome 16 as the chromosomal site associated with the disorder.

542759.long_answer: WAGR syndrome results from a contiguous-gene deletion in the 11p13 region of chromosome 11, removing genes such as WT1 and PAX6. Loss of these genes produces the characteristic features of Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and intellectual disability.

886038.long_answer: Hereditary angio-oedema, an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations in the SERPING1 (C1 inhibitor) gene on chromosome 11, is well known to have attacks precipitated by hormonal changes such as those that occur at ovulation. Thus, the chromosome associated with this ovulation-triggered disorder is chromosome 11.

529150.long_answer: Schmitt–Gillenwater–Kelly (hand-foot-genital) syndrome is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the HOXA13 gene. HOXA13 is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 7, band 7p15.2; alterations here lead to the characteristic limb abnormalities and urogenital defects such as hypospadias.

957915.long_answer: Marked hypersecretion of cortisol, as occurs in Cushing syndrome, can saturate and overwhelm renal 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (the enzyme that normally inactivates cortisol to cortisone). The unmetabolized cortisol then binds and activates mineralocorticoid receptors, producing low-renin hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis with suppressed aldosterone—clinical findings that closely mimic apparent mineralocorticoid excess syndrome.

677482.long_answer: Mutations in the PHEX gene, which is located on the X chromosome (Xp22.1), lead to X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets/osteomalacia. Because only one altered copy of the gene on the X chromosome is sufficient to produce the phenotype in both males and females, the disorder follows an X-linked dominant pattern of inheritance (affected fathers transmit the mutation to all daughters and no sons; affected mothers have a 50% risk of passing it to each child).

242984.long_answer: Adenosine monophosphate deaminase deficiency type 1 results from pathogenic variants in the AMPD1 gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle isoform of AMP deaminase. Cytogenetic mapping places AMPD1 at 1p13.2, establishing that the responsible gene resides on human chromosome 1.

768455.long_answer: Hereditary lactate dehydrogenase-A (LDH-A) deficiency—also called glycogen storage disease type XI—is caused by pathogenic mutations in the LDHA gene. A characteristic diagnostic test is a muscle biopsy with histochemical staining showing markedly reduced or absent lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity in muscle fibers, confirming the enzyme deficiency due to the LDHA mutation.

250625.long_answer: The classic gene first shown to cause Walker-Warburg syndrome is POMT1 (protein-O-mannosyltransferase 1), which is mapped to cytogenetic band 9q34 on human chromosome 9. Mutations in this chromosome-9 gene disrupt α-dystroglycan glycosylation, producing the characteristic brain, eye, and muscular defects of Walker-Warburg syndrome.

518632.long_answer: A condition that produces no noticeable signs or symptoms is described as “asymptomatic.” Growth-hormone deficiency can remain asymptomatic for long periods, with affected individuals showing no outward clinical manifestations despite underlying hormonal insufficiency.

430023.long_answer: The SDHAF1 gene, whose product is essential for the assembly of succinate dehydrogenase (mitochondrial complex II), is mutated in cases of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial complex II deficiency. SDHAF1 is situated on the long arm of chromosome 19 (19q13.12), making chromosome 19 the correct chromosomal location.

818437.long_answer: Steatocystoma multiplex presents as multiple subcutaneous cyst-like nodules. It is commonly linked to pathogenic variants in the keratin 17 gene (KRT17). Histopathology confirms the diagnosis by showing a thin squamous epithelium lacking a granular layer with adjacent sebaceous lobules, and definitive management options include total surgical excision or liposuction of the cysts. Therefore, the KRT17 mutation is the gene alteration frequently associated with this condition.

273645.long_answer: Chudley–Mccullough syndrome results from recessive mutations in the GPSM2 gene (G-protein signaling modulator 2). The GPSM2 locus is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 1, at band p13 (1p13.3). Thus, the gene associated with this syndrome is located on chromosome 1.

765834.long_answer: Granulomatous dermatitis seen in Blau syndrome is produced by gain-of-function mutations in the NOD2 (also called CARD15) gene, which encodes an intracellular pattern-recognition receptor. Constitutive activation of NOD2 drives NF-κB–mediated inflammatory pathways, leading to non-caseating granulomatous inflammation in skin, joints and eyes.

459782.long_answer: Crohn’s disease is a chronic, but benign, inflammatory bowel disorder whose transmural inflammation and subsequent fibrosis and scarring can form mass-like strictures that are easily mistaken for intestinal carcinoma. The condition shows a strong genetic association with loss-of-function mutations in the NOD2 (also called CARD15) gene, which encodes an intracellular pattern-recognition receptor important for bacterial sensing in innate immunity.

473470.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ALDH4A1 gene, which encodes Δ¹-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase (P5CDH), block the second step of proline catabolism. This defect causes hyperprolinemia type II, a congenital amino-acid–metabolism disorder characterized by markedly elevated plasma proline concentrations and accumulation of the intermediate P5C. Clinical manifestations often include seizures and variable intellectual disability, linking ALDH4A1 mutations directly to the described phenotype.

499780.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the KCNJ5 gene, which encodes the inward-rectifier potassium channel GIRK4, cause familial hyperaldosteronism type III. These mutations depolarize adrenal zona glomerulosa cells, drive excess aldosterone secretion, and clinically produce hyperaldosteronism with hypertension and hypokalemia.

520341.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome is produced by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the NBN (NBS1) gene, which encodes the DNA-repair protein nibrin. Cytogenetic and physical mapping place the NBN gene at band 8q21.3, meaning it resides on human chromosome 8. Therefore, chromosome 8 carries the gene responsible for this chromosomal-instability disorder.

269737.long_answer: Papillorenal (renal-coloboma) syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the PAX2 gene. PAX2 is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 10 (10q24-q25), so the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 10.

792521.long_answer: Chronic lithium therapy, used to treat mood disorders in the central nervous system, is a well-recognized risk factor for primary hyperparathyroidism because lithium alters the set-point of the calcium-sensing receptor, leading to parathyroid hyperplasia and excess parathyroid hormone secretion.

823024.long_answer: The nuclear gene most frequently implicated in Leigh syndrome is SURF1, which encodes a protein essential for cytochrome-c-oxidase (complex IV) assembly. SURF1 is located at cytogenetic band 9q34 on human chromosome 9; pathogenic variants in this locus account for the largest proportion of nuclear-encoded causes of Leigh syndrome.

334300.long_answer: Mutations in the RYR1 gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle ryanodine-receptor calcium-release channel, are a recognised cause of some forms of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita. The same mutations disrupt excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle, producing RYR1-related congenital myopathies such as central-core or multiminicore disease, in which muscle fibres cannot contract normally and therefore do not function properly.

826816.long_answer: Mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1, cause Marfan syndrome. This connective-tissue disorder commonly leads to spinal deformities, including scoliosis and thoracolumbar kyphosis, because weakened ligaments and supporting tissues allow abnormal curvature of the spine.

981001.long_answer: Costello syndrome is caused by activating mutations in the HRAS proto-oncogene. HRAS is located at cytogenetic band 11p15.5 on human chromosome 11; therefore, chromosome 11 harbors the gene responsible for Costello syndrome.

873704.long_answer: Mutations in the BTD gene, which encodes the enzyme biotinidase, cause biotinidase deficiency. Without functional biotinidase, free biotin cannot be released and recycled, leading to markedly reduced activity of all biotin-dependent carboxylases. Oral biotin supplementation bypasses the recycling defect and restores enzyme function, making the disorder effectively treatable with biotin.

772922.long_answer: Investigators at Great Ormond Street Hospital for Sick Children (London) examined myocardial specimens from infants with endocardial fibro-elastosis and demonstrated enteroviral (notably coxsackie-B) particles and high antiviral titres, thereby reinforcing that intra-uterine or early post-natal viral infection is a principal cause of endocardial fibroelastosis.

630524.long_answer: In mitral valve prolapse, the redundant or myxomatous valve leaflets and elongated chordae can prevent proper coaptation during systole, allowing blood to flow backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium. This complication—mitral regurgitation—is common and, when moderate to severe, increases ventricular volume load, progressive left-ventricular dilation, and ultimately heart failure.

615934.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ABCB4 gene, which encodes the canalicular phosphatidylcholine floppase MDR3, cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 3 (PFIC-3). PFIC-3 usually becomes clinically apparent in early childhood, when impaired phosphatidylcholine secretion renders bile acids toxic to the biliary epithelium, leading to cholestasis, high GGT, and progressive liver fibrosis.

180790.long_answer: Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome results from mutations in the DHCR7 gene (encoding 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase). The DHCR7 gene is located on human chromosome 11 (band 11q13.4), so chromosome 11 carries the causative gene for this disorder.

505334.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the X-linked FLNA gene, which encodes the actin-binding cytoskeletal protein filamin A, cause an inherited form of chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction. Mutations disrupt cytoskeletal organization in intestinal smooth muscle and enteric neurons, leading to severe, obstructive-type motility failure without mechanical blockage.

218184.long_answer: Collins–Pope syndrome derives its name from the British clinicians Collins and Pope, who published the initial description of the syndrome in a report on an affected family. Because that first report originated from their work in Britain, the syndrome was first described in the United Kingdom.

991799.long_answer: Congenital (transient) hyperinsulinism can be triggered by perinatal asphyxia—oxygen deprivation during labor or delivery. Hypoxic-ischemic stress damages pancreatic β-cell regulation, provoking excessive insulin secretion and resulting neonatal hypoglycaemia characteristic of congenital hyperinsulinism.

849991.long_answer: Young-Simpson syndrome (Ohdo syndrome, Young-Simpson type) is consistently linked to heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the KAT6B gene, which encodes lysine acetyltransferase 6B. Disruption of KAT6B alters histone acetylation and downstream gene expression, producing the characteristic craniofacial anomalies, intellectual disability, and congenital malformations that define this disorder.

729602.long_answer: The constellation of aplasia cutis congenita together with intestinal lymphangiectasia-induced generalized edema typifies Hennekam lymphangiectasia–lymphedema syndrome type 1. This syndrome is caused by loss-of-function variants in the CCBE1 gene, which is located at cytogenetic band 18q21.32; hence, chromosome 18 is the chromosome associated with this disorder.

421282.long_answer: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is an autosomal-recessive form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). The causative ADA gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 20 (locus 20q13.12). Mutations in this chromosome-20 gene impair ADA enzyme activity, leading to toxic accumulation of deoxyadenosine and resulting immunodeficiency in affected infants.

562716.long_answer: Arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARC) syndrome is an autosomal-recessive genodermatosis caused by loss-of-function mutations in the VPS33B gene, which encodes a protein essential for intracellular vesicle trafficking; defective VPS33B disrupts epithelial cell polarity and leads to the characteristic multisystem features of ARC.

846261.long_answer: Congenital dysfibrinogenemia often results from small insertions or deletions in one of the fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, or FGG). When these indels are not in multiples of three nucleotides, they shift the codon reading frame— a classic frameshift mutation— producing an aberrant fibrinogen polypeptide that impairs clot formation.

442505.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the OAT gene, which encodes the mitochondrial enzyme ornithine aminotransferase, abolish normal ornithine catabolism. The resulting enzyme deficiency causes hyper-ornithinemia (gyrate atrophy), a disorder characterized by large systemic accumulation of ornithine in blood and tissues.

504746.long_answer: Nance-Horan syndrome presents with dense congenital nuclear cataracts accompanied by characteristic dental abnormalities such as screwdriver-shaped incisors and supernumerary teeth. This X-linked disorder is consistently produced by loss-of-function mutations in the NHS gene, which encodes the Nance-Horan syndrome protein involved in eye and tooth development. Identification of pathogenic variants in NHS confirms the molecular basis of the syndrome.

751353.long_answer: During normal foregut development, paired tracheoesophageal folds fuse in the midline to form the tracheoesophageal septum, separating the ventral laryngotracheal tube from the dorsal esophagus. If this septum forms incorrectly or deviates, the trachea and esophagus are not completely separated, producing a tracheoesophageal fistula and often leaving the proximal esophagus blind-ending (esophageal atresia). Thus, maldevelopment of the tracheoesophageal septum is the embryological defect underlying these anomalies.

671422.long_answer: Haemochromatosis type 3 is caused by pathogenic variants in the TFR2 gene (transferrin receptor 2). The TFR2 gene is mapped to human chromosome 7q22, so the disease-causing gene for haemochromatosis type 3 resides on chromosome 7.

873111.long_answer: Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the FKTN (fukutin) gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 9 (region 9q31). This chromosomal location underlies the defective glycosylation of α-dystroglycan that impairs muscle integrity and brain development in the disorder.

749515.long_answer: Cryptorchidism-arachnodactyly-intellectual disability syndrome is classified by Orphanet as an ultra-rare disorder, with an estimated prevalence of fewer than 1 affected individual per 1,000,000 people; only a handful of cases have been reported in the medical literature.

335388.long_answer: Jansen’s metaphyseal chondrodysplasia is produced by activating mutations in the parathyroid hormone 1 receptor gene (PTH1R). The human PTH1R gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 3 (region 3p21-p22). Therefore, chromosome 3 carries the gene responsible for this disorder.

356779.long_answer: Sjögren–Larsson syndrome results from deficiency of the enzyme fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase (FALDH), encoded by the ALDH3A2 gene. This gene is located on chromosome 17p11.2, so mutations on chromosome 17 that disrupt FALDH activity underlie the clinical features of the syndrome.

699475.long_answer: Severe aortic stenosis is a frequent structural heart disease found in patients who suffer sudden cardiac arrest. The high-shear turbulence across the narrowed valve destroys large von Willebrand factor multimers, producing an acquired vWF deficiency that predisposes to bleeding from intestinal angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome). Consequently, the same underlying aortic stenosis that can lead to cardiac arrest can also manifest as gastrointestinal bleeding.

193891.long_answer: Early-onset parkinsonism-intellectual disability syndrome is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the RAB39B gene, which is mapped to band Xq28. Because RAB39B lies on the X chromosome, this chromosome carries the gene responsible for the disorder.

264662.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ABCB4 gene (encoding the canalicular phosphatidylcholine floppase MDR3) cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 3. Because little or no phosphatidylcholine is secreted into bile, the bile becomes detergent-rich, injuring the biliary epithelium and producing chronic cholangitis—an inflammatory condition of the bile ducts.

287615.long_answer: The F10 gene, located at 13q34 on human chromosome 13, encodes coagulation factor X. In the extrinsic clotting pathway, the tissue-factor–factor VIIa complex proteolytically activates factor X to factor Xa, initiating downstream thrombin generation. Hence, the chromosome carrying the gene for the protein activated by factor VIIa is chromosome 13.

657519.long_answer: Foreign accent syndrome is a rare speech disorder in which changes in prosody, timing and articulation after brain injury or other neurological insult make a person’s speech sound as though it carries a foreign accent. Although sometimes misclassified as a psychiatric issue, it is actually a well-documented neurogenic condition that alters the motor planning of speech, leading listeners to perceive a new accent.

712846.long_answer: Boils (furuncles) are deep skin infections of hair follicles most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Because these lesions are localized to the skin and can require incision-and-drainage, culture, and targeted antibiotic therapy, the specialist who routinely diagnoses and manages such cutaneous infections is a dermatologist.

133099.long_answer: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the PIGA (phosphatidylinositol glycan class A) gene. PIGA is located on the X chromosome (region Xp22), so this chromosome carries the gene whose mutation causes the disease.

740204.long_answer: In fetuses with congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), the development of hydrops fetalis signals severe intrathoracic mass effect and cardiovascular compromise. Published perinatal outcome series show that once hydrops is present, approximately 85–100 % of affected fetuses die, leaving a survival rate of no more than about 15 % despite supportive care. This contrasts sharply with the >90 % survival seen when hydrops is absent.

158591.long_answer: Lafora progressive myoclonus epilepsy (Lafora disease) is classically caused by loss-of-function mutations in the EPM2A gene, which encodes the dual-specificity phosphatase laforin. Absence of functional laforin impairs glycogen dephosphorylation, leading to intracellular accumulation of insoluble polyglucosan inclusions (Lafora bodies) that trigger the characteristic myoclonic epilepsy.

362952.long_answer: Most cases of medullary thyroid cancer are driven by activating mutations in the RET proto-oncogene, which is mapped to chromosome 10 (band 10q11.2). Germline RET mutations underlie MEN2-associated medullary thyroid carcinoma, and somatic RET mutations are common in sporadic cases, firmly linking chromosome 10 to the disease.

197455.long_answer: Australian paediatric pathologist Ralph Douglas Kenneth (R. D. K.) Reye published the first description of a congenital myopathy marked by rod-shaped ("nemaline") inclusions within skeletal-muscle fibres in the early 1960s. This distinctive histopathologic finding led to recognition of the condition that was subsequently named nemaline myopathy.

134812.long_answer: The majority of malignant hyperthermia cases are linked to pathogenic variants in the RYR1 gene (encoding the skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptor). RYR1 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 19 (19q13.2), making chromosome 19 the chromosome most commonly associated with malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.

527629.long_answer: Old analog CRT televisions refreshed the whole screen sequentially at 50–60 Hz, producing a large-area flicker in the most seizure-provoking frequency range for photosensitive epilepsy. Modern digital LCD/LED sets keep each pixel continuously lit and refresh at much higher effective rates (100 Hz+), eliminating the low-frequency, high-contrast flicker that triggers cortical hyper-synchronization. Without that 50–60 Hz raster flicker, digital TVs are far less likely to induce seizures.

889638.long_answer: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune exocrinopathy in which lymphocytic infiltration damages moisture-producing glands throughout the body. Besides the classic dry eyes and dry mouth, it often causes vaginal mucosal dryness due to reduced secretions from Bartholin’s and other glands. Persistent vaginal dryness can lead to irritation and neuropathic pain of the vulvar tissues, precipitating or exacerbating vulvodynia.

509340.long_answer: The FMR1 gene, located on the X chromosome at Xq27.3, is mutated in Fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. Expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats in FMR1 silences the gene, leading to loss of the FMRP protein and consequent cognitive impairment.

921140.long_answer: Alveolar soft part sarcoma is characterized by the recurrent translocation t(X;17)(p11;q25), which fuses the ASPSCR1 (formerly ASPL) gene on chromosome 17q25 to the TFE3 gene on chromosome Xp11.2. The resulting ASPSCR1-TFE3 fusion protein acts as an aberrant transcription factor that drives tumor development, making chromosomes X and 17 the two chromosomes involved in this oncogenic rearrangement.

806402.long_answer: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin are given by intravenous (IV) injection/infusion. If the IV line infiltrates and the drug extravasates into surrounding tissues, these agents act as potent vesicants, producing severe local inflammation and tissue necrosis.

773262.long_answer: Borrelia burgdorferi-sensu-lato spirochetes, the causative agents of Lyme disease, maintain their enzootic cycle primarily in hard ticks of the genus Ixodes. Species such as Ixodes scapularis in North America and Ixodes ricinus in Europe acquire the bacteria from infected vertebrate hosts and transmit them during subsequent blood meals, making Ixodes ticks the principal reservoir and vector for Lyme disease pathogens.

783566.long_answer: Maternal serum screening for abdominal wall defects (e.g., gastroschisis, omphalocele) measures the fetal protein alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). The AFP gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 4 (cytogenetic band 4q13.3), so chromosome 4 contains the gene encoding the screening protein.

318841.long_answer: Glycerate kinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of D-glyceric acid to 2-phosphoglycerate, and this enzyme is encoded by the GLYCTK gene. Pathogenic mutations in GLYCTK abolish or severely reduce glycerate kinase activity, leading to D-glyceric acid accumulation (D-glyceric aciduria) and defining the enzyme deficiency described.

426752.long_answer: Mineralization and fragmentation of elastic fibers in skin, retina, and arterial walls is the hallmark of the inherited disorder pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE). PXE is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ABCC6 gene, which encodes the ATP-binding cassette transporter C6; defective ABCC6 reduces systemic pyrophosphate levels, leading to inappropriate calcification of elastic tissues.

258239.long_answer: Inactivating mutations in the follicle-stimulating hormone receptor (FSHR) gene cause isolated FSH resistance. Only Sertoli cells express FSH receptors, so loss-of-function mutations selectively impair Sertoli-cell activity and spermatogenesis, while Leydig cells, which depend on LH and not FSH, remain unaffected and continue to produce normal testosterone.

696389.long_answer: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type IA (HSAN IA) is caused by mutations in the SPTLC1 gene. SPTLC1 encodes the long-chain-base subunit 1 of serine palmitoyltransferase, the enzyme that forms the catalytic domain responsible for the first, rate-limiting step of sphingolipid biosynthesis. Dysfunction of this sphingolipid-biosynthetic domain underlies the neuropathy seen in HSAN IA.

868206.long_answer: Familial sea-blue histiocytosis is caused by missense variants in the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene. APOE is mapped to 19q13.32 on human chromosome 19, so the gene responsible for this disorder resides on chromosome 19.

770063.long_answer: DOOR (Deafness, Onychodystrophy, Osteodystrophy, and mental Retardation) syndrome is most commonly caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the TBC1D24 gene. TBC1D24 encodes a protein involved in vesicle trafficking and neuronal development; pathogenic variants disrupt these processes, leading to the characteristic constellation of sensorineural deafness, nail and bone dysplasia, and intellectual disability observed in the syndrome.

690798.long_answer: The B-cell marker commonly used in immunohistochemistry to confirm and diagnose gastric (MALT) lymphoma is CD20. CD20 is encoded by the MS4A1 gene, which is situated on the long arm of human chromosome 11 (11q12). Therefore, the relevant gene—and hence the marker—resides on chromosome 11.

554914.long_answer: Missense or other pathogenic variants in the ACADM gene, which encodes medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD), cause MCAD deficiency. This fatty-acid β-oxidation disorder produces episodic hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, vomiting, liver dysfunction and encephalopathy after fasting or viral illness—clinical features that historically led many cases to be mistaken for Reye syndrome.

523325.long_answer: Mutations in the CBS gene, which encodes cystathionine β-synthase, cause classic homocystinuria—a metabolic disorder in the methionine pathway that leads to elevated homocysteine and methionine levels. Patients with CBS deficiency often show a Marfan-like (marfanoid) habitus, including pronounced arachnodactyly. Thus, the same CBS mutation is associated both with arachnodactyly and with a methionine-related metabolic disorder.

225128.long_answer: Bare lymphocyte syndrome type II (also called MHC class II deficiency) results from mutations in trans-acting regulatory genes such as CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP, or RFXANK that are required for transcription of MHC class II genes. Loss of these regulators abolishes MHC class II surface expression on antigen-presenting cells, leading to a severe combined immunodeficiency phenotype.

663095.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the TBX5 gene cause Holt-Oram syndrome, an autosomal-dominant disorder marked by upper-limb anomalies and a high frequency of atrial or ventricular septal defects and other congenital heart malformations. Because these cardiac defects are common and can be clinically significant, individuals with TBX5 mutations typically require evaluation and ongoing care by a cardiologist for congenital heart disease management.

335212.long_answer: The cellular prion protein (PrP), which is the key pathogenic factor in Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease and has also been shown to modulate tau aggregation in several tauopathies, is encoded by the PRNP gene. The PRNP gene is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 20 (20p13).

362773.long_answer: Weissenbacher-Zweymüller syndrome is produced by mutations in the COL11A2 gene situated on chromosome 6p21.3. Because chromosome 6 is one of the numbered (non-sex) chromosomes, the responsible gene resides on an autosomal chromosome, explaining the autosomal (usually recessive) inheritance pattern of the disorder.

476178.long_answer: Radiophobia is a specific anxiety disorder in which a person has an irrational and excessive fear of ionizing radiation (e.g., X-rays, gamma rays, nuclear fallout). Although acute radiation syndrome requires exposure to high doses of radiation, individuals with radiophobia can experience intense psychological distress and somatic symptoms that mimic or are mistaken for radiation illness. Thus, the psychological disorder linked to an irrational fear of ionizing radiation is radiophobia.

471904.long_answer: Mutations in the PANK2 gene (pantothenate kinase 2) cause pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration, historically termed Hallervorden-Spatz or “parkinsonism-hypertonia” syndrome. Affected individuals develop an early-onset parkinsonism-like disorder with pronounced muscle hypertonia (rigidity/dystonia) due to iron accumulation and neurodegeneration in the basal ganglia. Thus, PANK2 mutation is the well-established genetic link to this parkinsonism-hypertonia illness.

809957.long_answer: The GPR98 gene (also known as VLGR1 or ADGRV1) is one of the genes mutated in Usher syndrome type II (specifically the USH2C subtype). GPR98 encodes ‘very large G protein-coupled receptor 1’, a member of the adhesion GPCR family characterized by an extracellular N-terminal domain and a seven-transmembrane region that signals through heterotrimeric G proteins. Thus, among the Usher syndrome type II genes, GPR98 is the one whose product is a G protein-coupled receptor.

869721.long_answer: Hereditary haemochromatosis type 1 is caused by mutations in the HFE gene. The HFE gene is situated in the major histocompatibility complex region at 6p21.3 on human chromosome 6; thus chromosome 6 carries the gene responsible for this disorder.

412207.long_answer: Mutations in the FAM20C gene cause Raine syndrome, a congenital disorder marked by craniofacial anomalies (such as hypoplastic nose, proptosis and mid-face hypoplasia) together with generalized osteosclerosis. FAM20C encodes a secreted kinase essential for proper mineralization of bone; loss-of-function variants lead to the dense, sclerotic bones and characteristic craniofacial defects seen in this birth defect.

164954.long_answer: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL7A1 gene, which encodes the α-1 chain of type VII collagen that forms anchoring fibrils at the dermal–epidermal junction. The COL7A1 gene is mapped to human chromosome 3 (band 3p21.31). Thus, chromosome 3 harbors the gene responsible for this condition, whose chronic skin injury and inflammation can secondarily provoke small-fiber peripheral neuropathy.

777233.long_answer: Human serum albumin is commonly administered as a colloid for fluid resuscitation in patients with septic shock. The ALB gene, which encodes serum albumin, is located on human chromosome 4 (region 4q13). Therefore, chromosome 4 contains the gene encoding the protein used in this clinical setting.

324866.long_answer: Mutations in the ACAT1 gene, encoding mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase (β-ketothiolase), block a key step of ketolysis—cleaving acetoacetyl-CoA to two acetyl-CoA molecules. This enzymatic block prevents tissues from utilizing ketone bodies for energy, producing the autosomal-recessive disorder β-ketothiolase deficiency, the prototypic inborn error of ketone body utilization.

650044.long_answer: Linkage and association studies of developmental (congenital) hip dysplasia have repeatedly implicated the 17q21 region. Genes located on chromosome 17 in this interval (e.g., COL1A1 and HOXB9) carry variants that predispose to acetabular insufficiency and femoral-acetabular incongruity. When severe, the resulting dysplasia can be surgically managed with acetabular reconstruction or shelf procedures that utilise bone grafting, making chromosome 17 the chromosome classically linked with the heritable form of hip dysplasia treated by bone grafting.

509568.long_answer: Rett syndrome, an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder, is almost always caused by pathogenic mutations in the MECP2 gene located on Xq28. Affected individuals—predominantly females—commonly develop complications that include epileptic seizures and progressive scoliosis, linking MECP2 mutation directly to those clinical features.

117030.long_answer: Both fragile X syndrome and Down syndrome are well-established genetic conditions that characteristically include intellectual disability among their core clinical features. Fragile X syndrome, caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, is the most common inherited form of intellectual disability, with affected individuals typically exhibiting mild to severe cognitive impairment. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability; virtually all individuals with full trisomy 21 have some degree of cognitive delay, ranging from mild to moderate, with occasional severe impairment. Thus, the scientific and medical consensus is that both conditions lead to intellectual disability.

965622.long_answer: The precursor protein for high-molecular-weight kininogen is encoded by the KNG1 gene (kininogen 1). Cytogenetic mapping places KNG1 on the long arm of human chromosome 3 (band 3q27), making chromosome 3 the genomic location harboring the gene responsible for the HMW kininogen precursor.

939079.long_answer: Von Willebrand disease results from mutations in the VWF gene, which encodes von Willebrand factor. The VWF gene is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 12 (region 12p13.3). Hence, the causative gene for von Willebrand disease is located on chromosome 12.

367386.long_answer: The sarcoglycan complex in the muscle-cell plasma membrane is part of the larger dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. The transmembrane sarcoglycans bind to the cytoskeletal protein dystrophin, and the gene that encodes dystrophin is DMD, which is located on the short arm of the human X chromosome (Xp21).

165991.long_answer: Mutations in the ELN gene, which encodes elastin, cause autosomal-dominant cutis laxa. In this disorder defective or deficient elastin fibers lead to loose, wrinkled, and markedly inelastic skin because the dermis lacks normal elastic recoil.

148028.long_answer: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) with multiple mitochondrial DNA deletions can be caused by mutations in SLC25A4. This gene encodes adenine nucleotide translocator 1 (ANT1), the inner-mitochondrial-membrane carrier that exchanges ADP and ATP across the membrane. Defects in ANT1 impair mitochondrial energy exchange, leading to the clinical features of CPEO.

900893.long_answer: A leading hypothesis is that many cases of loin pain - hematuria syndrome are due to thinning or other structural defects of the glomerular basement membrane. This fragile filtration barrier within the renal glomerulus allows capillary rupture and red-cell leakage, producing recurrent hematuria and the associated flank (loin) pain.

470922.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the TRPS1 gene cause tricho-rhino-phalangeal syndrome (types I & III), a congenital disorder whose hallmark features include fine, sparse scalp hair that undergoes progressive thinning beginning in childhood. Thus, mutation of TRPS1 is the genetic defect associated with this syndrome of childhood‐onset hair loss.

370827.long_answer: Pathogenic mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes type II collagen, cause spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita. This skeletal dysplasia primarily involves malformed vertebral bodies and epiphyseal cartilage, leading to a short-trunk form of dwarfism. Because type II collagen is essential for normal cartilage and spinal development, COL2A1 defects disrupt vertebral growth plates and result in disproportionate short stature.

306851.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ANOS1 gene (formerly KAL1) cause X-linked Kallmann syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by defective migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons and the olfactory bulbs, leading to congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia. Thus, an ANOS1 mutation is a well-established genetic cause of a syndrome that produces hypogonadism.

309305.long_answer: Mutations in the SLC25A15 gene, encoding the mitochondrial ornithine transporter ORNT1, cause hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria (HHH) syndrome. In the neonatal period this disorder can present with isolated hyperornithinemia and low citrulline, findings that closely resemble those of ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) deficiency, thus mimicking that condition before hyperammonemia and homocitrullinuria become apparent.

494126.long_answer: Very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (VLCAD) deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the ACADVL gene, which encodes the mitochondrial enzyme needed for β-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids in muscle and other tissues. The ACADVL gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 17 (17p13).

851567.long_answer: During oogenesis, a nondisjunction error can leave the egg with two copies of the same chromosome. If, after fertilisation, the extra paternal copy is lost (trisomy-rescue), the child inherits both homologues from the mother and none from the father—an event called uniparental disomy (UPD). When the two maternal chromosomes are identical (isodisomy), any recessive pathogenic variant carried by the mother is present in two copies, unmasking rare autosomal-recessive disorders.

839966.long_answer: Genetic disorders such as Norrie disease and familial exudative vitreoretinopathy impair retinal blood-vessel development because of mutations in NDP (Norrin), FZD4, LRP5 or TSPAN12. These components form a ligand–receptor complex that activates the canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling cascade, which is essential for endothelial proliferation, tip-cell formation and vascular stabilization in the retina. Disruption of this Wnt/β-catenin pathway therefore underlies the defective retinal angiogenesis seen in these disorders.

526638.long_answer: Mutations in the CYP21A2 gene impair the 21-hydroxylase enzyme, the commonest cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. The enzymatic block prevents normal cortisol synthesis, diverting steroid precursors toward androgen production and causing markedly elevated serum androstenedione (and 17-hydroxyprogesterone). Thus, abnormal androstenedione levels are a direct biochemical signature of CYP21A2-related 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

100601.long_answer: Mitral valve prolapse can create myocardial and valvular stretch that predisposes to malignant ventricular arrhythmias—especially ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. These rapid, disorganized rhythms can abruptly halt effective cardiac output, making them a recognized mechanism for sudden cardiac death in patients with mitral valve prolapse.

527030.long_answer: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase causes Hurler syndrome (Mucopolysaccharidosis type I). In this disorder undegraded dermatan and heparan sulfates accumulate in many tissues, including the middle and inner ear. The progressive glycosaminoglycan storage leads to recurrent otitis media, conductive and sensorineural impairment, and can culminate in clinically significant deafness, making α-L-iduronidase deficiency a lysosomal storage disease that can lead to hearing loss.

673293.long_answer: D-bifunctional protein deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the HSD17B4 gene, which is located on the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q23.1).

403198.long_answer: Bart–Pumphrey syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder characterized by leukonychia, palmoplantar keratoderma, knuckle pads, and sensorineural deafness. Multiple families with this genodermatosis carry missense mutations (e.g., p.Asp50Asn) in the GJB2 gene, which encodes connexin-26, a gap-junction protein essential for epidermal and cochlear cell communication. These pathogenic GJB2 variants establish the gene’s causal role in Bart–Pumphrey syndrome.

870932.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the NF2 gene (which encodes the tumor-suppressor protein merlin) causes neurofibromatosis type 2.  This disorder leads to the formation of benign schwannomas—especially vestibular (acoustic) schwannomas—but the expanding tumors can compress cranial and peripheral nerves, resulting in hearing loss, balance problems and other nerve damage despite their histologically benign nature.

230620.long_answer: Best vitelliform macular dystrophy is most often produced by autosomal-dominant mutations in the BEST1 (VMD2) gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 11 at 11q12.3. Thus, chromosome 11 carries the gene responsible for BVMD.

982806.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the NF1 gene, which encodes the tumor-suppressor protein neurofibromin, causes Neurofibromatosis type 1. This neuro-cutaneous disorder presents with characteristic skin findings (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas) and is well documented to predispose affected individuals to cognitive deficits, learning disabilities, ADHD, autism-spectrum features, and other mental health problems. Thus, an NF1 gene mutation links the skin condition to both cognitive and psychiatric complications.

461426.long_answer: The association of anonychia-onychodystrophy with brachydactyly type B and ectrodactyly was first reported by Temtamy and co-workers in an Egyptian family. Their publication constituted the initial description of this distinct congenital limb-nail disorder, making Egypt the country of first description.

838588.long_answer: The two terms come from different fields—medicine and art—but both derive from the Greek roots “neo-” (new) and “plásis/plástos” (formation, molding). In medicine, a neoplasm is a new, abnormal growth of tissue (a tumor). In art theory, Neoplasticism (De Stijl) refers to creating a ‘new plastic’ visual language of abstract form and color. Apart from this common linguistic origin meaning ‘new formation,’ the concepts are unrelated.

309613.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ANTXR2 gene (also called CMG2, Capillary-Morphogenesis-Gene-2) cause hyaline fibromatosis syndrome, which encompasses juvenile hyaline fibromatosis and infantile systemic hyalinosis. This disorder is characterized by marked gingival overgrowth (gingival fibromatosis) and progressive, often painful joint stiffness and contractures due to hyaline material deposition around connective tissues. Hence, ANTXR2 mutation underlies the condition linking both clinical features.

160116.long_answer: The Sonic hedgehog (SHH) gene, whose product Shh is crucial for limb patterning and defects such as radial hypoplasia and abnormal thumb development, is located at cytogenetic band 7q36 on human chromosome 7.

667933.long_answer: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type II (LAD-II) is diagnosed by demonstrating loss of the fucosylated epitope sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes. Expression of this epitope depends on the GDP-fucose transporter protein encoded by the SLC35C1 gene. SLC35C1 is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 11 (11p11.2). Thus, the gene encoding the diagnostic protein for LAD-II resides on chromosome 11.

489247.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the FREM1 gene (FRAS1 related extracellular matrix protein 1) cause the autosomal-recessive disorder known as bifid nose, anorectal and renal anomalies (BNAR) syndrome. Patients with pathogenic variants in FREM1 typically present with a bifid or broad nasal tip together with malformations of the anorectal region and congenital renal abnormalities, establishing FREM1 as the gene responsible for this triad of defects.

990524.long_answer: I-cell (inclusion-cell) disease results from a deficiency of the Golgi-resident enzyme N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase, which normally adds the mannose-6-phosphate tag that directs hydrolases to lysosomes. The defect in this Golgi apparatus enzyme prevents proper targeting of lysosomal enzymes, leading to their extracellular secretion and the characteristic storage pathology of I-cell disease.

274298.long_answer: Li–Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germ-line mutations in the TP53 tumor-suppressor gene. TP53 is located at cytogenetic band 17p13.1 on human chromosome 17; hence this chromosome harbors the gene whose alteration confers the cancer-predisposition characteristic of the syndrome.

998654.long_answer: Most hypodysfibrinogenemia mutations are C→T transitions that arise at methyl-CpG ‘hot-spots’ in the fibrinogen genes; the original nucleotide that undergoes the pathogenic change is cytosine.

346355.long_answer: David Mitchell’s novel “Cloud Atlas” was adapted into the 2012 film of the same name, in which the same actors portray multiple, heavily-made-up characters across six different time periods. Because prosopagnosia impairs facial recognition, a viewer with the condition would have great difficulty following which character is which, making the film challenging to track.

340880.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the homeobox gene HLXB9, also known as MNX1, cause the Currarino/caudal regression sequence—partial or complete sacral agenesis with anorectal malformation and a presacral mass. Sacral/caudal regression can also arise sporadically after a vascular accident in utero that disrupts blood flow to the caudal mesoderm. Thus, HLXB9 mutation is the well-established genetic lesion linked to this congenital malformation that may alternatively be produced by an intra-uterine vascular insult.

810436.long_answer: Mutations in the HSD3B2 gene, which encodes the type II 3-β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase enzyme, cause the 3-β-HSD–deficiency form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Because this defect impairs the synthesis of all downstream steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, and androgens), both 46,XX and 46,XY fetuses can develop abnormal external genitalia—virilization of females and undervirilization of males—resulting in ambiguous genitalia in either genetic sex.

460489.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the PTF1A gene (Pancreas Transcription Factor 1 Subunit α) abolish normal cerebellar development, resulting in near-total or complete cerebellar agenesis. Affected infants present with profound developmental disability because the cerebellum fails to form; the same mutation typically also causes pancreatic agenesis. Thus, PTF1A mutation is a well-documented genetic cause of developmental disability characterized by absence of the cerebellum.

700505.long_answer: Anorexia nervosa and body dysmorphic disorder are separate DSM-5 diagnoses, but they share core psychopathology—severe body-image distortion and obsessive appearance concerns—and therefore commonly co-occur in the same patient population.

667771.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes type II collagen, cause spondylo-epiphyseal dysplasia congenita. This disorder disrupts vertebral and epiphyseal cartilage formation, leading to abnormal spine development and pronounced short-trunk dwarfism.

956505.long_answer: The NF2 gene, whose loss leads to multiple nervous system tumors such as vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas, is located on the long arm of chromosome 22 (region 22q12).

861391.long_answer: Sickle cell disease results from mutations in the β-globin gene (HBB). The HBB gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 11 (11p15.5). Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is an established curative therapy for this genetic hemoglobinopathy, so the disease-causing gene’s chromosomal location is chromosome 11.

872688.long_answer: Pseudoachondroplasia is caused by pathogenic variants in the COMP gene (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein). The human COMP gene is mapped to chromosome 19 at band 19p13.2-p13.1; therefore, chromosome 19 carries the gene responsible for this skeletal dysplasia.

179689.long_answer: May-Hegglin anomaly is caused by autosomal-dominant mutations in the MYH9 gene, which encodes non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA. The MYH9 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 22 (22q13), making chromosome 22 the chromosomal site responsible for this disorder.

314871.long_answer: Increased copy number of the BHLHA9 gene (duplication or triplication at 17p13.3) causes Split-Hand/Foot Malformation with Long-Bone Deficiency type 3 (SHFLD3). This dosage-sensitive syndrome presents with limb reduction defects that frequently include oligodactyly, along with split hand/foot malformations and tibial deficiency. Thus, duplication or triplication of BHLHA9 is the established genetic cause of the syndrome featuring oligodactyly.

133956.long_answer: Deficiency of Protein C, a vitamin K-dependent serine protease that inactivates coagulation factors Va and VIIIa, removes an important natural anticoagulant pathway. The resulting widespread microvascular thrombosis produces purpura fulminans—a rapidly spreading hemorrhagic skin necrosis that frequently progresses to tissue ischemia and gangrene.

347749.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the PCNT gene, which encodes the centrosomal protein pericentrin, cause microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPD II). A hallmark of this disorder is severe, progressively worsening microcephaly that begins prenatally and advances postnatally, reflecting impaired centrosome function and disrupted cell-cycle progression during brain growth.

200432.long_answer: Etiocholanolone, a 5β-reduced metabolite of testosterone, has been shown to bind and trigger the pyrin inflammasome in human monocytes. Its ability to induce IL-1β-dependent fever and neutrophilic inflammation produces an autoinflammatory picture that closely mimics familial Mediterranean fever attacks.

128648.long_answer: Subcortical band heterotopia (double-cortex syndrome) is most commonly produced by mutations in the DCX (doublecortin) gene, which is located on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq22–q23). Hence, the pathogenic mutation responsible for band heterotopia lies on the X chromosome.

104204.long_answer: Hennekam lymphangiectasia-lymphedema syndrome is caused by mutations in genes such as CCBE1, ADAMTS3 and FAT4 that regulate activation or signaling of vascular endothelial growth factor-C (VEGF-C). Impaired VEGF-C interaction with its receptor VEGFR-3 disrupts the VEGF-C/VEGFR-3 signaling pathway, leading to defective lymphangiogenesis and the lymphedema–lymphangiectasia phenotype characteristic of the syndrome.

822502.long_answer: The principal gene first linked to autosomal-recessive primary microcephaly is MCPH1 (microcephalin), which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 8 (region 8p23).

409488.long_answer: The enzyme that esterifies free cholesterol on high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles is lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). The human LCAT gene that encodes this enzyme is located on the long arm of chromosome 16 (region 16q22.1). Thus, chromosome 16 carries the gene responsible for HDL cholesterol esterification.

602867.long_answer: The tumor-suppressor gene TP53, whose germline mutations cause Li–Fraumeni syndrome, is located on the short arm of human chromosome 17 (band 17p13.1).

946489.long_answer: Erythropoietic protoporphyria results from loss-of-function mutations in the ferrochelatase (FECH) gene, the final enzyme of the heme-biosynthetic pathway whose transcription is modulated by steroid (sex-hormone) signals. The human FECH gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 18 (18q21), and pathogenic variants on this chromosome lead to the accumulation of protoporphyrin and the characteristic photosensitivity of the disease.

814039.long_answer: Fanconi anaemia, a hereditary disease characterized by progressive bone marrow failure, is most commonly linked to mutations in the FANCA gene. The FANCA gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 16 (16q24.3); hence chromosome 16 carries the gene associated with this bone-marrow-failure disorder.

393046.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in SMOC1 (SPARC-related modular calcium-binding protein 1) are a proven cause of an autosomal-recessive developmental disorder characterised by severe eye malformations (anophthalmia/microphthalmia) together with limb anomalies (syndactyly, brachydactyly). The original gene-discovery reports (e.g., Rainger et al., Nature Genetics 2011; Sousa et al., American Journal of Human Genetics 2011) described several consanguineous families from Turkey in whom homozygous SMOC1 truncating or splice-site variants segregated perfectly with the disorder. Subsequent studies have confirmed this association in additional Turkish and non-Turkish pedigrees. Thus, according to current biomedical consensus, SMOC1 is indeed associated with a developmental disorder that was first identified in (and remains prevalent among) Turkish families.

544451.long_answer: Familial studies have mapped the susceptibility locus for benign childhood epilepsy with centro-temporal (Rolandic) spikes to the 15q14 region of chromosome 15, implicating genes such as ELP4 located there. Thus, chromosome 15 is the chromosome linked to the genetic form of Rolandic epilepsy.

295358.long_answer: Morquio A syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA) is produced by pathogenic mutations in the GALNS gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase. Loss of functional GALNS impairs degradation of keratan sulfate and chondroitin-6-sulfate, leading to lysosomal storage and the characteristic skeletal abnormalities of the disorder.

923769.long_answer: The IL17F gene, located on chromosome 6p12, encodes the cytokine interleukin-17F. Loss-of-function mutations in IL17F cause autosomal dominant chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMCD type 4), an immunodeficiency syndrome marked by recurrent infections of skin, nails and mucous membranes—i.e., infections of the integumentary system.

171921.long_answer: Human adenoviruses are double-stranded DNA viruses whose primary transcripts are extensively and alternatively spliced in the host nucleus. A single adenoviral transcription unit can be processed into many distinct mRNAs (early and late transcripts), each encoding different viral proteins. The original discovery of RNA splicing was made in adenovirus-infected human cells, highlighting this virus as the classic example of alternative splicing generating multiple mRNAs from one genomic region.

142393.long_answer: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (Ritter disease) is a toxin-mediated infection by Staphylococcus aureus that primarily affects infants and young children. The exotoxins disrupt epidermal adhesion, producing a widespread exfoliative dermatitis; systemic signs such as irritability and high fever commonly accompany the skin lesions. Consequently, this bacterial infection is a well-recognized childhood form of dermatitis that can present with fever.

360753.long_answer: Atypical lipomatous tumors/well-differentiated liposarcomas consistently show high-level amplification of the 12q13-15 region, most notably involving the oncogenes MDM2 (an inhibitor of p53) and CDK4 (a G1-phase cyclin-dependent kinase). Detection of MDM2 and CDK4 amplification is a diagnostic hallmark that differentiates these tumors from benign lipomas.

379341.long_answer: Sebaceous nevi are congenital hamartomas of the skin that can later develop secondary tumors such as basal cell carcinoma or syringocystadenoma papilliferum. Diagnosis, surveillance, and treatment (e.g., dermatoscopic monitoring, surgical excision, or laser therapy) fall within the expertise of a dermatologist, the medical specialist trained to manage skin lesions and their potential complications.

443346.long_answer: Modern classifications divide histiocytic disorders into three broad groups: (1) Langerhans cell histiocytosis, (2) hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis/macrophage activation syndrome, and (3) malignant histiocytosis (including histiocytic sarcoma). Therefore, the type of histiocytosis that is not placed in either the HLH or LCH categories is malignant histiocytosis.

102188.long_answer: Genes implicated in age-related macular degeneration (e.g., CFH, ARMS2/HTRA1, C3) are turned on or off by transcription factors—DNA-binding regulatory proteins that control the initiation and rate of gene transcription. These proteins recognize specific promoter or enhancer sequences and recruit the transcriptional machinery, thereby governing the expression levels of AMD-associated genes.

627200.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome, the classic craniofacial dysostosis that involves premature fusion of skull sutures, is caused by pathogenic variants in the FGFR2 (and occasionally FGFR3) gene. These mutations are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, meaning a single mutated allele from an affected parent is sufficient to produce the disorder and it shows vertical inheritance through successive generations.

736382.long_answer: Hemophilia A is caused by pathogenic variants in the F8 gene, which encodes coagulation Factor VIII. The F8 gene is located on the long arm of the X chromosome at band Xq28, not on chromosome 22. Because hemophilia A is X-linked, the disorder is far more common in males and transmitted through carrier females—further evidence that the responsible gene resides on the X chromosome rather than an autosome such as chromosome 22.

914044.long_answer: Inherited Factor VII deficiency is caused by mutations in the F7 gene, which encodes coagulation Factor VII. The F7 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 13 at position 13q34; therefore, chromosome 13 carries the gene responsible for this hematologic disorder.

515682.long_answer: The REEP1 (Receptor Expression-Enhancing Protein 1) gene responsible for the autosomal-dominant form of hereditary spastic paraplegia SPG31 is located on human chromosome 2, specifically at band 2p11.2.

236988.long_answer: Costello syndrome is produced by heterozygous activating mutations in the HRAS proto-oncogene, most often the p.Gly12Ser substitution. These mutations impair the intrinsic GTPase activity of HRAS, leaving the protein locked in its GTP-bound conformation and therefore permanently active, which disrupts normal cell‐signalling pathways and leads to the characteristic features of the syndrome.

779505.long_answer: Female infertility seen in the systemic form of Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the SCNN1B gene, which encodes the β-subunit of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). SCNN1B is located at cytogenetic band 16p12 on human chromosome 16; consequently, chromosome 16 is the chromosomal location responsible for this infertility phenotype in PHA-1.

381924.long_answer: Pathogenic mutations causing schwannomatosis are most commonly found in the SMARCB1 (INI1) and LZTR1 genes, both of which are located on the long arm of human chromosome 22 (22q). Thus, chromosome 22 harbors the gene(s) whose alteration leads to the development of schwannomatosis.

737355.long_answer: In his work ‘Characters’ (4th century BC) the Greek philosopher and natural historian Theophrastus portrays “The Superstitious Man,” who repeatedly washes, sprinkles himself with water three times, avoids stepping on sacred spots, and performs elaborate checking and ritualistic behaviours to quell intrusive fears. These repeated, anxiety-driven cleansing and checking rituals strongly resemble the obsessions and compulsions that today define obsessive-compulsive disorder, making Theophrastus the earliest known author to describe such symptoms.

286540.long_answer: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic disorder caused by quantitative or qualitative deficiency of type I collagen. A key clinical distinction from rickets is that patients with osteogenesis imperfecta typically have normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels, whereas rickets presents with low calcium and/or phosphate due to impaired mineralization. Thus, deficiency of type I collagen underlies the genetic disorder not characterized by the low mineral levels seen in rickets.

379723.long_answer: Germ-line mutations in the MEN1 gene (encoding menin) cause Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1.  Besides endocrine tumours, MEN1 patients frequently develop numerous subcutaneous lipomas and have a documented excess of central-nervous-system tumours, especially astrocytomas and other gliomas.  Thus, a MEN1 mutation links the clinical combination of multiple lipomas with an increased risk of glioma formation.

187556.long_answer: Mutations in the human PAX6 gene, which encodes a paired-box/homeobox transcription factor essential for ocular development, can lead to microphthalmia. PAX6 is the direct human ortholog of the mouse Small-eye (Sey) gene; the two genes are homologous and perform the same key developmental roles, explaining why defects in either species produce similar small-eye phenotypes.

442699.long_answer: The anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), which causes regression of the Müllerian ducts during male embryonic development, is encoded by the AMH gene. In humans, the AMH gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 19 (region 19p13.3). Thus, chromosome 19 carries the gene responsible for producing the hormone that inhibits Müllerian duct formation in males.

673261.long_answer: Alpha-mannosidosis is caused by mutations in the MAN2B1 gene, which encodes lysosomal α-mannosidase. Cytogenetic and linkage studies have mapped MAN2B1 to human chromosome 19 (region 19p13/q13). Thus, chromosome 19 carries the gene responsible for alpha-mannosidosis.

204291.long_answer: The most common soft-tissue sarcoma in children is rhabdomyosarcoma. The hallmark alveolar subtype features the t(2;13)(q35;q14) translocation that fuses the PAX3 gene on chromosome 2 with the FOXO1 (FKHR) gene on chromosome 13. Because the critical PAX3 transcription-factor gene resides at 2q35, chromosome 2 is classically cited as the chromosomal location of the gene associated with paediatric rhabdomyosarcoma.

267570.long_answer: Familial multiple intestinal atresia is linked to pathogenic mutations in the TTC7A gene. TTC7A is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 2 (region 2p16), making chromosome 2 the chromosomal location of the gene associated with this hereditary disorder.

726797.long_answer: Ostravik-Lindemann-Solberg syndrome is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the TBX15 gene. TBX15 lies on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (cytogenetic band 1p13), so the responsible gene for this syndrome is located on chromosome 1.

320774.long_answer: Sturge-Weber syndrome, a neurocutaneous disorder characterized by facial capillary malformations, leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and early-onset glaucoma, is caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene (classically the p.R183Q variant). Thus, a GNAQ mutation is the genetic alteration associated with a condition that can present with both glaucoma and seizures.

333661.long_answer: The enzyme that converts testosterone to 5α-dihydrotestosterone in the prostate is 5α-reductase type 2, encoded by the SRD5A2 gene. SRD5A2 is located on human chromosome 2; thus chromosome 2 carries the gene responsible for this key androgen-activating step.

268927.long_answer: Tetra-amelia syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the WNT3 gene. The human WNT3 gene is situated at cytogenetic band 17q21 on chromosome 17, so the gene responsible for tetra-amelia syndrome resides on chromosome 17.

670392.long_answer: Condylomata lata are broad-based, smooth, moist, flat-topped lesions that arise in secondary syphilis due to Treponema pallidum, whereas condylomata acuminata are dry, verrucous, cauliflower-like genital warts caused by infection with human papillomavirus (most often HPV types 6 and 11). Thus they differ in etiology (T. pallidum vs. HPV) and in clinical morphology (flat-moist vs. papillomatous-verrucous).

955316.long_answer: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is an extremely rare disorder frequently misdiagnosed because of its rarity and atypical presentation. Virtually all classic cases are caused by a recurrent activating missense mutation (p.R206H) in the ACVR1 gene (also called ALK2), which encodes a bone morphogenetic protein type-I receptor. This mutation drives inappropriate ossification of soft tissues, explaining the disease’s hallmark progressive heterotopic bone formation.

392193.long_answer: The genetic form of the limb-reduction defect mimicking thalidomide embryopathy (phocomelia/Roberts or SC phocomelia syndrome) is produced by pathogenic variants in the ESCO2 gene, which is situated on chromosome 8 (8p21). Hence chromosome 8 is linked to the hereditary counterpart of the condition caused by thalidomide.

450311.long_answer: Hereditary pancreatitis is most commonly caused by gain-of-function mutations in the PRSS1 gene, which encodes cationic trypsinogen. PRSS1 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 7 (region 7q35), so chromosome 7 carries the gene responsible for this inherited form of pancreatitis.

672437.long_answer: Blue cone monochromacy is an X-linked disorder produced by deletions or rearrangements in the red (OPN1LW) and green (OPN1MW) cone opsin gene cluster. This tandem array resides on the long arm of the X chromosome at Xq28, so the gene cluster responsible for the disease is located on the X chromosome.

335137.long_answer: Ornithine translocase deficiency (hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome) results from pathogenic mutations in the SLC25A15 gene (also called ORNT1), which encodes the mitochondrial ornithine transporter. Loss of functional SLC25A15 impairs ornithine entry into mitochondria, disrupting the urea cycle and causing accumulation of ammonia, hence the hyperammonemia characteristic of the disorder.

698229.long_answer: The classic form of ocular albinism (OA1) is caused by mutations in the GPR143 (OA1) gene, which is located at Xp22 on the X chromosome. Because the critical ocular-albinism genes reside on this sex chromosome, the disorder shows X-linked inheritance.

560343.long_answer: CAPOS syndrome results from missense mutations in the ATP1A3 gene, which encodes the α3-subunit of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. The human ATP1A3 locus is situated on chromosome 19q13.31; consequently, chromosome 19 harbors the gene responsible for CAPOS syndrome.

164506.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked SRPX2 gene cause bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria. This malformation produces pseudobulbar palsy with severe oral motor and speech apraxia; affected individuals are often non-verbal and therefore depend on augmentative and alternative communication systems. Thus, SRPX2 is the gene linked to the polymicrogyria form requiring AAC due to profound speech impairment.

249253.long_answer: Both Denys–Drash syndrome and WAGR syndrome involve pathogenic alterations in the WT1 gene, which is located at band 11p13 on chromosome 11; therefore, chromosome 11 is the common chromosomal locus associated with these two syndromes.

923298.long_answer: The photosensitive ectodermal disorder trichothiodystrophy (IBIDS/PIBIDS) presents with ichthyotic skin, brittle sulfur-deficient hair, short stature and various skeletal abnormalities. It is caused by loss-of-function mutations in ERCC2, which encodes the XPD DNA helicase subunit of the TFIIH complex that functions in nucleotide-excision DNA repair. Thus, deficiency of the XPD DNA helicase enzyme underlies this skin-hair–skeletal syndrome.

285625.long_answer: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) is caused by an expanded CCTG repeat in the CNBP (formerly ZNF9) gene. This gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 3 (region 3q21.3), so chromosome 3 is the chromosome that contains the DM2-causing gene.

736203.long_answer: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), also known as human herpesvirus-4, infects B-lymphocytes and is etiologically linked to several lymphoid malignancies, notably Hodgkin lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders. Its latent infection in lymphoid cells and expression of viral oncogenes (e.g., LMP1, EBNA proteins) drive cellular proliferation and survival, establishing EBV as the canonical virus associated with Hodgkin lymphoma and related lymphoid diseases.

707418.long_answer: Camurati–Engelmann disease (progressive diaphyseal dysplasia) is caused by pathogenic variants in the TGFB1 gene. TGFB1 is mapped to cytogenetic band 19q13.2 on human chromosome 19, so this chromosome carries the disease-causing gene responsible for the skull-thickening phenotype.

546955.long_answer: Mutations in the UBR1 gene give rise to Johanson–Blizzard syndrome, which characteristically includes scalp defects of aplasia cutis congenita. The UBR1 gene is situated at cytogenetic band 15q15 on human chromosome 15, so the shared disease-linked gene resides on chromosome 15.

884285.long_answer: I-cell disease arises from a deficiency of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, the Golgi enzyme that adds mannose-6-phosphate tags to lysosomal hydrolases. Without this phosphorylation, the enzymes are secreted extracellularly instead of being targeted to lysosomes, leading to intracellular accumulation of undigested material and the characteristic lysosomal storage pathology.

984557.long_answer: Familial infantile myofibromatosis is most often caused by heterozygous activating variants in the PDGFRB gene. PDGFRB is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q32-q33.1), so the gene associated with this familial tumor disorder resides on chromosome 5.

424207.long_answer: Women’s wrists have a smaller cross-sectional area and a relatively narrower carpal tunnel than men’s. This reduced anatomical space means that the same amount of tendon swelling or repetitive friction produces higher intra-tunnel pressure, greater tendon–sheath irritation and earlier median-nerve compression. These biomechanical and anatomical differences, amplified at times by estrogen-related fluid retention, make women more susceptible to repetitive strain injuries such as tendinitis and carpal tunnel syndrome.

388586.long_answer: The human AOX1 gene, which encodes the molybdenum-containing enzyme aldehyde oxidase 1, is located on chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q23–q24). Aldehyde oxidase 1 catalyzes the oxidation of diverse xenobiotic compounds and participates in the catabolic degradation of folate derivatives, linking it to both xenobiotic metabolism and folate catabolism pathways. Therefore, the gene resides on human chromosome 2.

117173.long_answer: The congenital neurocutaneous disorder characterized by facial port-wine stains and early-onset seizures is Sturge-Weber syndrome. This condition is produced by a post-zygotic, somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene (most commonly the p.R183Q variant), which alters Gαq signaling and drives the vascular malformations seen in the skin and leptomeninges.

376729.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive mutations in the PAH gene, which encodes phenylalanine hydroxylase, cause phenylketonuria. Loss of this enzyme blocks conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, leading to toxic accumulation of phenylalanine and its metabolites. The resulting metabolic disorder damages the developing brain and commonly presents with intellectual disability and convulsions if dietary phenylalanine is not restricted.

362276.long_answer: The gene encoding the enzyme aspartoacylase is ASPA, which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 17 (region 17p13); mutations in ASPA on chromosome 17 cause Canavan disease.

992329.long_answer: The inborn error of GABA degradation most often refers to succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency. SSADH is encoded by the ALDH5A1 gene, which is located at cytogenetic band 6p22 on human chromosome 6. Mutations in ALDH5A1 abolish SSADH activity, blocking conversion of succinic semialdehyde to succinate and thus causing the characteristic enzyme deficiency in the GABA degradation pathway.

626687.long_answer: The gene encoding endothelin-converting enzyme-1 (ECE1)—the metalloprotease that cleaves pro-endothelin-1, ‑2 and ‑3 into their active forms—is located on human chromosome 1 (band 1p36). Mutations in ECE1 disrupt endothelin signaling and have been implicated in Hirschsprung’s disease.

942918.long_answer: Legius syndrome, frequently mistaken for neurofibromatosis type I because of multiple café-au-lait macules, is caused by pathogenic mutations in the SPRED1 gene. Genetic testing for SPRED1 confirms the diagnosis, but patients are sometimes incorrectly assigned the NF1 diagnostic code.

770105.long_answer: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (NAIT) is an immune‐mediated disorder in which maternal antibodies directed against fetal platelet antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal platelets. It is one of the most frequent causes of severe thrombocytopenia in otherwise healthy term newborns and is well recognized for predisposing affected neonates to life-threatening bleeding, particularly intracranial hemorrhage.

665422.long_answer: The natural reservoir for Machupo virus, the etiologic agent of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, is the large vesper mouse, scientifically named Calomys callosus. This cricetid rodent maintains the virus in endemic regions of Bolivia and transmits it to humans, typically through contact with its urine, feces, or aerosolized excreta.

413049.long_answer: The PLAT gene, situated at 8p11.21 on human chromosome 8, encodes tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), a serine protease that converts plasminogen to plasmin and thereby participates in the coagulation/fibrinolytic pathway. Trisomy of chromosome 8 is known as Warkany syndrome 2, linking this chromosome to the syndrome. Hence, the gene for the coagulation-related protein resides on chromosome 8.

490583.long_answer: Heterozygous inactivating mutations in the GNAS gene, which encodes the stimulatory G-protein α-subunit (Gsα), cause progressive osseous heteroplasia—a disorder marked by cutaneous and subcutaneous heterotopic ossification that can extend into deeper tissues. Thus, GNAS is the gene classically associated with disease featuring cutaneous or subcutaneous ossification.

614996.long_answer: Mutations in the GJA1 gene (encoding connexin-43) cause oculodentodigital dysplasia. This autosomal-dominant syndrome characteristically presents with digital anomalies such as syndactyly and dental abnormalities including microdontia, linking the GJA1 mutation to both features.

649907.long_answer: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease) is caused by pathogenic variants in the BTK gene located on the X chromosome. Because only one functional copy of BTK is needed, females with one mutant allele are typically asymptomatic carriers, while hemizygous males manifest the disease. This pattern—affected males, carrier females, and no male-to-male transmission—is characteristic of X-linked recessive inheritance.

857294.long_answer: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase B (also called N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase) causes mucopolysaccharidosis type VI (Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome). Arylsulfatase B is required for the stepwise degradation of the glycosaminoglycans dermatan sulfate and, critically, chondroitin 4-sulfate. Loss of this enzyme blocks chondroitin sulfate breakdown, leading to its accumulation and the characteristic clinical manifestations of this form of mucopolysaccharidosis.

999507.long_answer: Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis is caused by recessive mutations in the ANTXR2 (also called CMG2) gene, which is located at cytogenetic band 4q21 on human chromosome 4.

736017.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TWIST1 gene, located on chromosome 7p21, cause Saethre-Chotzen syndrome. This autosomal-dominant craniosynostosis syndrome is well recognised to account for roughly 8 % of all craniosynostosis cases.

562113.long_answer: Spinal muscular atrophy is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the Survival Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene, which is located at cytogenetic band 5q13 on human chromosome 5.
